Eight cipher leaves from the papal nuncio in Lisbon. George Lasry’s key and letter-by-letter decryption were on DECODE; here the text was divided into Italian words and 25 code groups fixed from three leaves deciphered at the time. The first leaf is the nuncio’s secret account of the attempt on King José I in September 1758. 43 2759 17 84 34 84 59 55 19 · 6 · 80 80 08 03 2300 43 2899 il Re si è levato [null] ma mai nel tutto il giorno a = 04 38 55 · e = 84 · il = 43 91 · 6 null · 2759 Re · 2778 Regina Lisbon → Rome · homophonic cipher of two-digit figures with a four-digit nomenclator · September 1758 – 1760 Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60 Go to the full text ↓ Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Portogallo 117, items 1–8 · DECODE R25, R195–R201, eight cipher leaves, ten pages · catalogued as partially decrypted (catalogue item 240) George Lasry recovered the key in 2020 and posted a letter-by-letter decryption with the code groups left as numbers. Here that decryption was divided into Italian words and its code groups were fixed from the three leaves deciphered at the time. The Secretariat of State’s clear decipherments of the other five, filed on DECODE as images, were transcribed and aligned with the figures; all eight letters now give Italian sentences. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letters Letters of Filippo Acciaiuoli, nuncio in Lisbon, and of the abbé Testa, 1757–61; eight cipher leaves. Where Portogallo 117. DECODE has the eight leaves, transcribed digit by digit in 2016–17, and kept them “partially decrypted”. The cipher Two-digit homophones, the digit 6 a null, and four-digit code words that all begin with 2. How it was read Lasry’s 2020 key and code-group decryption gave no Italian. Three leaves (10, 24, 31 October 1758) carry the Secretariat’s clear decipherment; lined up with the cipher it fixes 25 code words, and the other five leaves then read as running Italian. What it says On 12 September 1758 the nuncio reported that the king, coming back by night from a lady, had been fired on in his calesse and wounded in the right arm. Later letters follow the wound, the Jesuits and the 1760 marriage of the Princess of Brazil. Still open About eighty code groups that occur only once or twice, and a few passages in the two long leaves where the transcription has slipped. Credit George Lasry reconstructed the key in 2020. Portogallo 117/6 (f. 106r), 24 October 1758: the decipherment made in Rome, “Benche si dica il Rè assai meglio…”, written above the figures. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Portogallo 117/6 f. 106r, via DECODE R199.

The volume is “Lettere di mons. Acciaiuoli, nunzio in Portugallo, e dell’abbate Testa, 1757–1761”, ff. 2–585. DECODE dates all eight records 18 January 1757, which is the first date in the volume. The cipher leaves themselves run from 12 September 1758 to 1760: Item DECODE Folio Date Digits Clear on the leaf 117/1 R25 95r–v 12 Sept 1758 1918 no 117/2 R195 98r 19 Sept 1758 860 no 117/3 R196 101r 26 Sept [1758] 492 no 117/4 R197 103r 10 Oct [1758] 190 decipherment 117/5 R198 104r 31 Oct [1758] 577 decipherment 117/6 R199 106r 24 Oct [1758] 791 decipherment 117/7 R200 115r–v 28 Nov 1758 1999 no 117/8 R201 280r Lisbon, 12 Feb 1760 1499 no “Clear on the leaf” means the decipherment written above the figures. The Secretariat’s separate clear decipherments of R25 (ff. 90r–91r), R195 (f. 94r), R196 (f. 97r), R200 (ff. 108r–109r, second copy ff. 110r–111r) and R201 (f. 161, second text f. 162) are among the DECODE attachments of the records, with working drafts; they also give the dates of R195, R200 and R201. The key is Lasry’s reconstruction (DECODE, 24 October 2020). Letters and common syllables have fixed two-digit homophones: a 04 38 55, e 84, i 08 53, o 81, s 88, il 43 91, che 39, non 14, de 71 78, qu 70 87 90. The digit 6 is a null, scattered freely, and the code words are four digits beginning with 2. No two-digit element begins with 2 or contains a 6, so the figures cut up only one way.

The decipherments on 117/4–6 give them word for word: Code Reading Code Reading 2759, 2774 Re 2777 Re (of Spain) 2778 Regina 2813 Spagna 2300, 2845 tutto 2899 giorno 2171 molto 2510 lettere 2538 ministri 2799 ministro 2354 Camera 2138 avuto 2533 materia 2153 fatto 2315 altri 2518 maggiore 2188 quello 2140 benché 2134 assai 2178 e che 2395 contrario 2177 onde 2189 egli 2407 detto The clear decipherments of the other five letters give many more, consistent across the letters: 2740 prim- , 2530 Marchese / Marchesa (guessed as chirurgo in September), 2394 Conte , 2743 Principessa , 2803 Segretario , 2823 Sua Maestà , 2189 quest- , 2378 Città , 2398 Corte , 2817 Stato and others; the word lists are in the reading files. The first leaf (117/1, R25) is the longest. The reading follows the Secretariat’s clear decipherment (“Decif. li 11 Ottobre”), aligned word by word with the key decode of the figures; [?word] marks a word the decipherer wrote that the figures as transcribed do not confirm. … e si racconta che, venendo il Re da una visita di una Dama (della quale già molto per questo da anni vi si parlava) in calesse con Pietro Texeira, [?Vilasso], domestico favorito (perciò Cavaliere dell'Ordine di Cristo e sotto cavallerizzo), fossero sparate contro il calesse tre schioppettate, per le quali restò ferito malamente il cavalcante e la mula del bilancino che egli montava; il Texeira ferito a morte (essendosi detto domenica che lo avevano sagramentato), ed il Re con molte ferite nel braccio destro. … La Dama è delle primarie famiglie, sorella del Marchese di Tavora che fu Vice Re all'Indie, maritata al di lui figlio primogenito. Si parla che venga il colpo da di lei parenti, o che venga da nemici del Texeira, creduto si governatore nella sedia. Il fatto non si mette in dubbio. “…it is told that the King, coming back from a visit to a Lady (about whom, for this reason, people have been talking for years) in a calash with Pedro Teixeira, [?Vilasso], his favourite valet (for that reason Knight of the Order of Christ and under-equerry), three musket shots were fired at the calash, by which the postilion and the mule of the leader he was riding were badly wounded; Teixeira was wounded to death (it was said on Sunday that he had received the sacraments), and the King had several wounds in the right arm. … The Lady is of the first families, sister of the Marquis of Távora who was Viceroy of the Indies, married to his eldest son. It is said that the blow comes from her relatives, or from enemies of Teixeira, who is believed to be the governor [of the King] in the chair. The fact is not doubted.” The Marquis of Angeja, the King’s confidant, then took the King to the Real Barraca. This is the attempt of the night of 3 September 1758, which Carvalho turned two months later into the arrest of the Távoras and the Duke of Aveiro and, in 1759, their execution at Belém.
acciaiuoli1757.html#the-wound

117/2 (R195, 19 Sept). The illness is the public story; the king is now said to have come not from the Marchioness but from “altra donna non nobile”. The arm is said to be broken. The Queen “non muterà cosa alcuna, poiché non ha da durare”, and the fleets held back for a year by the Secretary’s negligence are made to sail, “con danno del Re, e de' mercanti, e de' poveri capitani”. 117/3 (R196, 26 Sept). “Continua la pubblica voce sulla causa del male del Re, che da nessuno più si dubita, e ciascuno se ne persuade dal sentire, che ancora Sua Maestà resta per tutto il giorno a letto: Molti certo lo vedono, ma nessuno vede il braccio, che è fasciato.” 117/4 (R197, 10 Oct). Deciphered at the time: “Il Rè si è levato, ma mai [esce] tutto il giorno. Vogliono i più, che sia molto guasto nel Braccio, e che almeno resterà perpetuamente impedito.” 117/6 (R199, 24 Oct) , deciphered at the time: “Benché si dica il Re assai meglio si vuole, che assolutamente il Braccio resterà impedito: parlando un suo confidente col Re sulla morte della Regina il Re gli disse: è stata buona Sorella, e che sono sicuro, che il Re sposerà la mia Figlia Maria Francisca, e che lo ha promesso alla Regina avanti, che ella morisse: ciò, che il Ministro di Spagna mostra è tutto il contrario … di tutto il resto non posso io compromettermi.” Barbara of Braganza, Queen of Spain and José’s sister, had died on 27 August 1758. The widowed Ferdinand VI did not marry Maria Francisca. 117/5 (R198, 31 Oct) , deciphered at the time: the king has not had erysipelas, “ma un sacco di materia, che ha fatto la piaga”, with fever as a result. The king is very apprehensive; “il credere il male maggiore di quello, che si dice” is universal.
acciaiuoli1757.html#carvalho

117/7 (R200, 28 Nov 1758) is the longest leaf; its cipher is crowded and much corrected, and the reading follows the Secretariat’s decipherment of 28 December, checked against a second copy and the draft. The Jesuits’ affair: the city is for them, but nobody dares speak. “La passione è tutta del Segretario de Carvalho, che veramente è dispotico, né ha chi gli resista, e pubblicamente si dice che il Re di Portogallo ne ha paura.” The Cardinal Patriarch trembles before him; the expulsion of Father Torres, the nuncio’s confessor, is “un altro motivo di diffidenza meco”. A lay brother “cacciato dalla Compagnia” by Torres “sta tutto il giorno da Carvalho, ed è quello che dà notizie, e con esso accende tutto il fuoco.” 117/8 (R201, 12 Feb 1760) is about the succession. The British ambassador is said to have no other errand than to thwart a marriage of the Princess of Brazil to the Infante Don Luis of Spain, and the Conde d’Oeiras (Carvalho) confers often with the Spanish ambassador; others think the king means her for Don Antonio, eldest of his legitimised brothers. The court of London “è molto allarmata” and fears for its trade from “uno della Casa di Spagna e di Borbone sul trono di Portogallo”. The letter ends: “Il paese freme, che vorrebbe la Principessa unita coll'Infante Don Pietro.” She married her uncle Pedro on 6 June 1760. Acciaiuoli was expelled from Portugal nine days later.
acciaiuoli1757.html#method

The DECODE records were fetched with a logged-in session: images, the NiLan/Midas digit transcriptions, Lasry’s key and his decryption, which is one file attached to every record. The decryption was flattened into one letter string per leaf and split into Italian words by hand. Code words were fixed by aligning the three clear decipherments with the cipher below them, and then checked for consistency wherever the same code recurs in the other five leaves (2759 Re 11 times, 2300 tutto 12). The September working text, leaf by leaf, is targets/acciaiuoli1757/READING.md . The reading audit of 22 October 2026 asked whether each letter builds sentences that can be translated. Four (R25, R195, R200, R201) did not: an open code broke almost every sentence. The same day the png attachments on their DECODE records, filed as “key and work images”, turned out to be the Secretariat’s clear decipherments and drafts. They were transcribed and aligned word by word with the key decode ( texts/R*_align.tsv ): in R25, 205 of 288 clear words are carried letter by letter by the figures and 53 by code groups whose values hold across the letters; the rest fall where DECODE’s digit transcription is garbled, and none is contradicted by the figures. R196’s decipherment (f. 97r) was transcribed on 23 October and agrees with the decode clause by clause. The readings and English translations are texts/R*_reading.md and texts/R*_en.md .

Code 2339 in R200: the decipherer left “l’Ambasciatore di . . .” blank; the draft has “di Spagna”, read as [?Spagna]. Words the decipherer wrote that the figures as transcribed do not confirm, marked [?] in the readings: “Vilasso” in R25, “solamente assicurato” and “della gente di quei paesi” in R195; DECODE’s digit transcription is garbled at those places. Code groups of R196 outside its decipherment’s wording. Grades: codes from the decipherments on the leaves and from the Secretariat’s separate decipherments are H; the word division of the letters follows those decipherments. The rest of Portogallo 117 (ff. 2–585) has more cipher than these eight leaves. It is not on DECODE and was not seen.

Stato Portogallo 117 ff. 90r-91r, on DECODE R25 as DOC_R25_D1107-D1109 (png). # Transcribed from the images 22 Oct 2026 (Claude Opus 5.5), line by line as written; a working draft of the same decipherment is DOC_R25_D944-D945 (f. 92-93). # Head (left column): Di Lisbona Da M.r Nunzio Acciajoli / 12. Sett.e 1758 / Decif. li 11. Ottobre Spiego nel Dispaccio il male del Re di Portogallo, e la causa, che se ne adduce, ma si vuole, che non sia la vera per tutta la Città, e si racconta, che venendo il Re da una visita di una Dama (della quale già molto per questo [struck word] da anni vi si parlava) in Ca- lesse con Pietro Texeira Vilasso Do- mestico favorito, (perciò Cavaliere dell' Ordine di Cristo, e Sotto Cavallerizzo) fossero sparate contro il Calesse tre Schioppettate, per le quali restò ferito malamente il Cavalcante, e la Mula del Bilancino, che egli montava; Il Texeira ferito a morte [essendosi detto, Domenica, che lo avevano sagramen- tato] ed il Re con molte ferite nel braccio destro: E con una sola Mula, chiamato il March.e d'Angeja Confi- dente del Re in Soccorso, in di lui Casa passando, lasciandovi il Texeira, se- guitando la Mula, il d.o March.e por- tasse il Re alla Real Baracca, non senza molto rumore. La materia è delicata, ma diventata pubblica in bocca d'ogni popolare, ho creduto do- verne avvisare V.E., perchè non se ne parli per altra parte. La Dama è delle primarie Famiglie, Sorella del March.e di Tavora, che fu Vice Re all'Indie, maritata al di lui Figlio Primogenito. Si parla, che ven- ga il colpo da di lei Parenti, o che ven- ga da Nemici del Texeira, creduto si Governatore nella Sedia: Il fatto non si mette in dubbio, si vuole che colpito nell'osso il braccio del Re, sia rotto, e che perciò non potendo per lungo tempo sottoscrivere, abbia com- messo il Governo alla Regina, come nel Dispaccio: L'Infante Don Em- manuele me ne parlò con il Sospetto degli altri. I Ministri e Cortigia- ni dicono ciò, che riferisco nella Lettera in piano: Nè più posso però riferire. [?word] = the decipherment has it but the figures as transcribed do not confirm it. --> # R25, Acciaiuoli to the Secretariat of State, Lisbon, 12 Sept 1758 (ff. 95r-95v) ## Reading Spiego nel Dispaccio il male del Re di Portogallo, e la causa che se ne adduce; ma si vuole che non sia la vera per tutta la Città, e si racconta che, venendo il Re da una visita di una Dama (della quale già molto per questo da anni vi si parlava) in calesse con Pietro Texeira, [?Vilasso], domestico favorito (perciò Cavaliere dell'Ordine di Cristo e sotto cavallerizzo), fossero sparate contro il calesse tre schioppettate, per le quali restò ferito malamente il cavalcante e la mula del bilancino che egli montava; il Texeira ferito a morte (essendosi detto domenica che lo avevano sagramentato), ed il Re con molte ferite nel braccio destro. E con una sola mula, chiamato il Marchese d'Angeja, confidente del Re, in soccorso, in di lui casa passando, lasciandovi il Texeira, seguitando la mula, il detto Marchese portasse il Re alla Real Baracca, non senza molto rumore. La materia è delicata, ma diventata pubblica in bocca d'ogni popolare; ho creduto doverne avvisare Vostra Eminenza, perché non se ne parli per altra parte. La Dama è delle primarie famiglie, sorella del Marchese di Tavora che fu Vice Re all'Indie, maritata al di lui figlio primogenito. Si parla che venga il colpo da di lei parenti, o che venga da nemici del Texeira, creduto si governatore nella sedia. Il fatto non si mette in dubbio. Si vuole che, colpito nell'osso, il braccio del Re sia rotto, e che perciò, non potendo per lungo tempo sottoscrivere, abbia commesso il governo alla Regina, come nel Dispaccio. Translation R25_en.md <!-- English translation of texts/R25_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 22 Oct 2026). --> # R25, Acciaiuoli to the Secretariat of State, Lisbon, 12 Sept 1758 In the despatch I explain the King of Portugal's illness and the cause given for it; but the whole city holds that it is not the true one, and it is told that the King, coming back from a visit to a Lady (about whom, for this reason, people have been talking for years) in a calash with Pedro Teixeira, [?Vilasso], his favourite valet (for that reason Knight of the Order of Christ and under-equerry), three musket shots were fired at the calash, by which the postilion and the mule of the leader he was riding were badly wounded; Teixeira was wounded to death (it was said on Sunday that he had received the sacraments), and the King had several wounds in the right arm. And with a single mule, having called the Marquis of Angeja, the King's confidant, to his help, passing by his house and leaving Teixeira there, following the mule, the said Marquis took the King to the Real Barraca, not without much noise. The matter is delicate, but having become public in the mouth of every commoner, I thought I should inform Your Eminence, so that it should not be told you from another quarter. The Lady is of the first families, sister of the Marquis of Távora who was Viceroy of the Indies, married to his eldest son. It is said that the blow comes from her relatives, or from enemies of Teixeira, who is believed to be the governor [of the King] in the chair. The fact is not doubted. It is held that, struck in the bone, the King's arm is broken, and that therefore, being unable to sign for a long time, he has entrusted the government to the Queen, as in the despatch. The Infante Don Manuel spoke of it to me with the suspicion of the others. The ministers and courtiers say what I report in the letter in clear; nor can I report more for now. 117/2 = R195, f. 98r, Sept 1758 The public version of the king's injury is illness; the arm is said to be broken. Fleets and ships are held back, to the merchants' loss. La Città tutta è per loro: il primo è l'Infante Don Pietro, seguitato dalle Principesse e da quasi tutta la Corte; ma né il primo né altri ardisce parlare. La passione è tutta del Segretario de Carvalho, che veramente è dispotico, né ha chi gli resista, e pubblicamente si dice che il Re di Portogallo ne ha paura. Temo che codesto Ministro e quel Domenicano che accompagnò costà il figlio del Signore Carvalho scrivino de' spropositi e delle falsità per aiutare. L'espulsione del P. Torres, eseguita senza avermene prevenuto, è un altro motivo di diffidenza meco e di confusione nel Cardinale. Un laico cacciato dalla Compagnia dal detto P. Torres, mio confessore allora, sono due o tre anni che sta tutto il giorno da Carvalho, ed è quello che dà notizie, e con esso accende tutto il fuoco. Egli era informatissimo, perché stato ministro della vendita delle robbe d'India che spacciano qui. Translation R200_en.md <!-- English translation of texts/R200_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 22 Oct 2026). --> # R200, Acciaiuoli to the Secretariat of State, Lisbon, 28 Nov 1758 The affair of the Jesuits is in the state I describe in the letters in clear. The whole city is for them: the first is the Infante Don Pedro, followed by the Princesses and almost the whole court; but neither the first nor anyone else dares to speak. The passion is all the Secretary de Carvalho's, who is truly despotic, and there is no one to resist him; and it is said openly that the King of Portugal is afraid of him. Before, he spoke of it for whole hours at a time without anyone being able to interrupt him, and the Ambassador of [?Spain] and the Emperor's Minister have told me in confidence that he also spoke of it with them a great deal and always at length; now he speaks of it much less. In the city no one dares to talk about it; in confidence, though, everyone calls it violence. With me, besides the long outburst he made to me, which I reported in clear, not only does he no longer speak of it, but when I deliberately brought it into the conversation he avoids it; as does the Cardinal too, who trembles before him and depends on him in everything. And this behaviour began with the suspension of the Fathers from confession and preaching made by the late Patriarch, when I spoke of it with Cardinal Saldanha the same evening, as I have already reported. I fear that that Minister there and the Dominican who accompanied Signor Carvalho's son to Rome may write nonsense and falsehoods to help. The expulsion of Father Torres, carried out without telling me beforehand, is another reason for distrust towards me and for confusion in the Cardinal. A lay brother dismissed from the Society by the said Father Torres, then my confessor, has for two or three years been at Carvalho's all day; he is the one who supplies information, and with it he stokes the whole fire. He was very well informed, having been an official of the sale of the goods from India that are sold here. This is the key to the present state of the affair, which I am persuaded, with many others, they would like, with honour, if it were possible, to withdraw from many steps taken, which are recognised as irregular. The Cardinal is at school and carries out the precepts of the said Signor, without ever answering back, let alone opposing. 117/8 = R201, f. 280r, Lisbon 12 [?] 1760 Conferences of the Conde d'Oeiras (Carvalho); the Princess of Brazil's marriage to Infante Don Luis of Spain or to Don Pedro; London is alarmed at a Bourbon on the Portuguese throne. The marriage to Don Pedro took place in June 1760. Translation R201_en.md <!-- English translation of texts/R201_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 22 Oct 2026). --> # R201, Cardinal Acciaiuoli to the Secretariat of State, Lisbon, 12 Feb 1760 The talk is becoming general at court and in the city that this English Ambassador has no other commission than to upset the marriage, the treaty for which is said to be well advanced, between this Princess of Brazil and the Infante Don Luis of Spain. Frequent conferences are seen between the Count of Oeiras and the Count of Masseda, Ambassador of Spain, with attentions from the first to the second that seem affected to everyone. Some on the contrary will have it that the King of Portugal, with the said Count of Oeiras, is not thinking of such a marriage, but rather of giving the Princess to Don Antonio, the eldest of His Majesty's three legitimised brothers, who in fact only this year, on the pretext of hunting, is staying at Salvaterra against custom, his brother the Inquisitor not even having been there. This now makes many talk, especially among the ministers of the princes, who are doing everything to find out what it really is. The English Ambassador will speak in appearance for the commerce that is harmed, but in substance the court of London is much alarmed, because it fears its own loss, particularly in commerce, from one of the House of Spain and of Bourbon on the throne of Portugal, given past times with Spain and past and present times with France. The country is seething; it would like the Princess united with the Infante Don Pedro. Key: DOC_R25_D3232_3232.txt , key.md

Two copies of the same letter, the body in cipher, the opening and closing formulas in clear; no decipherment was filed with them. Where Archivo Histórico de la Nobleza (Toledo), Osuna papers, OSUNA,CT.2,D.32(1-2): copy A on images 2–3, copy B on image 5 (PARES 3939398). A syllable is written as another syllable with the consonant changed and the vowel kept (mo = co, ne = de, ra = sa), numbers in series of five give more syllables (45–49 = ra re ri ro ru), and a few signs stand for words (a cross for que , sal for Su Santidad ). In 1648 Innocent X was renewing his nuncios. Philip IV wanted to keep his own at Madrid: Giulio Rospigliosi (1600–1669), titular Archbishop of Tarsus, nuncio in Spain since 1644. A royal letter of 10 January 1648 (OSUNA,C.1983,D.7, not digitised) had asked Cardinal Gil de Albornoz, the King’s ambassador to the Pope, to obtain that “the Archbishop of Tarsus, nuncio of Spain, continue his residence”. Albornoz answered on 24 March with what the Pope had said. This letter of 24 July is the King’s reply: the opening that acknowledges the March letter is in clear, the body in cipher, and the closing formulas, the date, Yo el Rey and the countersignature of Pedro Coloma are in clear again. The letter survives twice in the Osuna papers of the Archivo Histórico de la Nobleza: copy A on images 2–3 of the PARES record, copy B on image 5, the original and the duplicate, both in the same chancery hand. Copy A repeats half a line and cancels it with 4s written above it; copy B cancels one group inside sujeto . Otherwise the two copies agree group for group, apart from a few copying slips. No decipherment, interlinear or separate, was filed with either. The Albornoz embassy papers passed, with the cardinal’s successor in Rome, into the archive of the Dukes of the Infantado and then into that of the Dukes of Osuna. Catalogue no. 747 here lists 69 of their shelfmarks with cipher; only four are digitised on PARES, and the other three hold the plain copies from which the keys were rebuilt and tested. Copy B. The clear opening runs to de enero ; the cipher begins on the same line with 4 ro r 46 35 mo e 52 44 r mi or , sobre la continuación , and ends at 124 4 before the clear Y sea muy reverendo en Christo padre . A dark patch at the left edge hides the first groups of two lines; copy A has them. Image: Archivo Histórico de la Nobleza, OSUNA,CT.2,D.32 image 5 (copy B), via PARES (the copy published by Brice Dudout, Europe chiffrée).

The digitised pieces. Of the 69 shelfmarks of no. 747, four have images on PARES: CT.2,D.16 (Philip IV to Albornoz, 12 December 1644), CT.2,D.20 (26 January 1645), CT.2,D.32 (this letter) and CT.11,D.1 (1649). Brice Dudout wrote a protocol before computing anything: each key built on one text, frozen with a SHA-256 hash, and tested on text kept out of the work. A key that does not fit. D.16 keeps its cipher original (images 2–4) and a plain copy made at the time (images 6–8). Aligning them gave K1, the royal cipher of 1644–45, which was frozen and tested on D.20, transcribed before its plain copy was opened: K1 recovered 0.638 of D.20’s letters, against a median of 0.467 and a 99th percentile of 0.550 for 200 control keys with the values permuted. Applied to the 1648 letter, K1 gives nothing: the letter is made of syllable groups ( ne , mo , ma , so , ri ) and numbers from 2 to 61 that K1 does not have. The key from the 1649 chapter. CT.11,D.1 holds a chapter of a letter of Luis de Haro to the Count of Peñaranda, Madrid, 25 September 1649, on the army of Catalonia, enciphered “to send to Cardinal Albornoz” (image 3), with its plain copy (image 1). It is in the cipher of the 1648 letter. The words dentro de Cataluña y , enciphered twice in the same way, 2 ℓ48 ne ma so 39 40 g , opened the alignment. The key K2 was learnt on lines 1–12 only and frozen. Lines 13–23, decoded mechanically with the frozen key, recover 0.859 of the letters of the plain copy, against a median of 0.419 and a 99th percentile of 0.476 for 200 control keys with the values permuted. The protocol had named a word-level score; the test used a letter-level one (the longest common subsequence of normalised letters), because a mechanical syllabic decoding does not divide words reliably. Both tests clear their controls by a wide margin. The letter. Both copies of the 1648 letter were transcribed and decoded with K2. K2 left some single letters and series numbers without a value; 29 values were added on the letter (K2b), each attested at least twice, fitting its series of five, or confirmed by the other copy: e = n, r = a, 23 = o, the cross = que , 25 = fa, 54 = tu. Copy B, the cleaner, was then checked group by group against copy A, and copy A was followed where B departs from the key. The statistical check here. The project’s validator ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading of 636 groups (84 types) with a four-gram model of Golden Age Spanish, as mean log-probability per letter. The reading scores −2.038; random keys of the same shape −3.743 on average; a key annealed onto the shuffled ciphertext −2.535 at best; and the same annealer, started from random keys on the real text, reaches −2.246. Verdict: pass.

Rospigliosi did stay at Madrid until 1653. He later became Cardinal Secretary of State and, in 1667, Pope Clement IX. Albornoz was given leave to return to Spain in 1649 and died in December of that year.

Philip IV to Cardinal Albornoz, Madrid, 24 July 1648 (AHNOB OSUNA,CT.2,D.32) In 1648 Innocent X was renewing his nuncios. Philip IV wanted to keep his own: Giulio Rospigliosi, Archbishop of Tarsus, nuncio at Madrid since 1644 – the future Pope Clement IX. He wrote so to his ambassador to the Pope, Cardinal Gil de Albornoz, in a cipher nobody had read: “there can be no instrument more suitable” for the service of both courts, so the ambassador must not desist “in any case”. Ve{o} ‹74› [que] pasastis los oficios con Su Santidad, y lo que ‹el› respondió mostrando los ‹A›s que en ‹124› considera ; pero todavía, siendo este sujeto muy digno de favor por la atención con que acude a su ministerio y a la representación en que está, y que para las conveniencias del servicio [de] su príncipe y mío no puede haver instrumento más a propósito, buelvo a encargaros continuéis y esforcéis con Su {Be}atitud las instancias para su detención ‹✗11› en conformidad de las primeras órdenes, y que no desistáis por ningún caso, como en negocio que incluye en sí conveniencias del servicio de Su Santidad y mío ; y daréisme quenta de lo que resultare y se fuere ofreciendo en ‹124›. *Y sea muy reverendo en Christo padre cardenal Albornoz, mi muy charo y muy amado amigo, Nuestro Señor en vuestra continua guarda. De Madrid a 24 de julio de 1648.* *Yo el Rey.* *Pedro Coloma.* Translation translation.md # English translation [In your letter of 24 March you acknowledge receipt of the one written to you on 10 January] about the continuance of the Archbishop of Tarsus, even if the other nunciatures are filled. I see ‹…› [that] you made representations to His Holiness, and what he answered, showing the ‹…› that he considers in ‹…›; but nevertheless, this person being most worthy of favour for the care with which he attends to his ministry and to the representation he holds, and since for the interests of the service of his prince and mine there can be no instrument more suitable, I again charge you to continue and redouble with His Beatitude the requests for his retention ‹…›, in accordance with the first orders, and not to desist in any case, as in a business that contains interests of the service of His Holiness and mine; and you will report to me what results and whatever may arise in ‹…›. [Closing formulas in plain text:] Most reverend father in Christ, Cardinal Albornoz, my most dear and beloved friend, may Our Lord keep you. Madrid, 24 July 1648. I the King. Pedro Coloma. Four letters of October–December 1577 from Guillaume Ancel, French resident at the Imperial court, carry cipher passages with no contemporary decipherment (BnF Cinq Cents de Colbert 398). Harumi-Matsuba transcribed them with AI and applied Satoshi Tomokiyo’s reconstructed Vulcob–Ancel key; the text reports Matthias’s flight to the Low Countries and the Emperor’s double game with Spain. Measured here: 98.4% of tokens take a value and the decode scores as French; three lines agree with the images, but no person has checked the whole transcription. h + β (y 9 π (y 7 8 // 7 3 o β ω … = hors de sa chambre… saturnus = l’Empereur · Juno = le Roy d’Espagne Vienna → France · homophonic symbol cipher with plain-letter code words · October–December 1577 · contributed, partial Ancel’s cipher, Vienna 1577: Archduke Matthias leaves for the Low Countries Go to the full text ↓ Four letters from the French resident at the Emperor’s court, deciphered by an outside contributor with AI and a published key; the text reads as French, but no person has yet checked the transcription. Clear letters with long passages in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq Cents de Colbert 398, pp. 524–526, 539, 561–563 and 565 (Gallica views 558–599). Most other cipher pages in the volume carry a decipherment in the margin; these do not. No DECODE record. The cipher A symbol alphabet with two to four signs per letter, signs for double letters, a few word signs, and code words written in plain letters (saturnus, Juno, my) mixed with plain-letter nulls. How it was deciphered Harumi-Matsuba transcribed the signs with Claude and checked them with OpenAI Codex, then applied Satoshi Tomokiyo’s reconstructed key. Here the files were re-measured with this project’s language models and three lines were compared with the images. What it says Archduke Matthias slipped away to the Low Countries; Ancel thinks the Emperor will deny any part in it, but notes he plays both sides with Spain while Don John’s envoy Varambon waits for leave to levy troops. Credit Reading, transcription and checks: Harumi-Matsuba (issue #53, 20 October 2026), done with AI only (Claude and Codex). Key: Satoshi Tomokiyo. No human has checked the transcription. ancel1577.html#letters

Cinq Cents de Colbert 398 gathers original letters on German affairs addressed to Charles IX, Henri III, Catherine de Médicis and their ministers, among them the despatches of the two French residents at the Imperial court, Jean de Vulcob (1575–76) and Guillaume Ancel (1576–78, 1584). Most of their cipher passages were deciphered on arrival in the left margin. Four letters of late 1577 were not: 22 October 1577 (heading on p. 523; cipher from the end of p. 524 to p. 526): the flight of Archduke Matthias, the Emperor’s brother, to the Low Countries. 2 November 1577 (p. 539): six lines. 14 December 1577 (pp. 561–563): the Marquis of Varambon, Don John of Austria’s envoy, and the Spanish ambassador Borgia. It builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.8%, under the 95% bar. 21 December 1577 (p. 565). The letters open “Monseigneur” rather than “Sire”, so the addressee is not the King himself; who it is has not been settled. The single cipher line at the top of p. 570 turned out to be deciphered in the last margin line of p. 569, and the key gives the same words. The top of p. 525, the letter of 22 October 1577. Plain-letter words stand among the signs: Monseigneur is clear text, saturnus is the code word for the Emperor, Juno (start of the last line) the King of Spain. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq Cents de Colbert 398 p. 525, via Gallica (btv1b525218133, view 559).
ancel1577.html#key

Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed the cipher of Vulcob and Ancel (1575–1584) from the margin decipherments of this volume and published the table on Cryptiana (“French Ciphers for German (and Eastern) Affairs”, 15 March 2026), noting that it would allow the letters without a contemporary decipherment to be deciphered; he published no readings. The table has two to four homophones per letter (4, 7 and α for a ; ω and π for e ; ∂ and μ for i ), single signs for doubled letters (ss, tt, pp, rr, mm, nn), and word signs such as plus = que, ros = pour, ucl = est. He also notes that Vulcob’s letter of 2 August 1572 (BnF fr. 18989) uses it. George Lasry’s 1573 letter of Charles IX to Vulcob ( vulcob1573 ) is in a related cipher: he compared it with a key in this volume and found 14 shared letter forms. The contributor added a few values from context and from the margin of p. 33: an m-shaped sign = uu, a flat L-like sign = g, the crossed q = ff, a lone c = null. Names and titles hide in plain-letter code words. Those checked against margin decipherments elsewhere in the volume: saturnus = l’Empereur (p. 258), Juno = le Roy d’Espagne (p. 440), my = qu’il and my3θ = qu’ilz (pp. 258, 321).
ancel1577.html#the-reading

The contributor’s line-by-line key output and word division are in READING.en.md ; code words are in brackets. Two passages: 22 October 1577, p. 525 ll. 9–13: “…tellement que a peine pouvoit il faire un pas hors de sa chambre sans le congé d’iceluy seigneur [saturnus] son frere; tant s’en faut qu’a une telle heure il eust peu sortir du chasteau, qui ferme toute la nuit…” — Matthias could hardly step out of his room without his brother the Emperor’s leave, still less leave a castle shut all night; so, Ancel argues, the Emperor will deny any part in the escape. 14 December 1577, pp. 561–562: the Emperor must declare himself for the King of Spain [Juno] or for the Archduke; if for the first, he will show it by giving Don John leave to levy troops in Germany, as Varambon has asked; meanwhile Borgia says that if the Emperor backs his brother he must do it in earnest, “d’autant que le roy catholique fera toutes les provisions possibles pour maintenir son droit”. On 2 November the Emperor “fait toute la demonstration [qu’il] luy est possible pour persuader les Espagnolz que tel depart est advenu a son desceu”; on 21 December Varambon is back from Archduke Charles’s court with nothing, and the Emperor waits for the King of Spain’s answer. p. 565, 21 December 1577: “…se remettant [saturnus] a la response qu’il attend du [Juno] sur ce qu’il luy a rescrit depuis le partement de l’archiduc Mathias”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq Cents de Colbert 398 p. 565, via Gallica (btv1b525218133, view 599).
ancel1577.html#checks

By the contributor (all with AI): a first transcription in sign names by Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 from enlarged tiles; a cross-check transcription by OpenAI Codex from the line images, without the key; two rounds of image adjudication by Claude Sonnet; then three independent Codex transcriptions, which agree with the final one on 95.2–96.1% of values (lowest page 88.8%, p. 565). With 1,000 shuffled keys, none scores as well as the real key on any page. As a calibration, two pages that do have a margin decipherment (pp. 258 and 285) were run through the same procedure without the margin being seen: 85.9% of letters agree with the margin. Here (21 October 2026): the files were copied into the repository and re-measured ( measure.py ). Of 4,385 cipher tokens on the seven pages, 98.4% get a value from the key or a checked code word. Under the project’s 16th-century French model the key output scores −1.8 to −2.3 per character, against −6.3 to −6.6 for shuffled keys. Split into words of a 16th-century vocabulary, 95.4% of tokens fall inside words, against 50% for shuffled keys; this is a lenient measure, an upper bound on what reads. Recomputing the calibration from the contributor’s files gives 472 of 556 letters, 84.9%. Three lines were compared sign by sign with the BnF images (p. 525 ll. 9–10, p. 565 l. 5): all 126 signs agree in order and count; two ∂/δ (i/n) choices could not be told apart at 2,400 pixels and rest on context, as the contributor says of that pair. The figures support the reading as French and the key as right. They do not make it a checked reading: the transcription is AI-made throughout, the adjudications are AI judgements, and the contributor marks 29 of 125 lines as conjecture or unclear syntax. The extent therefore stays partial.

A human check of the transcription against the images, starting with the 29 conjectural lines. Code words without a meaning: manua/manue (a person), mare , grinter , totum (probably l’Empire), nez , bel , mim ; probable nulls fec, sec, sanc, sane, pome, estre, roc, vib . Look-alike sign pairs settled by context: 3/ʒ (m/r), p/φ (f/m), ∂/δ (i/n), 9/q (d/l), the cross/4 (o/a). Unclear stretches: p. 526 ll. 9–14, p. 539 ll. 2–3, p. 561 ll. 1–4 and 18–19, p. 562 ll. 25–26 (line ends lost in the gutter), p. 565 ll. 9 and 15–16. The addressee (“Monseigneur”) and the signatures were not checked.

Je ne voy icy personne qui monstre de douter en sa conscience que telle chose n'aye esté pour pensé d'iceluy seigneur, deliberé et conclue en son conseil, nonobstant toutes les autres conjectures qu'on veuille amener a l'encontre, rien que plusieurs pretendent {my: qu'il} n'aye eu occasion d'avancer en tel cas un frere pour despouiller son oncle, ses neveu[x] ce que il leur appartient davantage. J'entend [au] lieu qu'on a eu assez de peine a inciter pour ce ledit seigneur archiduc, le que l'autrement … trop grande … ; l'on a adjousté aussi que [le]dit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur} eust desiré le faire ar[rester] il eust peu depescher lesdusditz gentilzh[ommes] plus matin, comme il ne feut rien ; le temps les ne partirent qu'environ le midy … en donnant soupçon ; sur ce {my: qu'il} escrivit toutes les lettres {my: qu'il} envoya aux princes. But considering the gentle nature of the young prince, and his upbringing, who has always been in fear and [re]verence, so much so that he could hardly take a step out of his room without the leave of that lord the Emperor his brother — so far was he from being able to leave the castle, which is shut all night, at such an hour — and likewise never having had anyone about him in whom he had [mim] confidence, so as to take such a resolution without the knowledge of His Imperial Majesty, with whom on the contrary it is certain that he has communicated more in the last few days than he used to; considering also that the Sieur de Malstet, as has since been verified, had asked the Emperor himself for him, not as governor, as some said, but outright as lord of the said Low Countries, and was negotiating with His Imperial Majesty, not with the said lord Archduke [pur]. I see no one here who shows any doubt in his conscience that such a thing was not thought out by that lord, deliberated and concluded in his council, notwithstanding all the other conjectures that one may wish to bring against it, except that several claim that he had no occasion in such a case to advance one brother in order to strip his uncle, his nephew[s], of what belongs to them more. I understand [instead] that it took a good deal of trouble to incite the said lord Archduke to this, the that otherwise … too great …; it is also added that if the said lord the Emperor had wished to have him stop[ped], he could have despatched the said gentle[men] earlier in the morning, which was not done; the time, they left only about noon … giving suspicion; whereupon he wrote all the letters that he sent to the princes. 2 Nov 1577, p. 539 The Emperor does all he can to persuade the Spaniards that Matthias's departure happened without his knowledge (contributor's summary). Spelling as the contributor gives it. ## Reading Je n'ay peu entendre ce {my3: qu'il} … traité, mais iceluy [manue] a dit a un personnage qu'il a visité, luy parlant de l'archiduc Mathias, {my3: qu'il} ne faut pas doresnav[ant] …nt que {saturnus: l'Empereur} marche si froidement comme il a commencé ; {my3: qu'il} est necessaire {my3: qu'il} se resolve de quel party il voudra estre, ou du dit {Juno: le Roy d'Espagne} ou du dit seigneur archiduc ; si du premier, {my3: qu'il} le monstre par les effetz, donnant permission de lever gens de guerre par l'Alemagne, comme l'en a supplié le marquiz de Varembon au nom de dom Jehan d'Austriche, offrant mesme de bailler caution satisfaire entierement a tout ce qui a esté ordonné touchant la gendarmerie es deux dernieres dietes imperiales tenues a Spire [et] Ratisbone ; ce que observant, ledit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur} ne le peut directement refuser, ainsi {my3: qu'il} [bel] specialement contenues […] esdessusdites dietes. Ce nonobstant sa magesté imperiale a entretenu icy plus de trois semaines ledit marquiz, se remettant a l'arrivée du dit sieur Borgia luy donner response … les tient en longueur le plus qu'il peut. [D'au]tre part iceluy Borgia a dit que si l'Empereur veut soustenir son frere, il luy sera besoin de faire a bon escient, d'autant que le roy cath[olique] fera toutes les provisions possibles pour [conser]ver/maintenir son droit. Par cela, Monseig[neur], vous pouvez juger en quelz termes se tro[uve] [le]dit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur}, lequel, comme aucuns pr[e]tendent, n'avoit possible estimé qu'iceluy {Juno: le Roy d'Espagne} prendroit cest affaire par le bout {my: qu'il} semble m[ain]tenant vouloir faire, ains plustost esperoi[t], voyant son payz quasi en proye, il se cont[entero]it que l'archiduc Mathias y fust son gouver[neur]. [On] ne peut on encores savoir de quel costé [il] tournera, car il entretient les Espagnol[z] [de] belles parolles, fait neantmoins secre[tement] plusieurs petites choses qui descouvr[ent] [la] bonne affection {my: qu'il} a defavoriser son fre[re]… se presente quelque officier qui le veu[ille] aller trouver, il est incontinant remuneré de ces passez, on luy fournit outre cela ar[gent]… son voyage, ce qui est advenu a plusieurs autres nagueres, a un ingenieur neapolitan bien experimenté ; ces jours cy pareillement il a chanté en la chambre dudit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur} … [une chan]son au desavantage des Espagnolz … ledit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur} monstra recevoir un singulier plaisir, tost apres l'envoya a l'archiduc Erneste pour luy faire avoir part du passetemps. Je vous say ces menues particularitez, Monseigneur, attendant que je sache asseurement quelle sera la derniere resolution dudit seigneur {saturnus: l'Empereur}, lequel a la verité, comme jugent plusieurs sages personnages, n'a aucunement besoin de mauvaise intelligence, moins de guerre avec ledit seigneur {Juno: le Roy d'Espagne}, n'estant trop bien pourveu de finances, estant dificile d'attirer les estatz de l'empire a quelque secours extraordinaire, veu mesme qu'on ne peut obtenir deux leurs taxes ordinaires, si ce n'est possible les Electeurs de Saxe, Brandebourg, lesquelz toutesfois ne se voudront de beaucoup affoiblir. Translation p561-563_en.md <!-- English translation of texts/p561-563_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes; bracketed part-words completed in the reading are translated as words; unresolved code words stay [code]; "…" is an unreadable stretch. --> # Ancel, pp. 561-563: English translation I have not been able to learn what he … negotiated, but this [manue] said to a person he visited, speaking to him of Archduke Matthias, that from now on it is not right …that the Emperor should proceed as coldly as he has begun; that it is necessary that he decide which party he will be of, either of the said King of Spain or of the said lord Archduke; if of the first, that he show it by deeds, giving permission to raise soldiers throughout Germany, as the Marquis of Varambon has begged him in the name of Don John of Austria, even offering to give security to comply fully with everything that was ordained concerning men-at-arms in the last two imperial diets held at Speyer [and] Regensburg; which being observed, the said lord the Emperor cannot refuse it directly, since he [bel] specially contained […] in the aforesaid diets. Notwithstanding this, His Imperial Majesty has kept the said Marquis here more than three weeks, putting off giving him an answer until the arrival of the said Sieur Borgia … he keeps them waiting as long as he can. [On the] other hand, this Borgia has said that if the Emperor means to support his brother, he will have to do it in earnest, since the Catholic King will make every possible provision to [pre]serve/maintain his right. From this, Monseigneur, you can judge in what position the said lord the Emperor finds himself, who, as some claim, had perhaps not thought that the King of Spain would take this affair by the end that he now seems to wish to, but rather hoped that, seeing his country almost a prey, he would be content to have Archduke Matthias as his governor there. [One] cannot yet know which way [he] will turn, for he entertains the Spaniards with fine words, yet secretly does several little things that reveal the good will he has to favour his brother… if some officer presents himself who wishes to go and join him, he is at once rewarded for his past services, he is furnished besides with [money]… his journey, which has lately happened to several others, to a very experienced Neapolitan engineer; these last days likewise he sang in the said lord the Emperor's chamber … [a so]ng to the disadvantage of the Spaniards … the said lord the Emperor showed that he took singular pleasure in it, and soon after sent him to Archduke Ernest to let him share the entertainment. I tell you these small particulars, Monseigneur, while waiting to know for certain what will be the final resolution of the said lord the Emperor, who in truth, as several wise persons judge, has no need at all of ill understanding, still less of war, with the said lord the King of Spain, not being too well provided with finances, and it being difficult to draw the estates of the Empire into any extraordinary aid, seeing that one cannot even obtain their ordinary taxes from two of them, except perhaps the Electors of Saxony and Brandenburg, who however will not want to weaken themselves much. 21 Dec 1577, p. 565 Varambon is back from Archduke Charles's court with nothing; the Emperor waits for the King of Spain's [Juno] answer (contributor's summary). bagno1652.html#context

Written from Paris on 5 January 1652, during the Fronde, the despatch concerns opposition to Cardinal Mazarin's return to France. Guidi di Bagno reports the Parlement's death sentence and 150,000-livre bounty, threats against Mazarin, and an appeal for papal intervention. The central dispute is whether a secular court can punish a cardinal or whether that authority belongs to the pope. The submission covers all four cipher pages, ff. 6r–7v, in reading order P3, P4, P5, P1. The record also includes a clear opening leaf, f. 5r; it is not included in the four-page cipher reading. The opening cipher page, with Italian words interspersed among numerical groups. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 104 f. 6r, via DECODE R5622. This letter was not part of George Lasry, Beáta Megyesi and Nils Kopal, "Deciphering papal ciphers from the 16th to the 18th Century", Cryptologia 45(6), 479–540 (2021; published online 2020), DOI 10.1080/01611194.2020.1755915 (scope confirmed by George Lasry).
bagno1652.html#method

The attack recovered the grouping of a continuous digit stream into single-digit letters, two-digit letters and syllables, and four-digit word/name codes. Repeated Italian words and crib testing constrained the values; the roughly alphabetical nomenclator helped extend them. The manuscript was revisited to correct touching-digit ligatures, duplicated boxes, and the marked 04 = qu versus plain 04 = che. Values were checked across the four cipher pages. No matching historical key or decipherment was used. Clear words interspersed in the letter supply context, not a parallel decipherment of the cipher passages. The September repository attempt had excluded the Francia 346 key and found OCR too noisy. Lasry's CTTS transcription enabled a new attack. No generic null-5 rule was accepted.

The nuncio rejects the Parlement's jurisdiction over a cardinal; a speaker tentatively identified as the Duke of Orléans threatens that Mazarin will be killed in his cardinal's robes unless the pope summons or deprives him. [f. 6r] Two days after the departure of the last ordinary [post], with which I informed Your Eminence of the resolution taken in the Parlement against Mazarin, the arrêt was printed; I send it to Your Eminence with the present letter. It contains the death penalty and the bounty of one hundred and fifty thousand livres placed on his head. It declares him [2149: to have?] incurred them by violating the prohibitions issued by [2517: His Majesty?] the King against his returning to [2416: France?]. It is grounded in the earlier arrêts, which stipulated that, if he contravened them, he would fall into the penalty of lèse-majesté. They claim he is guilty of this crime [2148: since?] he was lodged at Sedan on the twenty-[2698: ?] of last month. [They also claim] that the Parlement is the competent judge of the crime of lèse-majesté of any person whatsoever, [2400: even if?] constituted in the highest rank. And I told those who spoke to me, in plain conversation, that neither the Parlement nor any temporal [2560: power?] has this faculty, which is entirely reserved to the Supreme Pontiff. And [I told them] that I hold it for certain that the King will annul it. [2609: Lord?] [2393: Duke of Orléans?] has charged me to inform His Holiness that in [...], in which [2635: His Royal Highness?] took part (he being greatly devoted to [f. 6v] [2601: the Holy See?] and to His Holiness), [he] has [2158: never?] had the intention, by declaring the said penalty, of offending the dignity of cardinal, but only the person of a common enemy and of a man more reckless than any there has ever [2630: been?] at any time, and of the greatest harm to the Crown and to all [2354: Christendom?]. And [he is] begging His Holiness to free this [2580: kingdom?], the King and the royal house from [2080: a?] perverse man, by recalling him to [2600: Rome?] under penalty of deprivation of the [2334: cardinalate?]. And [they] fully(?) believe that he will not obey; [2165: so that?], when he is condemned by His Holiness, he will be utterly despised. And His Holiness will gain the universal goodwill of [2416: France?], relieving the King, a minor, from the oppression of so fierce a tyrant. And even if the Queen [2141: too?] were to [2157: take?] exceptional(?) offence at this, on considering the [2143: harm?] to herself and to the said cardinal she would have reason to welcome it (tentative: several underlying readings are uncertain), because otherwise he will undoubtedly be killed, and that dignity [the cardinalate] would be all the more offended; and the Queen will be forced to withdraw, or will see the total ruin of her children. [The Duke] added that the Prince and he will unite [f. 7r] their [2305: forces?], and that they are determined that Mazarin should perish unless he leaves and goes so far away that his return need no longer be feared. And he begs His Holiness to take this decision at once, and to dispatch an envoy by the relay-post service to execute his command, at which [2635: His Royal Highness?] will assist. And if [His Holiness] wished, before [2150: making/giving?] this declaration, that the Prince and he should petition for it by a judicial act, they will do so before the person whom His Holiness will send. His Holiness could dispatch him secretly, so that he should meet no hindrance on the journey. And he promises that the Parlement itself will support him. And I promised to write everything to Your Eminence, and I raised objections with him concerning the respect owed to royal persons, whatever the faults of the [2483: minister?]. [I also mentioned] the cardinal's disobedience to the paternal admonitions that His Holiness will have given him in his papal brief, and that this disobedience, if His Holiness resolved to have a formal injunction [2150: issued?] to him, could reach such a point that it would be worse than turning a blind eye to his misconduct. [f. 7v] [The last words of f. 7r and the first of f. 7v form one sentence, joined above.] And [2393: the Duke of Orléans?] replied: "I tell you, we will have him killed in his cardinal's habit, if the Pope does not summon him [to Rome] or does not deprive him of that dignity; and I formally declare this to you, as his [2483: minister?] [= representative]." And [2393: the Duke of Orléans?] [2140: also?] told me that the Queen had already promised that Mazarin would not return, and had had the King write this to the Parlement, [2140: also?] in the last [2463: letter?] of [2638: His Majesty?], which was read when the arrêt was made. And [he said] that she then broke her word so shamefully that everyone is scandalized by it, and that no one will trust her any more. [...] Historical check ---------------- The Parlement of Paris's arrêt of 29 December 1651 set a price of 150,000 livres on Mazarin's head and declared him guilty of lèse-majesté for re-entering France against the earlier arrêts (February and September 1651). Mazarin re-entered France at the turn of the year 1651/52 with troops raised in Germany, by way of Sedan. Gaston d'Orléans ("Monsieur") and Condé ("il Principe") were then allied against him. This historical setting is consistent with the proposed reading. It does not independently establish the unresolved date or the personal names. Key: key.txt

breves1603.html#letters

François Savary de Brèves was Henri IV’s ambassador at the Porte from 1591 to 1605. In 1604 he negotiated the renewal of the Capitulations. The BnF notice for fr. 3541 lists the King’s letters to him, several marked “avec chiffre”. For 1603 there are twelve. Berger de Xivrey’s source lines give the folios. 1603 Written at Fol. In Berger, Lettres missives VI 18 February Paris 60 full text, pp. 31–32 31 March Metz 63 full text, pp. 63–65 17 April Fontainebleau 66 full text, pp. 76–78 1 May Fontainebleau 69 summary, p. 668 13 May Fontainebleau 72 summary, pp. 669–70 22 June Paris 75 summary, pp. 670–71 22 July Nanteuil 78 summary, p. 672 6 August Saint-Germain 81 summary, p. 673 15 September Caen 84 summary, pp. 676–77 15 October Fontainebleau 104 summary, p. 678 (“chiffré à moitié”) 9 November Fontainebleau 87 summary, pp. 678–79 23 December Paris 90 summary, p. 680 (the BnF notice has the 24th) The letter usually cited as f. 63 of “1 March” is the Metz letter of 31 March, le dernier jour de mars . The same volume also has a fully ciphered letter of 5 January 1610 (f. 8) and a Puisieux letter with cipher (f. 39). Both date from Brèves’s later embassy in Rome and probably use another key. They were not examined.
breves1603.html#key

Tomokiyo rebuilt this cipher from Brèves’s letters to the King in BnF fr. 16144, and then noticed that the original is in fr. 3462, a volume of keys and jargons. The leaf is f. 103 (Gallica canvas 109). The next leaf, f. 104, is not the same key. It is the “Chiffre reformé pour Levant”, sent to Brèves in April 1604, after these letters. BnF fr. 3462 f. 103, the whole table: the persons on the left (from le Pape sa Saincteté to les Spahis gens de cheval ), the alphabet across the top, the nomenclator below, and the doubles and nulls at the foot of the last column. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). BnF fr. 3462 f. 103, the alphabet. Each letter has two to four substitutes: figures ( a = 7, 3, 5; b = 8, 9; e = 2, 3, 4), crosses and pseudo-letters. The long bar at the right end of the row belongs to the table. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). The table has five parts: An alphabet of homophones, figures and signs. A nomenclator in initial-letter blocks, numbered 10–99 for words in a – g ( aussi 11, avec 12, capitullations 57, Constantinople 59, corsaires 61, faire 92, fault 93, guerre 98), with signs for the rest ( le , que , qui , pour , vous , Turcs , galleres , vaisseaux , la mer ). A column of persons , each a single sign: the Pope, the King, the Emperor, the kings of Spain, Poland, Persia, Fez and Tartary, the Grand Seigneur, the Sultana his mother, the grand bassa, the viziers, the general of the sea, the aga of the janissaries, the beglerbey, the nissangi, the tesquitar and the spahis. Doubles , the figures 13, 49, 57, 30, 97, 38 and 70 marked with a caret. Two lists of nulls. Part of the nomenclator: aussi 11, avec 12, au 13 … capitulle 56, capitullations 57, Constantinople 59, corsaires 61 … faire 92, fault 93. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). The figures agree with the values Tomokiyo recovered from the ciphertext ( aussi 11, avec 12, faire 92, fault 93, a = 7/3/5), which confirms that this is the key of the letters. A transcription is in targets/breves1603/key.md . Its numeric entries are firm. Its names for the signs are provisional until they can be checked against the ciphertext.
breves1603.html#print

Berger de Xivrey’s sixth volume of the Recueil des lettres missives de Henri IV (1853) cites each of these letters as “Orig. — B. N. Fonds Béthune, Ms. 9021, fol. …”, with a second source: “Cop. — Biblioth. de M. Monmerqué, Ms. intitulé Lettres à l’ambassadeur du Levant ”. That copy was in clear, and Berger printed from it. He gives the February, March and April letters whole. He lists the other nine in the table of unprinted letters at the end of the volume, each marked “(En chiffres)” and summarised. The Monmerqué manuscript has not been traced. It was probably dispersed with his library. The OCR of the 17 April letter garbles exactly those passages Berger seems to have set in italic, which may be how he marked what was in cipher. This is not checked against the printed page.

breves1603.html#says

Berger’s text of 18 February, from “que les desordres”, the stretch Tomokiyo’s overlay covers … les desordres de l’empire de ce Seigneur vont continuant et augmentant, à sa honte et au grand prejudice d’iceluy, et ay bien consideré et pris le conseil que vous me donnés sur cela, duquel je me serviray le mieux qu’il me sera possible; mais la juste jalousie que j’ay de mes voisins ne me permet de faire pour ce regard tout ce que je desirerois et seroit necessaire. Je ne me puis persuader que cest empire soit pour tomber ou faire naufrage si tost que vous l’apprehendés, joinct que j’ay l’opinion, s’il y avoit du changement, que ce sera sur la personne du prince plustost qu’en autre chose; car les ennemys du dict empire ne sont mieux conseillez et servys que luy, et ont des incommoditez qui les combattent, qui ne sont de petite importance; mais ils doivent plustost craindre les armes du revolteur d’Asie que celles des autres. February. Brèves had written that the Ottoman empire might collapse. The King does not believe it: if anything changes, it will be the person of the sultan, not the empire. Its Christian enemies are no better led than it is, and the real danger is the rebel in Asia, the Celali rising. France is at peace. Bouillon has had to withdraw to Germany, finding no Protestant willing to rise for him. The King is leaving for Metz, where war threatens between the Protestants and Catholics of Germany over the bishopric of Strasbourg, disputed between Brandenburg and Lorraine. March, from Metz. He wants to know how the remuement at the Porte has ended, “car il en succedera un grand bien ou un grand mal” to the sultan and his empire. The Emperor is recruiting Frenchmen: Nevers, wounded at the assault on Buda, has vowed to go back. The King will not be drawn into mediating a peace between the Emperor and the sultan. He has ordered his subjects in the Levant to sail armed against English pirates. He reports that Elizabeth is gravely ill. April. The revolt of Mamoucte Bassa and the spahis against the sultan and his first vizier has been put down. The King regrets the fall of the mufti and his brother. Brèves is to congratulate the sultan, but not to ask for an Ottoman fleet, and to get out of the peace negotiation gently. The Emperor will not hear of peace, and the King of Spain is urging him against it so as to have a free hand at Algiers. Elizabeth is dead, and James has been proclaimed without opposition. May to December , from Berger’s summaries only; the letters themselves are not in the repository: the war in Hungary and Transylvania, with Moses Székely driving out Basta; the King’s wish that the Frenchmen serving the sultan withdraw, quietly and in Brèves’s own name; Spain’s enterprise on Algiers, taken up, dropped and taken up again; a treaty with James I disowning his subjects’ piracy, and Marseille ships to be armed against Barbary and English corsairs; the sultan’s chiaoux waiting at Marseille for a royal journey to Provence that did not happen that year; in August, surprise at the execution of the sultan’s son on a mere suspicion; in December, unease at “certain changement survenu à la Porte”, which the King fears favours the house of Austria. Mehmed III died on 22 December 1603, the day before the last of these letters was written. The renewal of the Capitulations in May 1604 falls after the series.
breves1603.html#remains

The ciphertext. Fr. 3541 is not on Gallica: there are no records under its shelfmark or its old Béthune number, and the BnF notice has no link to a digital copy. Desenclos 2018 has no plates, and Tomokiyo does not say where his images came from. A reproduction of ff. 60–104 would let the nine summarised letters be decrypted in full with the key. The three printed letters give about two pages of known plaintext to settle the key’s signs first. The full texts are at the BnF. Fr. 4029 (anc. 8962(3), olim Supplément français 500), a 17th-century “Recueil de copies de lettres”, holds 158 letters of Henri IV to Brèves from 1592 to 1608. Its nos. 131–142 are this series, from 18 February to 23 December 1603, one folio each on ff. 118–128. No. 130 is a letter of 6 January 1603 that has no ciphered original in fr. 3541. The volume is not on Gallica. Eleven folios of it would give the full text of the nine summarised letters, and a reproduction order for them is the cheapest way to finish this series. The Monmerqué copy that Berger used, Lettres à l’ambassadeur du Levant , is not needed. Guadet’s supplement (t. VIII–IX, 1872–76) does not print the nine in full. Checking the key’s signs. Brèves’s own letters to the King in the same cipher are online. Fr. 15578 f. 185 ( Gallica canvas 196 ) is fully ciphered, with the recipient’s decipherment written between the lines (“Je n’adjousteray a ma derniere … que la mort du grand …”). That makes it known plaintext for settling the provisional sign names in key.md before any images of fr. 3541 are obtained. It has not been transcribed yet. A loose end in Berger. His table (p. 667) also lists a “dépêche entièrement chiffrée” to Brèves of 17 April, “fol. 60”, with no copy cited. It is either a second April dispatch or a misprint. Only the manuscript can say which.

Monsieur de Brèves, since my last, written on the 4th of this month, I have received yours of the 3rd, 15th and 17th of December, from which I have learned that the disorders of this Lord's [the Sultan's] empire go on continuing and increasing, to his shame and to its great harm; and I have well considered and taken the advice you give me on this, which I shall use as best I can; but the just jealousy I have of my neighbours does not allow me to do in this regard all that I would wish and that would be necessary. I cannot persuade myself that this empire is about to fall or be wrecked as soon as you fear, besides which I am of the opinion that, if there were a change, it would fall on the person of the prince rather than on anything else; for the enemies of the said empire are no better advised and served than he is, and they have difficulties fighting them that are of no small importance; but they should fear the arms of the rebel of Asia more than those of the others. So I shall be glad to know what progress it makes, and you will know that my kingdom is at present very peaceful. The Duke of Bouillon has been forced to withdraw to Germany, having found my subjects of the Religion not disposed to follow his counsels and rise for him. I shall leave in two days to go to Metz, to settle a certain dispute that troubles the peace of that town and to be ready on that frontier, where it seems that matters are on the point of a war beginning between the Protestants and Catholics of Germany, founded on the dispute over the bishopric of Strasbourg, which is contested between the houses of Brandenburg and Lorraine — the latter favoured by the Emperor and the other by the said Protestants, arms being already ready on both sides. You will be informed of what comes of it, as I also wish to be of what happens over there. I pray God, Monsieur de Brèves, to keep you in His holy and worthy care. Written at Paris, the 18th day of February 1603. HENRY. Translation 1603-03-31_en.md <!-- English translation of berger/1603-03-31_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the letter as printed by Berger de Xivrey (1853) from the contemporary clear copy of the ciphered original. --> # Henri IV to Brèves, Metz, 31 March 1603: English translation To Monsieur de Brèves, gentleman in ordinary of my chamber and my ambassador in the Levant. Monsieur de Brèves, I greatly wish to know what the outcome has been of the commotion begun at this Lord's Porte, of which you informed me by your letter of 3 January, which I received with that of 29 December on the 19th of this month; for great good or great harm will come of it to the person of this Lord and to his empire, which, being attacked and harried on all sides, must succumb if he suffers harm and his principal officers fall into disorder and take sides. The Emperor is preparing to attack him more powerfully than ever, even to the point of enlisting my own subjects for that purpose. Last year the Duke of Nevers was in his army, and was wounded at the assault on Buda by a great arquebus shot that he received in the body, of which he nearly died. He now says that during his wound he vowed to God to go back there if he recovered from the said shot, so that, being again solicited by the said Emperor, I foresee that it will be difficult for me to prevent him from going back. Nevertheless I have resolved to do all I can in this regard. The first time he was accompanied by only five or six gentlemen, as adventurers; but I have learned that the said Emperor wishes to give him a command, so as to oblige him to go this time with a larger following; which will be cut down on my part as far as possible. I am sorry for the disgrace of the Mufti and of his brother, given the confidence you have in them, and I wish to hope that this change will soon bring about others which may perhaps be the cause of their restoration; but know that I do not wish to be engaged in the negotiation of peace with the said Emperor, as they had proposed to you, for I could not bring it to an end, and besides I would displease the Pope and others by undertaking it. I also know that the said Emperor will have no wish to hear of it, so that it would be shameful for me and for this said Lord to speak of it. I shall have the Grand Duke spoken to about the prisoner, this Lord's porter, whom he recommended to me, and shall send his answer. Meanwhile do not promise them his release, for the said Grand Duke might make difficulties about it. I will not promise what I do not keep. I have ordered my subjects in those ports of the Levant to sail there armed, for protection against the English pirates; but it will be necessary to resolve to summon this Lord to give me satisfaction for it, because of the refuge they find in that country; and if he will not or cannot do so, my said subjects will abstain from trading there. For the rest, I have finished in this town what I came here for, for I have changed its governors as I wished, both for the good of my service and for the relief of the citizens, so that I shall leave within two days to return to Paris. I have had word that the Queen of England has fallen gravely ill; nevertheless I hope she will not die this time. I pray God, Monsieur de Brèves, to keep you in His holy care. Written at Metz, the last day of March 1603. HENRY. Monsieur de Brèves, I have learned, from your letter of the [?29th] of January and from those of the [?11th] and [?20th] of February, the beginning, the progress and the end of the rising and conspiracy made by Mamoucte Pasha and some Spahis against this Lord, his first vizier and his principal officers and servants; praising God that the outcome has been such as you wrote in your last, and also as regards the Mufti and his brother, for the reasons given in your said letter; and I shall be glad to learn by your next, as I expect, that all this commotion has been entirely appeased and the authors punished to His Highness's satisfaction; and I do not doubt, this having so turned out, that you will have rejoiced at it on my behalf, both with this Lord and with his said first Pasha and others as you think fit. But if, on receiving the present letter, you have not yet done this office, do it as soon as you have received it, and let him understand that I commanded you to do so, as one who wishes this prince to keep in his empire his authority and power, as his predecessors of glorious memory did. But since no certain reliance is to be placed on their assistance and promises, as you have written to me in your letters, refrain from soliciting and pressing for an armament at sea, and from letting them see that I need their assistance, or that I expect [it] in any way, so that this does not oblige me to engage myself with them; for I recognise well that there is neither gain nor honour in it. Nor commit me either to the negotiation of peace with the Emperor; for I know for certain that the said Emperor will hear nothing of it, both because of the advantages he has gained and hopes God will continue to give him hereafter against this Lord, and because the King of Spain dissuades him from it, so as to facilitate the enterprise he has always had against Algiers, to which he invites the kings of [?Kuku] and their like. Therefore withdraw gently from this negotiation, as I wrote to you in my last, and continue to inform me of all occurrences. You will know that the Queen of England having died on the [?3rd] of this month, the King of Scotland has been proclaimed and declared her legitimate successor and king of the said kingdom and of that of Ireland, with the common consent of all the English, without any opposition up to this hour, and he was expected in London with much devotion to be crowned king; at which I have been very glad, for I have always had a particular and brotherly friendship with the said king, having favoured and assisted him on this occasion as far as I could. For the rest, I returned here yesterday evening, having completed my journey to Metz very happily and usefully for my service, for which I praise God, praying Him, Monsieur de Brèves, to keep you in His holy care. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letters Ten despatches of Gaspar Méndez de Haro, Marqués del Carpio, Spanish ambassador in Rome, to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, Spanish envoy at Copenhagen, 4 September to 11 December 1677. Each opens with clear compliments and turns to cipher. Where Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559; DECODE R1002–R1011, 29 pages. DECODE lists eight as partly decrypted (the decipherment is in the margin) and two, R1004 and R1005, as not decrypted. The cipher A syllabic nomenclator: numbers 9–30 for letters, 31–60 for consonant-vowel syllables, struck numbers for a second syllable table, letter pairs with a disguised consonant ( ge = de, ma = la), and about twenty three-letter code words for names and frequent words. How it was deciphered The key was recovered by lining up the 4 September letter with its contemporary marginal decipherment, then applied to all ten. On 22 October 2026 the eight margins were transcribed from the images and aligned word by word with the key’s output; each letter was written out as Spanish and translated into English. R1004 and R1005 carry a faint margin too, and it agrees with the key. What it says The French fleet off Messina and Catania; Orange raising the siege of Charleroi; riots against Spaniards in Rome, guns on Castel Sant’Angelo and French press-gangs at Civitavecchia; Innocent XI refusing Carpio an audience; the fall of Freiburg; d’Estrées at Turin threatening war in the Milanese. Still open Two place names at the end of R1006, illegible in the margin; one misread group in R1002 and one unwritten verb in R1003; struck 55 and a few struck numbers not placed in the key table.
carpio1677.html#the-letters

The file is one of several in SEG 2559 holding letters to Fuenmayor from Spanish diplomats, 1674–79. DECODE describes Carpio’s ten as partly decrypted: “the solution is written in the margin, without revealing the key.” R1004 and R1005 are marked as not decrypted, meaning DECODE saw no decipherment on them. Each letter opens with a clear paragraph of compliments, then turns to cipher. The cipher is in one hand, in point-separated groups, with the null groups N, R, g and 4 struck through at the start and end of each block. The decipherment runs vertically in the left margin. R1005, 20 November 1677. DECODE lists this letter as not decrypted; a faint decipherment runs down the left margin: “mas que nos tienen con gran cuidado las apariencias y evidentes señales de que la proxima campaña havrá guerra en Milán…”. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 20 November 1677, via DECODE R1005.

Token Value 9–30 single letters: a 9, b 10, c 11, d 12, e 13, f 14, g 15, h 16, i 17, l 18, m 19, n 20, o 21, p 22, q 23, r 24, s 25, t 26, u 27, x 28, y 29, z 30. In practice they spell word-final consonants: n, r and s are the commonest tokens in the file. 31–60 consonant + vowel, rows of five in the order a e i o u: m 31–35, n 36–40, p 41–45, r 46–50, s 51–55, t 56–60 (33 mi, 36 na, 39 no, 48 ri, 52 se) struck numbers t row 15–19, f row 20–24, vowel + l 30–34 (31 el), vowel + s 35–39 (36 es), vowel + n 40–44 (41 en, 42 in, 43 on), vowel + r 45–49, que 50, qua 51, qui 52; struck 14 = ju ( ajuste , justicia , justamente , confirmed by the margins); struck N, R, g, 4 are nulls letter pairs a syllable with its consonant changed and its vowel kept. Cipher b → c, c → b/v, g → d, l → g, m → l, so ge de, gi di, bo co, ci vi, ma la, la ga, lu gu. Also ag ha, eg he, and a separate sign for lle 116 V.S. (Vuestra Señoría) code words sen = Rey; gin/jin/jen = S.M.; gus = Príncipe [de Orange]; quol = Inglaterra; ana = Nápoles; ten = Francia; tin = Francia, franceses; pon = armada; san = Bruselas; tan = Flandes; gon = señor(es); ran, xan = gobernador; ren, xen = gobierno; cen = Duque [de Lorena]; cun = España (cun iles = españoles); xin = gente; gen = enemigos; xon = guerra; men = Reino; lun = cartas; 110 = cuando. Those found on 22 October 2026 from the margins: cen, ren/xen, xin, cun, tin, gen and 110. R1010, 4 September 1677. Margin: “La Armada de Francia salió de Mecina y haviendo corrido voz de que se encaminava a imbadir a Brindis en el Reyno de Nápoles…”.
