13 November 1677 (R1004). Normalised; bracketed words are uncertain. … [y al mesmo tiempo devo] lamentarme con V.S. de lo que en todas partes nos persigue nuestra mala fortuna, pues con la llegada del Cardenal de Estrées a Turín se teme alguna gran novedad en Italia; y las cosas de [Flandes] se hallan en el estado que V.S. sabe. Si bien en las materias del Congreso parece debemos suspender el juicio hasta ver lo que resulte del abocamiento del Príncipe de Orange con el Rey de Inglaterra. En los embarazos de esta corte no se me ofrece qué añadir a lo que diré a V.S. en mis antecedentes, sino que, si bien aguardaba este correo las órdenes de S.M., no las he recibido; pero no dudo las traerá el siguiente, pues de Madrid me avisan que habían llegado allá las cartas en que di los primeros avisos sobre estas dependencias. “…to lament with Your Lordship how our ill fortune pursues us everywhere: with Cardinal d’Estrées come to Turin some great novelty is feared in Italy … in the Congress [of Nijmegen] we must suspend judgement until we see what comes of the Prince of Orange’s meeting with the King of England … I expected His Majesty’s orders by this post and have not had them.” 20 November 1677 (R1005). … más de que nos tienen con gran cuidado las apariencias y evidentes señales de que la próxima campaña habrá guerra en Milán, pues el Cardenal de Estrées, que está en Turín, no se descuida. “…except that we are much concerned by the appearances and evident signs that next campaign there will be war in the Milanese, for Cardinal d’Estrées, who is at Turin, is not idle.”
carpio1677.html#the-other-eight-in-brief

These eight letters have the contemporary decipherment in the left margin. Each margin was transcribed from the images and set word by word against the key’s output; where the two differ, the sense decides and the choice is noted in the reading file. The Spanish of every letter and its English translation are under Full texts below. 4 Sept (R1010). The French fleet has left Messina. It was said to be bound for Brindisi, but its design is to surprise Catania, and “given their great good fortune we must fear the success of whatever operation they undertake” ( debemos temer el logro : the key gives temer , DECODE’s margin transcription tener ). Carpio is dismayed by letters from Brussels that the Prince of Orange raised the siege of Charleroi intempestivamente . 18 Sept (R1011). Balbases reports the effect of Charleroi at Nijmegen, and it is felt in Rome too. Those ill-disposed to Spain spread the rumour that Spaniards were raising men by force for Sicily; the populace has insulted and stoned Spaniards in the streets for more than fifteen days, and the Pope does nothing. Militia cavalry is brought in and more guns are mounted on Castel Sant’Angelo. Carpio contrasts this with the French: when their galleys were last at Civitavecchia they pressed more than a hundred men aboard, “without sparing the reapers on their way to work in the fields”, and Rome tolerated it. 25 Sept (R1009). The rumours were false and fomented by Spain’s enemies, yet the Pope applied no remedy and would not even inquire. After conferring with the cardinals of the Spanish party, Carpio has reported to the viceroy of Naples and the governor of Milan and awaits their answers. 2 Oct (R1006). The Pope and his ministers still give no satisfaction; Carpio awaits the governor of Milan’s advice before taking a final resolution with the cardinals of the party. The French fleet and galleys, after keeping station off Catania, are said to have turned back towards two places that are uncertain, probably Toulon and Hyères, the galleys badly knocked about. 9 Oct (R1007). “This government” still withholds the satisfaction owed. Carpio waits for the viceroy of Naples’ answer and, on the cardinals’ advice, keeps away from the Pope’s audiences. 16 Oct (R1008). Nothing new: the government stands firm, and Carpio will not move until the King’s orders arrive. 4 Dec (R1002). On the King’s orders he asked Innocent XI for an audience on Tuesday 30 November and again on 1 December. Both times the Pope refused, without giving a reason, and said the King’s business should go through a cardinal. Carpio will not ask again nor treat the principal business until this point is settled, “a point as unbecoming to His Majesty’s service as the first”. 11 Dec (R1003). The loss of Freiburg (taken by Créqui, 16 November) may change the plan of the winter quarters, the Duke of Lorraine having to recross the Rhine, and leaves Flanders in a miserable state. On the audiences he recalls the two refusals already reported; he has not asked again and waits for the advice of the Marqués de los Vélez, viceroy of Naples.
carpio1677.html#method

DECODE’s ciphertext transcriptions (by RP and MEG, 2020) were parsed into tokens. The 4 September letter has a legible marginal decipherment, and lining its first lines up against the cipher showed the layout. The letter pairs looked like Spanish syllables with the wrong consonant. ca 9 [42] ca gi 24 against “va a imbadir” fixed a = 9 and r = 24, and 36 = na in both Mecina and encaminava. The rows of five followed from 33 mi, 36 na, 39 no and 48 ri. Every token of all ten letters was then tallied in context, which settled the consonant changes ( gi-os Dios, lu-ar-de guarde, ne-lo-cios negocios). The decoder ( targets/carpio1677/dec.py ) applies the tables mechanically. The code words were first identified from context and from the historical events they fit: Charleroi, Freiburg, d’Estrées at Turin, Orange in London. The decoder’s output is a stream of syllables, with stray letters where DECODE’s transcription has a slip. A reading audit on 22 October 2026 (George Lasry’s test: the text must form sentences that can be translated) found that only R1004 and R1005 had been written out as Spanish; the other eight had been summarised from the syllable stream. The same day the eight margins were transcribed from the DECODE images, DECODE’s partial margin transcriptions were checked against them, and each margin was aligned word by word with the decoder’s output. The two agree almost throughout. The alignment fixed seven code words ( cen , ren / xen , xin , cun , tin , gen , 110) and struck 14 = ju , and corrected three of the earlier summaries: R1010’s “temer el logro”, the stonings and the Civitavecchia press-gangs in R1011, and the fleet’s return in R1006. Every letter was then written out as Spanish and translated into English; on 23 October 2026 the writer’s spelling was restored word by word from the margins ( agrauios , recivido , governador , bolvio ), without changing a word. All 3,504 cipher tokens are in letters that give continuous sentences; the holes are the few words listed below.
carpio1677.html#what-remains-uncertain

R1006, last sentence: two places the fleet returned to, the code word rin and the spelled vi ve re s . The margin is illegible there on the DECODE scan. Toulon fits the fleet’s return in autumn 1677 and the margin’s capital T (C); Hyères for Vieres is a guess (I). A better image of the original would settle both. R1002: one misread group after “que Dios guarde”; the margin runs on without it, and the words supplied there are a guess at the construction. R1003: one verb (“[dejo]”) written neither in the cipher nor in the margin. The cipher transcriptions are DECODE’s. The margins were transcribed from the images, but the cipher groups were not re-transcribed; a few misread numbers remain as untranscribed tokens ( {..} ) in the raw decoder files, and the margin covers them. Key table: struck 55 (in Papa ) and a few struck numbers ([25], [80]) are each read from context in their letter but not placed in the table. The three code words that were conjectures before the margins were aligned are now confirmed by them: tan = Flandes (R1003), cun iles = españoles (R1011) and lun = cartas (R1010).

As soon as the news arrived, those ill-disposed to Spain spread the rumour that we were raising men here by force for Sicily, and having [thereby] got the populace stirred up against our nation, they have insulted various Spaniards in the streets these days. And although I have proved these rumours false, and the Pope and his ministers are not unaware of it, I have not been able to obtain justice or satisfaction: not only is there [?no move] to punish the seditious, there is [none] to find out the truth either. Such is my forbearance that for more than fifteen days I have been putting up with their stoning the King's subjects, so as to put myself in the right and because I see that their only aim has been to provoke me into a rash step. And they have brought in some cavalry of the militia of this district, and mounted more guns on the Castel Sant'Angelo than there were before. This happens in plain view of the irregularity and inequality with which they treat the French: the last time their galleys were at [?Civitavecchia] they raised more than a hundred men and put them aboard, picking them by force, without sparing the reapers on their way to work in the fields. This is proved, and it was tolerated, the Pope and everyone knowing it better than I. So Your Lordship can infer the just displeasure I am left in, not knowing where these disorders will end, when the use of all the gentlest means is not enough, and I must see to my own safety, to the dignity of my post and to that of the King's subjects. A two-page report of his audience with the Venetian Signoria, in clear, with nine lines in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 148 (the Sforza archive taken to France in 1499–1500). DECODE R7911, catalogued there with no decipherment and no names. The cipher Graphic signs: two to five signs for the common letters, signs for syllables and common words (per, che, con, quale, et), and code words for names ( stat for the Duke of Milan). How it was deciphered With the envoys' own key, an 18th-century copy in Milan headed with their names (Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1597 no. 14, DECODE R5314). A decipherment written at the time over the two lines on the back agrees with it word for word. What it says Venice and Florence wanted to settle with Sforza "the destruction of the Duke of Milan", his losses and their compensation, and a peace with a power hidden behind a code word; and twice Cosimo de' Medici is quoted on what to offer and say. Still open One code word, utinam , which is not on the key copy. The catalogue entry this page closes (no. 1309) also named ff. 151 and 152 of the same volume. Neither has any cipher: see the documents . The Duke of Milan's own cipher slips of the same months, in the same volume, are in another key and have their own page ; so do two Sforza letters of May 1446 , in a third.

f. 148r. The cipher sits in two places: the five lines below the middle, and the two lines at the foot, partly under the library stamp. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 148r, via DECODE R7911. Mazzatinti's inventory of the Sforza papers in Paris (1883) lists three letters from Sforza's envoys at Venice dated 7 December 1446: f. 148 (DECODE R7911): "Lettera di Contucio a Fr. Sforza (Venezia 7 decembre). In cifre." Two pages and an address. Contucio reports his audience: the Signoria will send Ser Pasquale [Malipiero] to the Count as its ambassador, Florence will send another, and he gives the Count's speech of congratulation on the Venetian victories over the Duke's troops, with news from Lombardy. Nine lines are in cipher. f. 151 (DECODE R7912): "di Giovanni Stavoli, M. Giordani, V. Amidani, Agostino, Contucio a F. Sforza", not marked as cipher. The DECODE photograph shows clear leaves only: a heavily corrected minute in Sforza's voice and his letter of the same day from Pesaro to Boccaccino and Nicodemo, with the foot of the envoys' joint letter laid over it. f. 152 (DECODE R7913): the envoys' joint letter of 7 December, all in clear ("Questa matina la Ill. S. ne respose ad lambassiata exposta per mi Contucio ..."), signed by Giovanni Stavoli, Agostino, Contucio, Matteo and Vincenzo. So the cipher of the entry is all on f. 148. The ital. 1583 volume is not digitised by the BnF (microfilm only), and these DECODE images are binarized microfilm scans.

The Milan State Archives keep 18th-century copies of the Sforza chancery's 15th-century keys (Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1597, on DECODE as anonymous key records). No. 14 is headed Angelus cum cifra Vincentij and names its users: Johannes de Stavolis, Augustinus, Baptista, Matheus, et Vincentius . These are Sforza's envoys at Venice in 1446, the men who sign with Contucio. The project had looked at this key in September for another letter and set it aside; in October it turned up on a sibling letter of Angelo Simonetta's from Venice (f. 89, "Cum cifra Vincentii", DECODE R7900), whose clear text is filed with it (f. 90). The key gives two to five signs for most letters (a: o, -o, ϙ; e: ƅ, 5, ʒ; o: four forms of q; u: Π, ⊏, ⊔, E), a table of vowel-and-consonant syllables, fifteen word signs, a column of names ( stat = lo Duca de Milano, Δ = la Signoria Vostra, pp = the Signoria of Venice, ppp = the Count) and nulls. Its code word stat appears twice in f. 148, and the first cipher line reads at once: "tanto per la desfatione del Duca de Milano". The writer draws some signs in his own way (the key's ƅ for e as an h with a hooked bowl, its h for s as a k, its "kp" for q as "xp"); the table is in targets/contucio1446/key.md . f. 148v, lines 5–7: the two cipher lines on the back, with the decipherment written over them at the time: questa · parte · parve · a cosimo · se devesse · dire . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 148v, via DECODE R7911. A hand of the time wrote a decipherment above the two cipher lines on the back. It agrees with the key sign for sign, and it supplies one code word missing from the copy: pec = Cosimo. The recto passages have no such gloss.

At the foot of the page, after the Count's offer to the Signoria (he would give up what little he has left for the Duke's ruin, "as he has done the other times when it was needed for the state of Your Serenity and of the League"): ... quando e bisognato per lo stato dela V. Ser.ta e dela lega. Questa tale oferta parve[?] a Cosimo che in ogni modo se devesse fare. In English. This offer, Cosimo thought, should in any case be made. And on the back, after the Count asks the Signoria where it wants him in the coming season: Essendone advisato fara di buona voglia ogni cosa che debbia essere stato e di piacere ala V. Ser.ta. Ancora: questa parte parve a Cosimo se devesse dire. In English. Once told, he will gladly do whatever is to the state's and Your Serenity's pleasure. Further: this part too, Cosimo thought, should be said. In the war of 1446–47 Venice and Florence were allied with Sforza against Duke Filippo Maria Visconti, who was at the same time trying to win his son-in-law back. The cipher keeps out of reach of a reader the allies' war aims ("the destruction of the Duke of Milan", with Sforza present in person), Sforza's claim for his losses, and the fact that Cosimo de' Medici had a hand in what the envoys offered and said at Venice.

Images: DECODE R7911 (recto, verso, address), R7912 and R7913, fetched in the project's sweep of the ital. 1583 records on 23 October 2026; the key R5314 from the same sweep of the Milan keys. Every cipher sign was transcribed from crops at three to four times size, line by line, as a key value plus a variant number (226 signs, 42 distinct, and one null). Three pairs of look-alikes were told apart on the image: a round u (p) and a box u (u) in line 26, which give "vostra" and "perdeta"; an o with a bar at the left (a) and an o crossed by a bar (et) in line 27; a double t (r) and a double t with a flourish (con) in line 28. Deciphered with decode.py : 225 of the 226 signs take a value from the key or the gloss (99.6%), and every one of them stands in a word of the reading above. The verso passage agrees with the contemporary interlinear decipherment over its 31 signs. Statistical check against a 16th-century Italian letter model ( docs/_validate.py ): the reading scores −1.865 per letter, random keys −4.04 (z 5.6): pass. The key identification was also checked on the sibling pair R7900/R7901: the cipher's "che lo stato de stat " stands where the clear text has "che lo stato del Duca de Milan".

Mostly clear French, with runs of cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3077 no. 23, pp. 145–147 (DECODE R4254, listed there with no decipherment); a copy is Clairambault 328 f. 291 (DECODE R2287). Catalogue item 4, where the BnF notice gives no year. The cipher Du Bellay’s first cipher: drawn signs, with meaningless sign groups and uncoded phrases shut between two fixed marks that cancel them. It is not the cipher of his letters of 1529. How it was deciphered V.-L. Bourrilly and P. de Vaissière recovered the lost key and printed the letter in clear in 1905. George Lasry solved the cipher again in 2022. Here the letter was dated and matched to the edition; no key was applied. What it says Du Bellay expects no peace from the Emperor’s envoys if the divorce goes ahead: the Queen has said privately that the Emperor would then never rest until he had ruined the King of England. Credit Bourrilly and de Vaissière (key and text, 1905); George Lasry (the cipher solved again, 2022); Satoshi Tomokiyo (who published Lasry’s key). Until 14 October 2026 this letter shared a page with du Bellay’s letters of 1529, which are in his cipher of that year, a different cipher, with their own page .

BnF fr. 3077 binds du Bellay’s despatches to Montmorency by day and month across several years, and the notice for no. 23 reads only “avec chiffre, XXVIIIe d’octobre”. Its content dates it to 1528, the first year of du Bellay’s embassy: Campeggio’s reception by Henry VIII, the two legates’ first interview with Queen Catherine, Montpezat’s coming. Bourrilly and de Vaissière print it as no. 156 of Ambassades en Angleterre de Jean du Bellay (1905), pp. 430–434; it is also in Le Grand’s Histoire du divorce III (1688) pp. 188–192 and calendared in Letters and Papers IV 4879. The clear text opens Monseigneur, je croy que me pensez si peu paresseux es affaires du Roy . fr. 3077 p. 146: “par mer. Quant a moy, Monseigneur,” then the cipher. Some of the clear words between the runs are in Bourrilly’s text ( je tiens de bon lieu que ); others, such as et la seigneurie de Venise and du port de Savonne , are not, and look like the cancelled decoy phrases his note describes. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3077 p. 146, via DECODE R4254 (crop P6).
dubellay1528.html#cipher

Bourrilly’s editors describe it in a note (p. 432): it is the first cipher du Bellay used, and only two of his letters in it were known to them, this one and one of 28 May 1529. They found its key, which was lost, but could not identify with certainty the persons meant by some signs that occur only once. To make it harder, the ciphered text is broken at intervals by groups of meaningless signs, or by uncoded phrases about other business, each shut between two marks that act as brackets and cancel what they hold. They did not print their key. George Lasry solved the cipher again in 2022, on Clairambault 329 f. 9, a letter annotated as du Bellay’s. Satoshi Tomokiyo, who published the solution on Cryptiana (“Bayonne’s Cipher (1528–1529)”), notes that the same key fits Clairambault 328 f. 291, the copy of this letter, and that it differs from the cipher of du Bellay’s 1529 letters. That is why DECODE’s note on R2287 says Tomokiyo’s 1529 table does not fit.
dubellay1528.html#reading

From Bourrilly’s text. After a clear sentence on the Emperor’s two envoys with offers of peace, one by land and one by sea, du Bellay writes that if the marriage goes ahead he does not expect peace through them. He has it from a good place that the Queen said in private that, if it does, the Emperor will never stop until he has ruined the King of England, even if he had to give the King of France back his sons on reasonable terms to do it. He then wonders whether something could be worked up through the Duke of Gueldres or Margaret of Austria, and warns that the Pope is not to be trusted, leaning as he does on the English.
dubellay1528.html#open

Nothing in the text: the 1905 edition prints the cipher passages in full. Here, no transcription was made and no key applied, so this page has no sign-by-sign replay. Neither key is printed: Bourrilly’s is lost again, Lasry’s is an image on Cryptiana. The letter of 28 May 1529 in the same cipher and Clairambault 329 f. 9 were not opened.

Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba’s price for taking the fleet against the Turk: harbours in Italy for his sick, wounded and stores (BnF Espagnol 318 no. 92). The cipher is the Cifra general printed by Galende Díaz, confirmed against a later hand’s interlinear glosses; about three quarters of the letter is deciphered with it. The volume’s other ciphered letters, in other ciphers, have their own pages. h boy · zez · xiz 7 · xuy · baz · xix zol · xup · zuy · zik · bob · yuy y tiempo · por · estar · en · tanto · el negoçio · de · puede · no · que · lo Naples → Venice · homophonic symbol alphabet with CVC code groups, the Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos · 17 August 1500 · known key applied, partial The Great Captain to Lorenzo Suárez, 17 August 1500 (Espagnol 318 no. 92) from Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba Go to the transcriptions ↓ Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba’s price for taking the fleet against the Turk, in the Catholic Monarchs’ general cipher; the key, proved against a later hand’s glosses, gives a value to about three quarters of the words, but the decode does not yet build sentences: decoded, not read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 17 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Credits · Juan Carlos Galende Díaz (key or decipherment used) · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source, key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, the Great Captain, to Lorenzo Suárez de Figueroa, Spain’s ambassador at Venice, 17 August 1500. This is the copy sent to the secretary Almazán. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 318 no. 92, f. 116r–v (Gallica, canvases 440–441). It is one of five ciphered letters in the volume, catalogue item 9. The cipher The Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos : invented signs for letters, up to five for a vowel, mixed with three-letter code groups (683 in the key) for words and names. How it was deciphered Galende Díaz printed the key in 1994 and Tomokiyo assigned the letter to it. A later hand’s glosses between the lines confirm it: eight words, no misses. Both pages were then transcribed and deciphered with the key. What it says He will take the fleet against the Turk, but at a price. He wants harbours in Italy for his sick, his wounded and his stores, as the Pope had given him before. Still open Six code groups that contradict the printed key, and about ten stretches of letter signs. With them, f. 116r ll. 8–11, 16, 18–21, 26–31 and 34 are sign strings rather than sentences, so most cipher sentences have holes and the letter is decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026); “What it says” is a gist. Other letters The other ciphered letters of the volume use other ciphers and have their own pages: no. 5 (Escrivà’s cipher), no. 95 (Lasry’s alphabet) and nos. 93–94 (key not identified).
esp318.html#five

The volume (ark btv1b52503046q , 486 canvases, 127 folios) is the autograph collection of the Ruffo di Scilla princes, sold in 1854 and bought by the BnF in 1857; Morel-Fatio catalogued it in 1892 as no. 172. Its hundred items are letters to Ferdinand and Isabella from most of the crowned heads of Europe. Five are wholly or partly in cipher, and the catalogue had listed four. Until 14 October 2026 this page covered all five. They use at least four different ciphers, so each now has its own page: Item ff. Letter Cipher Page no. 5 5–6v Federico III of Naples to the Catholic Monarchs, San Germano, 11 Jan 1497 Joan Ram Escrivà’s cipher no. 1 federico1497 no. 92 116–116v Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba to Lorenzo Suárez, 17 Aug 1500 Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos this page no. 93 118–118v Lorenzo Suárez to the Catholic Monarchs, Venice, 24 Feb 1504 not identified esp318no93 no. 94 120–121v The viceroy of Sicily to Ferdinand, Messina, 27 Apr 1503 not identified esp318no93 no. 95 122–122v Unaddressed cipher, 8 Jan 1497 George Lasry’s 2022 alphabet esp318no95 All five are in one office’s style. A cipher of Ferdinand’s secretariat is two things at once: a homophonic alphabet , three to five invented symbols per letter, and a nomenclator of two-, three- and four-letter groups ( consonant, vowel, consonant ) written in ordinary Latin letters in the same hand, standing for words, names and syllables. The nomenclator is one-part: the vocabulary runs alphabetically and the groups run in a fixed order beside it, so the initial letter of a group tells you roughly where in the alphabet its plaintext sits.
esp318.html#no92

F. 116 is headed by its sender, la respuesta q[ue] enbio a los s[eño]res en xbij de ag[osto] 1500 , and opens in clear: Muy mag[nifico] Señor: a los xiiij d[e]l presente recebi v[uest]ra letra con hun breve d[e]l papa y otras dos cartas del embax[ad]or veneçiano con uno suyo, dando priesa en my yda a la resistençia del turco. E porq[ue] esto es conforme a la voluntad e mandami[ento] q[ue] yo tengo de sus al[teza]s, en virtud de Jhu Xpo yo me dispongo a ello con toda la celeridad y presteza q[ue] el caso requiere… and then alternates clear and cipher for two pages. It is Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, the Great Captain, writing to the Lorenzo Suárez of the notice (Lorenzo Suárez de Figueroa, Spain’s ambassador at Venice until his death there in 1506, whose own ciphered letters Galende Díaz lists), about the expedition against the Turk. This is the copy kept for the secretary Miguel Pérez de Almazán. Tomokiyo’s page on the Spanish ciphers notes that the Great Captain “used this cipher” (Ferdinand and Isabella’s general cipher of about 1500–02) in this letter, and lists the letter itself as having no known decipherment. This could be tested, because a later hand wrote a partial decipherment between the lines of f. 116r. The glossator deciphered a few words and stopped; his words are the control. BnF Espagnol 318 f. 116r. Between the two ciphered lines, in a later and lighter hand, y tpo — por — estar — en — tanto . They gloss the line below: h boy zez xiz 7 xuy baz . In the printed key boy is Tiempo , zez Por , xiz Esta , xuy En , baz Tanto ; 7 is the alphabet’s r and h its e , the conjunction the glossator spelled y . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 318 f. 116r, via Gallica (btv1b52503046q). Juan Carlos Galende Díaz printed the key in 1994, from a file of twelve ciphers in the Real Academia de la Historia (B.R.A.H. 9/15): his appendix 1 is the Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos , ff. 7–9 of that file. Checked against the glosses, its plates give eight independent matches and no conflict: Gloss on the leaf Cipher In the printed key lo yuy Lo y · tpo h · boy (alphabet e ) · Tiempo por zez Por estar xiz + 7 Esta + r en xuy En tanto baz Tanto el negoçio xix zol El · Negocio de xup De puede zuy Puede no zik No — bob Que A gloss-anchored line then decodes straight through: ct h boy zez xiz 7 xuy baz ff k … pt y tiempo por esta r en tanto p g … giving …y tiempo, por estar en tanto… , which is what the glossator wrote above it. F. 116v ends half in clear, and the codes sit inside sentences whose sense is clear without the key: …no desconfio que mucho se pudiera aprovechar … esta var … zin se ha ofreçido … yo me desnudo y descargo y me satisfago en que n[uest]r[o]… , with zin = Nápoles , xar = después , biz = toda , xuy = en . Below that a later inventory hand: Inventº 11 Ottº 53 . The key is transcribed here as keys/cifra_general.txt : 683 code groups from the plates (pp. 167–173), plus the twenty-one personal signs: Papa = A, Emperador = B, Rey de Françia = F, Rey de Spanya = G, Reyna de Spanya = 4, Principe de Spanya = C, Rey de Inglaterra = S, Rey de Napoles = □, Duque de Calabria = R, Infanta doña Juana = oTT, Don Fadrique prinçipe de Altamira = S†.
esp318.html#the-reading

Both pages were transcribed line by line on 21 September 2026, 36 lines on the recto and 11 on the verso, against the symbol alphabet Galende prints on p. 167. The hand leans on a few forms the specimen line had not shown: the fifth form of A (a reversed C with a hash) and the fifth form of E (a q with a k written below it) carry most of the vowels, the crossed T is the key’s “duplicate” sign for LL ( vituallas , Pulla , llamó ), and the clear hand’s con- abbreviation turns up inside the cipher ( contenté con el , con color de ). About three quarters of the words are deciphered. On 23 October 2026 the line table was written out as running Spanish with the clear passages ( texts/f116_running_reading.md , English texts/f116_en.md ); it is a partial reading, with unread groups in brackets. Two passages: Mas parece me que si buena obra como esta, con tanto diferencia e trabajo desto armada, no deve pasar caso, solo cargo, sin grande remuneracion. … que sera bien que nos de [?nardo] aquella se […] puertos de Italia donde esta armada se pueda recoger quando el tiempo lo requiriese, por no aver de bolver tan lexos, para si al tiempo menester ha de aprovechar, y aun para poner nuestros dolientes y heridos y ropa e vituallas, y estos navios si les […] reparar algo. De manera que podamos estar a […] nuestro, sin los ynconvenientes de estar en casas agenas; [?adelante] crecer; y el parescer no se [zog] […] esta [?demandado], por que quando el me llamo para el cerco de Ostia le demande lo mismo por [?medio] de Garcilaso, y lo ovo por bien “But it seems to me that so good a work as this, with so much difference and labour of this fleet, should not pass as a mere duty without great reward. … that it will be well that they give us […] ports of Italy where this fleet can shelter when the season requires, so as not to have to go back so far, … and also to put our sick and wounded, and clothing and victuals, and these ships, if they […] to repair something. So that we may be at […] ours, without the inconveniences of being in other men’s houses … because when he [the Pope] called me to the siege of Ostia I asked him the same through Garcilaso, and he was content.” The group zems , first taken for a misprint, is Galende’s Ostia after all: the 1497 siege for Alexander VI. Lines 31–32 give “ciudad … [?Tarachina]” (Terracina). Lines 8–14 and 18–21 still do not build sentences, so the letter remains decoded, not read. That is Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba bargaining with Venice, through the Spanish ambassador there, before the joint campaign against the Turks at Cephalonia in the autumn of 1500: he will bring the fleet, but he wants Italian harbours of his own for it, as the Pope had given him. The full line-by-line transcription and decipherment are in f116_reading.md . Two outside checks. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page carries, commented out in its source, his own partial decipherment of the opening, “[paresce?] me que tan buena obra como esta con tanto diferencia e trabaio desto armada no deve pasar caso solo cargo sin grande [r]emuneración” , which corrects three groups first taken for misprints here: zap is zag = me , bac is vac = armada , and xie = cargo as printed. Sanuto’s Diarii (vol. III, cols. ~708–709) report the same demand from the Venetian side eight days later: the Spanish ambassador told the Venetian envoy in Rome that Gonsalvo wanted a cruciata , precedence, “qualli porto li piace a li bisogni” and victuals; off Corfù in October he told the Venetian proveditor he wanted a harbour “seperato” from theirs. A third pass tested Sanuto’s terms ( cruciata , jubileo , precedence) as cribs on recto lines 8–11. They are not there, since those lines weigh whether the enterprise suits Their Highnesses, but the pass settled zie as parescer , the value Tomokiyo guessed: zie followed by the letters R I A and tener gives pareceria tener , and the same value fits all five places. Lines 8–11 now decipher as si empresa a propósito de sus altezas … no hablo en ello … segun la necesidad dellos ay … en semejante acatamiento pareceria tener mas respeto a … .
esp318.html#open

Six code groups still contradict Galende’s printed values wherever they stand: bog (three times, printed Rey de Portugal , probably boz = todo ), and zeb , xob , zer , zog , bue (twice); zems , once among them, was settled as Ostia on 23 October 2026. Either the 1994 plates misprint them, as they visibly misprint others, or the letter used a variant copy of the table; the manuscript, BRAH 9/15 ff. 7–9, which is not digitised, would settle it. About ten stretches of letter signs are also unplaced (grade I), mostly where the q-shaped N and the reversed-9 S cannot be told apart at this resolution. Words in the blockquote are grade C where the signs are certain and the Spanish runs, M where a word was completed from context. The share of about three quarters is an estimate by line from the prose reading; no token count was kept.
esp318.html#method

Almost all of the work was bibliographic, and the order mattered: shelfmark first, cipher second. Searching for the cipher family found Galende Díaz’s appendix, which is the key; the interlinear glosses proved it; the reading is transcription against the printed alphabet. No key was recovered here. Line pitch comes from the autocorrelation of the ink profile (113 px on f. 116r), and three-line half-width strips at 2.6–3× are the readable unit for this hand. The replay below follows the steps recorded for this letter.

Galende prints *Mercadoria* against `zie` and *Paresce* against `zix`; either his plate slips or the table the secretariat issued differed. * l. 8 *si empresa a propósito de sus altezas* (`xuy` + P R E S A, the ß sign = P); l. 9 *no hablo en ello* (crossed T = LL again); l. 10 *segun la necesidad dellos ay*; l. 11 *en semejante acatamiento pareceria tener mas respeto a* (`vog` = *acatamiento* as printed; `zer` read as `zec` = *mas*, r and c being close in this hand). ## Open points 1. (23 Oct 2026: `zems` = *Ostia* fits after all, "el cerco de Ostia"; see texts/f116_corrections.tsv.) Codes still not resolved after the second and third passes (which settled `zap` = `zag`, `bac` = `vac`, `xie`, `zie` = *parescer*, `vog`, and `zer` as `zec`): `zeb`, `zems`, `xob`, `boe`/`boc` in l. 8, `bog` (×3; probably `boz` = todo), `bue`, `bi?`, `yeb`+R A in l. 10. 2. Stretches of letter signs not resolved: ll. 11, 18, 20, 21, 27, 28, 31–32, 34, 36 of f. 116r; f. 116v l. 10. 3. The q-with-o sign reads R in *remuneración*/*remito* and N in *necesidad* (v4, v9): either two signs the eye merges at this resolution or a scribal slip. 4. The personal-symbol and duplicate tables (p. 167 *Duplicate*, p. 173) were not needed except for LL (Ŧ). Status: read in part. The subject, the argument and about three quarters of the words are secure; the remainder needs a sign-by-sign pass at higher magnification, or a comparison with BRAH 9/15 ff. 7–9 itself for the misprinted codes. A leaf of dense signs with no clear word (BnF Espagnol 318 no. 95), dated 8 January 1497. George Lasry recovered its homophonic alphabet from the ciphertext alone with CTTS and in October 2026 deciphered the whole recto; Michael Brackx deciphered the verso with the same alphabet. Famine, the French bid for the city’s silk workers, the King’s slowness and the cardinal of Santa Cruz’s peace mission. Five name codes stay unidentified. ÷ ϵ ʮ def ϟ π ⁷ ≐ · x ʮ ϵ σ x ϟ ϟ x del [def] no se … en Alemanna N = ϟ · O = π · L = ʮ · A = x Unaddressed, from Italy · homophonic symbol alphabet with code groups, George Lasry’s 2022 reconstruction · 8 January 1497 · key recovered by George Lasry An unaddressed Spanish cipher of 8 January 1497 (Espagnol 318 no. 95) Go to the full text ↓ A leaf of dense signs about famine, the French and a peace mission to France. George Lasry recovered its alphabet from the cipher alone and has now deciphered the whole leaf, recto and verso; Michael Brackx’s earlier reading of lines 14–33 and the verso agrees with it but for four words. Measured on its words, Lasry’s reading builds coherent sentences but stays under the 95% bar at 91.5% (code groups read from context count as supplied words); the 2022 lines 1–13 measure 88.0%. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) With George Lasry (solution, key or decipherment used, earlier solution) and Michael Brackx (solution, key corrected, pointer to a source) · Also credited · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (100% of the cipher) The letter An unaddressed Spanish cipher letter from an Italian city with a Señoría, dated 8 January 1497, three days before Federico of Naples’s letter in the same volume. Wholly in cipher except the date line and signature on the verso. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 318 no. 95, f. 122r–v (Gallica, canvases 458–459). Part of catalogue item 9. Not on DECODE. The cipher A homophonic alphabet of 43 invented symbols for 21 letters, one to four each, and 11 code groups written in ordinary letters ( bac , bnh , bon …) for words and names. How it was solved George Lasry transcribed the leaf in CTTS and recovered the alphabet with its built-in cryptanalysis (2021–22); in October 2026 he corrected two values with Claude Opus 5.5, read the code groups from context and deciphered the whole recto, then the verso (pull request 85). Re-checked here mechanically and statistically. What it says Bread cannot be had even for money; the French court the city’s silk workers with trade licences; the King provides “muy tarde y muy poco”; the Pope wants the cardinal of Santa Cruz to seek peace in France; the writer asks for a force to defend the city. Credit Key and complete reading by George Lasry (pull requests 75, recto, and 85, verso). The first full reading of lines 14–33 and the verso by Michael Brackx (issue #63), now superseded, which Lasry’s confirms almost everywhere. Still open Five name codes, used once each; three tentative readings; one word at a burn hole; the year of the clear date. Other letters The other ciphered letters of the volume use other ciphers and have their own pages: no. 92 (the Cifra general ), no. 5 (Escrivà’s cipher), no. 93 and no. 94 .

Y [null?] de lo de aquí no ay que dezir, remitiéndome a lo dicho, sino que crece cada día la carestía, y espérase que no se podrá aver pan por dinero ni sin él. Y los franceses traen muchas vituallas y licencia para los que hazen la seda, que es un tercio desta [ciudad] , que puedan mercadear en Francia; y piensan con estas dos cosas traer esta [gente] a su opinión. Y junto con esto diz que vienen con la más [gente] que pueden, y aun dinero; y [aunque?] el [rey] provee como suele, muy tarde y muy poco, todo lo quiere conplir con palabras. Y la Señoría parece que está dispuesta en esto, porque le toca mucho, pero espera a que el [rey] haga. [y?] Con esto están las cosas en no buen estado. Y a micer Juan Luys avemos traído acá con harta fatiga, y muestra que está enemigo de Francia. Y el [rey de romanos?] cada día trata con estos que goviernan y les promete muy grandes cosas, pero no creo que se concertarán, pues que de todo me dan parte, aunque del [rey] se encubren. Y parece que se quieren governar como [Name1?] se sirva, y en al (?) grandes malos pensamientos contra el [rey] . No sé si pornán algo por obra. Y creo que Claver avrá sentido algo; lo escrevirá a [Name2?] . Y yo estorvo quanto puedo el daño del [rey] , pero no puedo hablar en ello sino con mucha dificultad. Y el [papa] diz que quiere que el [cardenal] de Santa Cruz vaya a Francia a procurar paz. Y ciertamente, para alcançarla qual conviene, lo mejor sería que la Liga hiziese lo que deve, para que [Name3?] por allá hiziese lo que puede, y así el [rey de romanos?] rogaría a los que le ruegan; de otra manera pienso que causará esto más daño que provecho. Devría [Name4?] mandar a [Name5?] que, si necesario fuese, viniese aquí a defender esto, pues si se perdiese, lo … [f. 122v] … que Dios no quiera, no avía cosa segura en Ytalia. Y del [rey de romanos?] no sé que diga, sino que está en Alemaña; y no supo nadie de su ida, ni ay esperança de su venida. A viij de enero [year not legible]. [rubric] English translation (George Lasry) And [null?] of matters here there is nothing to say, referring myself to what I wrote before, except that the dearth grows every day, and it is expected that bread will not be had for money or without it. And the French are bringing in many victuals, and a licence for those who make silk, who are a third of this [city] , to trade in France; and with these two things they mean to bring these [people] over to their side. And besides this, it is said that they are coming with as many [troops] as they can, and money too; and [although?] the [king] provides, as he usually does, very late and very little, he wants to settle everything with words. And the Signoria seems well disposed in this, because it concerns it greatly, but it is waiting for the [king] to act. [And?] With this, things are in no good state. And we have brought Messer Juan Luys here with great difficulty, and he shows himself an enemy of France. And the [King of the Romans?] deals every day with those who govern and promises them very great things; but I do not believe they will come to terms, since they tell me everything, although they hide from the [king] . And it seems that they want to govern themselves as [Name1?] pleases, and [have?] great evil designs against the [king] . I do not know whether they will put anything into effect. And I believe that Claver will have sensed something; he will write it to [Name2?] . And I hinder the harm to the [king] as much as I can, but I cannot speak of it except with great difficulty. And the [Pope] says that he wants the [Cardinal] of Santa Cruz to go to France to procure peace. And certainly, to obtain it as it should be, the best would be for the League to do what it ought, so that [Name3?] over there would do what he can, and so the [King of the Romans?] would entreat those who entreat him; otherwise I think this will do more harm than good. [Name4?] ought to order [Name5?] to come here, if it were necessary, to defend this place, for if it were lost, … [f. 122v] … which God forbid, nothing in Italy would be safe. And of the [King of the Romans?] I do not know what to say, except that he is in Germany; and nobody knew of his going, nor is there any hope of his coming. On 8 January [year not legible]. [rubric] Lasry’s 2026 key corrects two values of his 2022 table: the small solid circle is z , not b ( dezir, hazen, diz, paz ), and the ℓ-shaped symbol is r , not s ( aver pan, micer, Claver ). His recto agrees with every correction Michael Brackx had proposed to the 2022 lines 1–13 (section 03), and with Brackx’s reading of lines 14–33 except rogaría a los que le ruegan (Brackx: logaria … llegan ), para que ( parece que ) and Claver avrá ( Claue haura ). His verso (pull request 85, the fourth photograph f122v) agrees with Brackx’s (section 04) except no sé que diga ( que siga ); it has the King of the Romans gone to Germany, which supports reading dif (written def on the verso) as Maximilian I. The leaf spells the country alemanna (Lasry’s own decryption, and Brackx); his edition prints Alemaña , normalising nn to ñ as it does in daño . The edition is left as he has it; whether to keep the leaf’s spelling is a question for him. Lasry’s key as revised in 2026. Readings with a question mark are tentative; [NameN?] are unidentified names. Image: George Lasry, CTTS key snapshot for BnF Espagnol 318 f. 122r. Checked here on 24 October 2026, after pull request 85: decode.py applies the key file to Lasry’s transcription and gives 1,364 symbols, 1,246 on the recto (the two lines photographed twice are now transcribed once) and 118 on the verso, every one with a value. Statistically ( docs/_validate.py , Spanish letter model, code groups left out) the reading scores −1.97 per letter, against −5.99 for random keys of the same shape (7.8 standard deviations lower) and −3.44 for a key fitted to the same symbols shuffled (43.9 lower). Verdict: pass.

F. 122 is a single leaf of dense signs, 31 lines by the segmentation (33 line bands as Brackx cuts them), with four more cipher lines on the verso above a clear date line and signature. It has no address and no salutation. In May 2022 George Lasry sent Tomokiyo an “approximate” solution, and Tomokiyo published it as two images. One is the alphabet, one to three signs per letter, with a row of unassigned signs and the code groups bac bnh bon dah daf dae oht bed dal boo del . The other is Lasry’s decipherment of lines 1–13, in red over the scan. Until October 2026 this page said no plaintext had been published. That was wrong: the second image had been missed, and Brackx pointed it out. F. 122r, line 17, from the project’s machine reading of September 2026, with the letter each sign cluster carries printed beneath: …muy grandes cosas … pero no… . Blanks are places where two signs touch. Image: Annotated here on BnF Espagnol 318 f. 122r, line 17 (Gallica).

In September 2026, before Brackx’s reading, the project applied Lasry’s key through image processing, because matching the signs by eye was unreliable (÷ against ≐, three forms of 7). The leaf was binarised and its connected components grouped into 963 glyphs over 31 lines. These were clustered by shape, and the clusters were labelled from contact sheets against the key. The clean clusters give the Spanish frequency ranking (e–a–o–n–s) with no language information. A Spanish 5-gram decoder then filled the uncertain boxes. Three independent decoders agreed on the same two thirds of the recto and failed on the same third, where two signs touch. Two of Lasry’s signs were corrected on the way: the n with a cross-tail is m , not y . The pipeline lives in targets/esp318/ .

ghinucci1527.html#letters

Ghinucci was Henry VIII’s envoy at Charles V’s court in Spain from 1527 to 1529, with Edward Lee and, in 1527, Francis Poyntz. Lee wrote his despatches in an English letter cipher (the Poyntz 1527 page has one). Ghinucci, an Italian, wrote his own Latin reports in a different system of his own. Four of them are on DECODE: R8476 , Cotton Vesp. C III f. 304: Poissy, 24 December 1526. Printed with its deciphered passages in State Papers of Henry VIII VI (1849) pp. 552–556, from the decipherment kept in the Record Office ( L&P IV 2727). R8589 , Vesp. C IV f. 313: Valladolid, 12 February 1529. L&P IV 5282 prints the Latin decipherment of the whole cipher passage. The decipherer struck each null through with a light stroke. R8590 , Vesp. C IV f. 315: Valladolid, 15 February 1529, deciphered between the lines ( L&P IV 5300). R8613 , Vesp. C IV f. 363 (old f. 332): headed “Dupplicata sub die xxii Julii 1527”. The binder’s “1529” at the top is where DECODE’s date comes from. L&P IV 3291 lists it as the duplicate of a letter whose original, Cotton Vitellius B IX f. 127, is damaged (“mutilated”), and describes the duplicate as “partly in cipher” with no decipherment beside it. The editors summarised the original in English. The head of R8613: the clerk’s “Dupplicata sub die xxii Julii 1527”, the binder’s “Hispania 1529”, and the first line of the letter, cipher signs with their superscript digits between clear words ( videntes potissime , Curare et aliqua- ). Image: British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV f. 363r, via DECODE R8613. Another letter bound in the same volume, ff. 214–218, is sometimes grouped with these because its cipher also writes numbers above the signs: Gilino’s report to Francesco II Sforza of 15 September 1527 (DECODE R8572). It is a different, Milanese cipher with its own key and has its own page .
ghinucci1527.html#system

Each base sign stands for a consonant row; the small digit above it chooses the syllable, and the order of vowels differs from row to row, with several digits for some syllables. In the K row (r), 2 is ro , 3 ri , 4 ru , 8 ra , and 7 and 9 are both re . In the L row (t), 2 is tu , 3 ta , 4 te , 6 to , 9 ti . A sign with no digit is a single letter, and not the consonant of its row: bare o is p , bare z is t . Two-digit superscripts (12–19) are mostly nulls, and so are some ordinary signs (L7, struck as a null by the decipherer of R8589). A few signs are code words: L8 Regia Majestas , K5 Rex Gallorum , n2 Caesar , y6 Pontifex , d4 Gallia , x1 Hispania , a reversed c with 7 for Dominatio Vestra Reverendissima . There is no word division. The letters drop doubled consonants ( comisionis , milionem ). The key was recovered in three steps. R8589’s cipher was transcribed and aligned with the Latin that L&P prints, the decipherer’s strokes marking the nulls. That fixed the system and the commonest syllables. R8590’s interlinear added more. Then R8476 (845 signs) was aligned with the italic passages of State Papers VI, which gave the code words and confirmed the rows; all 42 of its struck signs aligned as nulls. The merged table ( key.tsv , about 210 entries) was applied to R8613, and the gaps were filled from R8613’s own context. Each such value was checked wherever it recurs. The scribe of the duplicate was not consistent with the signs. Two forms collapse in the transcription: h is o in oblatum and milliones but s in fratris and spes , as it is throughout R8476; m serves for r and for x . These are marked in the reading below.

Ego quidem parum huic rei fidei adhibui, donec Tarbensis , volens hoc purgare, id iudicio meo magis approbavit: nuncium .N. fratre in domo sua [invento], voluit ipsumque coram Nobis dicere quod circa hoc mandatum fuerat. Ipse autem , non incipiens, ut mihi visum fuit, a principio sed a fine sue commissionis, dixit de Lautrec in discessu ipsius fratris sibi dixisse quod non erat parcendum pro liberatione filiorum, et quod offerret et usque ad millionem . Cum autem, quas audivi, numquam antea fuisset oblatum minus millione , sed bene […] satis plus , nullo modo videtur verisimile quod de uno tantum millione Lautrec ageret, sed potius de millione ultra id oblata , quod etiam satis videtur approbari, quod eo tempore non tamen forsan sibi de Regia Majestate pollicebantur. Videtur etiam satis verisimilitudinis rei dari quod Nobis innuit Caesar , videlicet fuisse petitam longam dilationem ad illos tres milliones solvendos, solutionemque dividendam in plures […] pagas , quod forsan magis Regi Gallorum expediet . Quicquid sit, non dubito D.V.R. de veritate certum lumen habituram. Graves viri putant eum qui a Caesare ad Pontificem mittitu[r] in nulla habere commissionem super eius liberatione, et hic […] divulgari ad obturandum [?ora] obloquentium tam hic quam alibi de Pontificis detentione . A gravi viro intellexi disseminari […] is[?tos] quod D.V.R.ma veniat in Galliam curaturam inter alia ut ecclesia Anglicana et Gallicana a Romana separetur , non quidem durante Pontificis captivitate et ad [?iuvandum] eius liberationem , ut dicitur, […] sed ad perpetuam divisionem . In English. The Imperialists seem above all to want to draw the King’s Majesty to themselves by some means, at least so as to part him from the King of the French; and as long as they persuade themselves they can hope for that, I believe they are thinking of anything rather than peace, even if they were offered better conditions, though for the sake of appearances they say they want nothing else. I am sure that if this hope did not feed them, they could well be expected to come to terms once better conditions were offered; and much more could be hoped, in my judgement, if they did not hold for certain that the friendship and union between the King’s Majesty and the King of the French will not last long. The French seem to want [peace] greatly, if not too much. When they meet the Emperor’s councillors they try to leave some handle by which they or we can always return to talks, and they often press us to urge this on the councillors as if of our own accord, showing openly that they very much want the treaty not to be shut off. From this excessive desire, I believe, came the offer of three millions through Avemaria that the Emperor told us of. I gave it little credit until the bishop of Tarbes, wanting to clear the matter, rather confirmed it: he found the messenger, a friar, at his house and had him say before us what he had been ordered. The friar began not at the beginning but at the end of his commission, and said that Lautrec, when he left, told him that nothing was to be spared for the release of the King’s sons, and to offer up to a million. Since, as I hear, never less than a million had been offered before, it seems unlikely that Lautrec was talking of one million only, rather of a million over what had been offered. The Emperor’s hint to us lends this some likelihood: that a long respite was asked for paying the three millions, and that the payment be divided into several instalments, which perhaps suits the King of the French better. Serious men think that the envoy the Emperor is sending to the Pope has no commission at all for his release, and that this is put about here to stop the mouths of those who speak ill of the Pope’s detention. I heard from a serious man that it is being spread that Your Most Reverend Lordship is coming into France to see to it, among other things, that the English and French churches are separated from the Roman, not only during the Pope’s captivity and to help free him, as is said, but for a perpetual division. Lines 5–7 of the first page: “Bene credo quod nisi” in clear, then hec eos spes nutriret, oblatis eis … pinguioribus conditionibus in cipher, then “satis”. The ten signs of spes nutriret were the last long gap to be settled. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV f. 363r, via DECODE R8613. The content agrees point by point with the English summary that L&P IV 3291 gives of the burnt original: the Imperialists’ wish to separate England from France, the three millions offered through Avemaria, the bishop of Tarbes, the friar, Lautrec and the million for the children, the envoy to the Pope without a commission for his release, and the rumour of Wolsey’s journey to divide the churches from Rome. The summary was known before the work began and was used only as a check; the Latin of the cipher passages had not been recovered before.

Ego quidem parum huic rei fidei adhibui, donec ⟨Tarbensis⟩, volens hoc purgare, id iudicio meo magis approbavit: nuncium .N. ⟨fratre in domo sua [invento], voluit⟩ ipsumque coram Nobis dicere quod circa hoc mandatum fuerat. ⟨Ipse autem⟩, non incipiens, ut mihi visum fuit, a principio sed a fine ⟨sue commissionis, dixit de Lautrec in discessu ipsius fratris⟩ sibi dixisse quod non erat ⟨parcendum pro liberatione filiorum, et quod offerret et usque ad millionem⟩. Cum autem, quas audivi, numquam antea fuisset ⟨oblatum minus millione⟩, sed bene ⟨[…] satis plus⟩, nullo modo videtur verisimile quod ⟨de uno⟩ tantum ⟨millione Lautrec⟩ ageret, sed potius ⟨de millione⟩ ultra id ⟨oblata⟩, quod etiam satis videtur approbari, quod eo tempore non tamen forsan ⟨sibi de Regia Majestate⟩ pollicebantur. Videtur etiam satis verisimilitudinis rei dari quod Nobis innuit ⟨Caesar⟩, videlicet fuisse petitam ⟨longam dilationem⟩ ad illos ⟨tres milliones solvendos, solutionemque⟩ dividendam in plures ⟨[…] pagas⟩, quod forsan magis ⟨Regi Gallorum expediet⟩. Quicquid sit, non dubito D.V.R. de veritate certum lumen habituram. Graves viri putant ⟨eum qui a Caesare ad Pontificem mittitu[r]⟩ in nulla habere commissionem ⟨super eius liberatione, et hic […] divulgari ad obturandum [?ora] obloquentium⟩ tam hic quam alibi ⟨de Pontificis detentione⟩. A gravi viro intellexi ⟨disseminari […] is[?tos]⟩ quod D.V.R.ma veniat in Galliam curaturam inter alia ut ⟨ecclesia Anglicana et Gallicana a Romana separetur⟩, non quidem ⟨durante Pontificis captivitate⟩ et ad [?iuvandum] ⟨eius liberationem⟩, ut dicitur, ⟨[…] sed ad perpetuam divisionem⟩. "D.V.R." is Dominatio Vestra Reverendissima, Your Most Reverend Lordship (Wolsey). ## Translation ⟨The Imperialists⟩ seem above all ⟨to wish to have […], ho[…]⟩ to take care and in some way to hope that by some means ⟨they may draw the King's Majesty to themselves⟩, so that at least ⟨they may separate him from the King of the French; and as long as⟩ he has persuaded himself that he can hope for this, ⟨I believe they⟩ think of nothing ⟨less⟩ than ⟨of peace⟩. And if he offered ⟨them richer conditions⟩, although for a certain show of honesty ⟨they say in words that they want nothing else⟩. I well believe that, if ⟨this hope did not feed them, richer conditions having been offered them […]⟩, it could be hoped well enough ⟨that […] they would come to [?peace]⟩. And much more could be hoped, in my judgement, if ⟨they did not hold it for certain that the friendship and union between the King's Majesty [and] the King of the French will not last long⟩. ⟨The French⟩ seem much, ⟨if not too much, to desire […]⟩. And they strive as much as they can, when they meet ⟨with the Emperor's councillors⟩, since they hold the [?discussion] divided, that some ⟨handle [?be left] by which⟩ they themselves ⟨or we⟩ can always ⟨return to the talks; and they often press us⟩ to insist particularly on this ⟨with the Emperor's councillors⟩ as if on Our own account, showing quite openly ⟨that they⟩ greatly ⟨desire that the treaty⟩ be ⟨not⟩ altogether ⟨excluded⟩. From this ⟨excessive desire⟩ I believe comes the reason why, ⟨through Avemaria⟩, in the past days ⟨the Emperor⟩ told Us ⟨that three millions had been offered⟩, if only that be true. I for my part gave little credence to this matter, until ⟨Tarbes⟩, wishing to clear it up, rather confirmed it in my judgement: ⟨having [found] the messenger N., a friar, in his house, he wanted⟩ him to say before Us what he had been instructed on this. ⟨He, however⟩, beginning, as it seemed to me, not from the beginning but from the end ⟨of his commission, said that de Lautrec, at the said friar's departure⟩, had told him that ⟨nothing was to be spared for the liberation of the sons, and that he should offer even up to a million⟩. But since, from what I have heard, ⟨less than a million⟩ had never before been ⟨offered⟩, but rather ⟨[…] a good deal more⟩, it seems in no way likely that ⟨Lautrec⟩ was dealing about one ⟨million⟩ only, but rather about ⟨a million⟩ beyond what had been ⟨offered⟩; which also seems borne out well enough, since at that time they perhaps did not yet ⟨count on the King's Majesty for themselves⟩. Some likelihood also seems to be given to what ⟨the Emperor⟩ hinted to Us, namely that ⟨a long delay⟩ had been asked for paying those ⟨three millions, and that the payment⟩ be divided into several ⟨[…] instalments⟩, which perhaps ⟨will suit the King of the French⟩ better. Whatever it be, I do not doubt that Your Most Reverend Lordship will have certain light on the truth. Serious men think that ⟨the man who is being sent by the Emperor to the Pope⟩ has no commission at all ⟨concerning his liberation, and that this […] is put about to stop the [?mouths] of those who speak ill⟩, here as elsewhere, ⟨of the Pope's detention⟩. I have understood from a serious man that ⟨it is spread […] by th[?ese men]⟩ that Your Most Reverend Lordship is coming into France to see to it, among other things, that ⟨the English and the Gallican Church be separated from the Roman⟩, not indeed ⟨during the Pope's captivity⟩ and to [?help] ⟨his liberation⟩, as is said, ⟨[…] but for a perpetual division⟩. DECODE R8505, catalogued with no author, date or language, is identified as a French memoir on Henri de Navarre’s party, filed among Stafford’s papers. Its key, a homophonic alphabet of about fifty graphic symbols in which m is written as a group of dots, was recovered from the ciphertext alone. 95.1% of the deciphered characters fall in French words; ten nomenclator numbers for names are open. DECODE has no title, no date, no author, and gives the language as “English?”. The document was identified and transcribed here, and the key recovered from the ciphertext alone; no key or decipherment was found on DECODE, in Tomokiyo or in print. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Credits · Brice Dudout (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · none (key obtained, text not read) The document A French political memoir, L’Estat du Roy de Navarre & de son party en France , dated after 1580. The catalogue paired it with R8501 as “unknown sender to unknown recipient”; R8501 is a separate Stafford despatch ( Stafford, 20 August 1586 ). Where Harley 1582, DECODE R8505; no key or decipherment on DECODE, in the volume’s other records or in print. The cipher A homophonic cipher of about 3,600 symbols over four sides. How it was read Key recovered from the ciphertext alone, with no crib. A control on real French failed the same way as the first runs, so the fault was in the solver. The recovered alphabet had no m or b, which exposed a transcription error: dot groups are m, a closed oval pierced by a stem is b. What it says The prince of Parma, a party of malcontents, an Italian engineer at Lisbon, Beaucaire, Béziers, Carcassonne, Montmorency, d’Épernon. Still open The ten nomenclator numbers, which are names, and about 5% of scattered characters where the ink is faint or two shapes cannot be told apart.

The catalogue item covered DECODE R8501 and R8505, both in BL, Harley MS 1582, both “Non-decrypted” on DECODE (for R8501 this is wrong: a contemporary decipherment exists). Harley 1582 is a made-up volume of state papers, and the two records have nothing in common but the shelfmark. R8501 (ff. 71–72) is cipher in a Stafford despatch of 1586 whose contemporary decipherment is written out in clear on f. 72r. That page was transcribed, and Stafford’s key rebuilt from it, for the neighbouring letter: see Stafford to Walsingham, 20 August 1586 . Nothing there is open. R8505 (ff. 263–264, four images) is the subject of this page. f. 263r: the heading L’Estat du Roy de Navarre & de son party en France , and the first cipher run, which begins in mid-sentence after “Joinct que” and carries the nomenclator numbers ·81· and ·21·. The clear French, which is most of the four sides, surveys Henri de Navarre as a political asset. It gives his two “qualitez”: first prince of the blood, so that his authority can only grow while the king has no children, and chief of the reformed churches of France. It then lists the places he holds and their garrisons in Guyenne, Languedoc, Dauphiné and Provence, the counts and viscounts of his following, the harquebusiers each region can raise, the Catholic party, the German and Swiss alliances, and the marriage question. Internal dates run to 1576, 1577 and 1580; La Rochelle, Brouage and Saint-Jean-d’Angély are current concerns. That places it among Navarre’s embassies to the Protestant powers in the early and middle 1580s (this repository holds the numerical cipher of one of them, in Ségur 1585–86 ), and explains how the paper came to rest in an English secretary’s file.

A homophonic alphabet of about fifty graphic shapes (Greek-looking and geometric forms, written spaced out symbol by symbol with no word division), plus ten nomenclator numbers written between dots (6, 21, 26, 36, 51, 57, 72, 81, 99, 721), which are names and are not decoded. The frequent letters have three to six homophones each and the rare ones one symbol each, an ordinary chancery design of the 1580s. letter signs letter signs a lunate ε, ψ, ∂, ∅, ъ-with-cup m the dot groups (two, three, four dots) b φ (oval pierced by a long stem) n loop-foot stem, σ c ⌠, reversed L, crossbars, + o Π, three-legged Π, &Sha; d #, ⨺, ≢ (three bar-shapes) p hourglass e L, 7, Γ, I q c+y ligature, plain ω f stem with a dot cluster at its upper right r ω with a bar, the same crossed g square bracket, square U s two-bowled ε, η, R, Ƶ, II … h Ω t β, crossed ε, ωſ, F i ∂-loop, 9-shape, y, c, V u ъ, long-s, ϝ l χ, χ with a hanging o y v The dot groups are a letter. Every earlier transcription of these pages, the first pass here included, took the clusters of two, three and four dots for punctuation or word division and dropped them. They are the letter m , which is why the first recovered key had no m. The first attack failed. All four sides were transcribed (about 3,600 symbols) and run through a homophonic solver (simulated annealing) against the repository’s French language models. No French came out. Under English, Spanish and Italian models every language scored alike, the pattern of a solver that has found no key. A control located the fault. Real French was enciphered with a fifty-symbol homophonic key of the same shape and run through the same solver ( control.py ). It failed in the same way, so the obstacle was the solver, not the manuscript. There were two faults: a Sukhotin vowel/consonant constraint that is wrong for a key of this shape, and a temperature scale far too small for log-probability differences of this size. With both corrected the control recovers 100% of its key, and still 95.5% of its characters when 15% of its symbols are randomly corrupted. Transcription noise at the level this manuscript produces is therefore tolerable. The key of the manuscript. The corrected solver returned French at once (“et qu’ils attendent”, “à l’avenir”, “duquel”), and basin-hopping with a word-segmentation objective recovered the alphabet. The key corrected the transcription. A French key with no symbol for m and none for b is impossible. The images were checked again, and the dot groups, φ and the two epsilons accounted for the gap. ff. 263v and 264v were re-transcribed symbol by symbol against the key, changing 29% and 31% of their symbols. On 23 October 2026 f. 263r was re-read on the better images of DECODE R8010, a duplicate record of the same leaves.

The whole memoir, clear text and cipher together with holes marked, is in R8505_reading.md (with English), rebuilt on 23 October 2026. DECODE R8010, a second record of the same leaves with better images, was found that day: f. 263r was re-read sign by sign on it (eight labels corrected), f. 264r compared with it, the clear French of ff. 263r, 263v and 264r transcribed in full, and the versos found to have been labelled the wrong way round (the Languedoc side is f. 263v, the side with the Lisbon engineer f. 264v). The memoir is still decoded, not read: f. 263r builds sentences, but the cipher clauses of ff. 264r and 264v do not (about half the sentences of the whole are clean). [?word] marks a doubtful word, […] an unread place, a bracketed number a nomenclator name. The cipher carries what the writer would not put in clear: a Spanish drift, a marriage, an army of reiters, and the people who might be bought. f. 264v: “… c'est de se rendre ou [?chef] ou instrument principal de la ruine de ceus de la religion, come ainsi soit qu'il ne peut [?desguiser] ce faict …”; “… avec le prince de Parme pour lui rendre les places …”; “… frere craindra qu'il ne releve contre luy un parti de malcontens …”. f. 264v, one passage with its clear context: “Et je scay que des l'an passé le Roy d'Espagne faisoit traicter a la soubz main avec luy par un certain italien qui sert d'ingenieur a Lisbone, dont les letres me sont venues es mains. Maintenant aussi la Roine sa mere va traicter avec luy le mariage de sa fille [?de] Lorraine, pour le reioindre avec [?ceste] maison ennemie de la chrestienté [?et] particulierement de l'estat d'Angleterre, a quoi, veu les pratiques ordinaires de [?ceus] de Guise en Escosse, [6] doit remedier.” The prince in question is the one this paragraph discusses, whose mother is “la Roine”. f. 264v: “… se [?deffiant] du roi son frere qu'il [?ne] la charge d'une armee a sa devotion …”; “… sortir de la une [?armee] de reistres pour la ieter et espandre sur le pais de celui qui la voudroit troubler … tandis que le parti de ceus de la religion demeurera ferme en [72] …”. f. 263v, on Languedoc: “et maintenant iouissant de l'amitie estroite de Monsieur de Mon[?tmorency], auquel la leur est necessaire […] asseurer hors […] places de toute la province de Languedoc, qui est la plus riche e importante de toute la France, estant icelui asseure de Beaucaire sur le Rosne et de la seneschaussee de Besiers […] de Carcassonne”. f. 263r names Espernon in cipher (“Qu'ilz ont plongé devant Espernon et Ioieuse”), and f. 264r has “la guerre […] de nos provinces” among its unread clauses.

95.1% of the 3,551 deciphered characters fall inside French words , measured by Viterbi segmentation against a 37,000-word vocabulary built from the repository’s French corpora. The measure is conservative: sixteenth-century spellings and proper names the vocabulary does not hold count as not deciphered. But it counts characters, not sentences: a word-division search finds short French words in a string of fragments. Read line by line, the cipher clauses do not build sentences (some lines of f. 263v are almost noise), so the memoir is decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). The figure is kept as evidence that the key is real, not as a reading. Two things are left. The ten nomenclator numbers are names. Three have contexts that narrow them: 72 is a country and almost certainly France (“la guere contre ceus dela religion en 72 ”, “demeurera ferme en 72 ”); 81 is a person and probably the King (“le 81 son frere”); 21 is a feminine noun, the League or the army (“ 21 ch[ar]gee dela guere”). None is fixed by the text. About 5% of the characters do not resolve into French words: faint ink, and shapes ambiguous within one family. A note on method, since it bears on the figure. ff. 263v and 264v were re-transcribed symbol by symbol from the images against the recovered key. On ff. 263r and 264r the first-pass transcription was corrected only by a constrained pass. A token could be swapped only between shapes that the second transcription proved confusable (the dot groups and the f symbol, a stem with a dot cluster at its upper right, so a faint stem looks like a bare cluster; φ and the long-s; the two epsilons; the two stem-loops; χ and the hourglass; the three bar-shapes; the bracket and Π), and only where the word model gained clearly. That is 77 tokens, 2% of the text, each listed in emendations_all.txt so it can be checked against the manuscript.

R8505, "L'Estat du Roy de Navarre et de son party en France" (Harley MS 1582 ff. 263-264) decoded, not read A French political memoir, written after 1580, surveying Henri de Navarre as a political asset for an outside reader: his two 'qualitez' (first prince of the blood, chief of the reformed churches), the places and garrisons he holds in Guyenne, Languedoc, Dauphiné and Provence, his following, his alliances and the marriage question; it belongs with Navarre's embassies to the Protestant powers in the mid-1580s. The cipher carries the sensitive clauses inline in the clear French (d'Espernon, Beaucaire sur le Rosne, Besiers, Carcassonne). A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. Transcription f1.txt 1.1|sa faveur. Sir Simonds D’Ewes (1602–1650), the parliamentary antiquary whose manuscripts make up much of the Harleian collection, wrote his private papers in an alphabet of his own. His diary of 1622–24 (Harley MS 481) is partly in it, and a 1915 University of Minnesota thesis deciphered that diary without printing the key. Folio 61 is a small slip mounted on a larger leaf, headed 1635 in ordinary figures, with the margin dates 1635/1636 in clear beside the January entry and a running count in cipher, huc usque xxxii , “thus far 32”, at the end of the August entries. A rule separates the summer entries from those of September and January. The foot of the slip runs under the mount and its last line is cut. Harley MS 286 f. 61: the whole slip, 30 lines. The margin note at the rule is huc usque xxxii ; the last line is trimmed under the mount. Image: British Library, Harley MS 286 f. 61, via DECODE R7759 (image 1).

The images of R7759 were fetched from DECODE; the second image is only the verso showing through. A search of the BL catalogue named D’Ewes. No key to D’Ewes’s alphabet was found in print: the Minnesota thesis on his diary and Notestein’s 1923 edition of his parliamentary journal mention the cipher but give no table. Probable words: a long word recurring on almost every line, <oηSSθ2ro , fits convulsio ; a two-word phrase 9θcηd θSηd fits plena luna ; Xrφφr<rθr2 fits difficilis . The month names and numerals at the start of each line supplied the rest. Checks against the calendar: 3 April 1635 was a Friday ( die Veneris ), 23 April a Thursday ( die Iovis ), 23 May a Saturday ( die Saturni ). The moon was full on 23 April, 19 July and 18 August and new on 2 August, as the slip says. On 25 May (“plena luna”) and 12 June (“decrescente”) it was not; the numerals are unambiguous at high magnification, so these are D’Ewes’s own slips or loose wording. The Autobiography (Halliwell’s edition, 1845) confirmed the start on 3 April 1635 and the count of forty-four fits. Two full transcription passes over line crops: 92.7% of words deciphered after the first, 96.5% after re-cropping the doubtful words at three times the size. Measured on the words of the running Latin reading (October 2026), 89.4% read as sense, under the 95% bar.

In the morning about the ninth hour he had a convulsion. Friday. April 23. In the afternoon he had convulsions twice. Thursday. With the full moon. May 14. At the end of three weeks [?nine] convulsions again. The moon [?then] changed. May 23. Saturday, an open flux. May 25. Between the hours of 12 and 1 he had a convulsion, the full moon being on that day. June 12. With the moon waning [?] he felt the first convulsion. June 13. Another mild [?] convulsion followed. And on June 14 another. July 17. Before the full moon, which fell on the 19th following, two mild convulsions. July 23. Another severe convulsion. August 2. The moon [?then] new, a severe [struck] convulsion. August 3. A mild convulsion in the morning. About the first hour, when he was in the arms of my people, another terrible convulsion, which after dinner [?shook] him with no slight, great trembling. In the afternoon again [?afterwards] another severe convulsion. Aug. 24. In the morning another severe convulsion. Aug. 20. A little after the full moon (which fell on the 18th of this month) three very severe convulsions, in the third of which his mouth was drawn almost to the right ear, which I had never observed before. Where Existing DECODE transcriptions and images. Fagel inventory 5206 is catalogued as digitized copies of deciphered Hellen letters from 1752–1753. How it was tried Existing transcriptions and images were reviewed, parallel texts searched, and the parsing of the earlier attempt audited. No key was recovered and no enciphered passage decoded. What was added The audit found errors that turned uncertain numbers into definite ones, lost some ciphertext and overstated the illegible groups. The previous parser removed question marks before recognizing numbers: 2 1 ? ? , for example, became the definite value 21 . It also counted empty newline fragments as unreadable groups, included the heading year 1752 as ciphertext, and discarded cipher before a cleartext tag on the same line. The letters are provisionally grouped into 1752, 1756 and 1763 code families. The Nationaal Archief catalogue lists collection 1.10.29, Familie Fagel, inventory 5206 as digitized copies of deciphered Hellen letters from 1752–1753 . A matching text for 4 January 1752 could provide known plaintext for reconstructing and checking that letter’s code. The date range alone does not establish that this particular letter is included. During the 20 September 2026 access check, the old scan link returned 404, the catalogue service timed out, and the current viewer displayed an empty content area with a maintenance notice. This was an access failure on that date; it does not show that the documents are permanently unavailable. Open the current archive viewer . De Leeuw’s study points to Fagel 5177 for British decipherments with Lyonet’s additions, and Boerhaave Museum Arch 162-r for Lyonet and Croiset’s account. He reports no Prussian codes broken between April 1757 and October 1763. That makes a surviving Dutch decipherment a less secure expectation for the 1763 letters than for the earlier material; it does not prove that no parallel text survives elsewhere.
hellen1752.html#limits

None of the enciphered passages was decoded. No plaintext value has been verified. The clear passages give context; they are not decipherments. A search of the printed Politische Correspondenz found replies and contextual references, but no matching plaintext for these targets. The next steps are to retrieve Fagel 5206, check the 4 January date and opening against R1953, and use any genuine parallel text to derive mappings that can be tested on further passages. The source images also need a fuller collation of doubtful digits, missing separators and marks. A key catalogued as “Prussia 1746” in DECODE R2824 proved to be for a Dutch envoy going to Prussia, so it was rejected as a Prussian chancery-key lead.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) With Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) and Arya Sanketbhai Patel (identification) At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Don Diego de Ibarra, Spanish agent in Paris, 10 July 1593; three lines in clear, then twenty lines of cipher. Where BnF français 3984 no. 68, f. 145 (Gallica, canvas 268). Catalogue item 19, with three despatches in the Spanish office cipher. The cipher The syllabic cipher of the Duke of Feria and the Count of Mansfeld (1593): numbers for syllables, single signs for letters, three-letter symbols for words. How it was deciphered Tomokiyo’s key image, which cites this folio, was transcribed and applied to a full transcription of the leaf; a shuffled-key control confirms it, and one more value (57 = li ) was fixed by a constrained search. What it says Fragments and a few sentences: waiting for the cavalry, “A mi no me parece que puede con esta gente”, “No estamos desesperados”, danger, “espero en Dios que ha de acudir”, the size of the army in Flanders. Still open Most three-letter word codes ( pra, dur, gar, var, tor, vis, xur … ); seven were fixed on 23 October 2026 from the contemporary decipherment of a sibling letter, f. 130–131. Two numbers the model cannot separate. This letter was filed with three despatches of 1593 in the Spanish office cipher, a different cipher with its own page: Miranda and Sessa, 1593 .
