N.S. = Our Lord (the Pope). --> # R158, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 16 February 1718 (Spagna 364D/5, ff. 63r-66v): English translation ## Translation Your Most Illustrious Lordship will recognise from the enclosed sheets the conduct held by Cardinal Acquaviva because Our Lord has, not refused, but merely deferred the proposal of the Church of Seville, and the steps taken by Our Lord's ministers for the pure and simple [?preservation] of the incontestable reasons that support the Holy See and His Holiness in this business. Three things, besides the protest, have justly increased the bitterness of Our Lord, who hopes that they too can in no way be approved by the King. The first appears from the sheet marked A. It is enough to read it to agree on the strange claim of Monsignor Herrera, as if the Royal Ministers should be free to defend, in whatever manner they please, the alleged and unfounded royal prerogatives so as to burden the Pope, while Our Lord's ministers, on the contrary, were prevented from upholding their own very strong and irrefutable reasons with those acts that are proper to preserve them. To answer protests is a defence granted to everyone, and an unshaken usage among all nations, practised also by Cardinal Corradini in 1710, when he was Auditor, as appears from the sheet marked letter B; and it is indeed a grace and favour that the Pope allowed the one made on behalf of Cardinal Acquaviva to be received by his own ministers in the present case, in which, since no prejudice to the King's rights was implied, as I wrote at length to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with the last despatch, it could have been rejected without any wrong or injury. The second regards the four reasons adduced in the act of protest which is sent marked letter C, made by Monsignor Herrera in the name of Cardinal Acquaviva to Our Lord's Monsignor Auditor, and then executed in the Chancery and registered in that tribunal. Four are brought forward. It is false, in the first place, that the proposals of Churches to which princes have the right of nomination or presentation have never been deferred; and there are many examples of it, it being enough to see the acts of the Consistory to be convinced. As for translations, what is asserted is so false that in earlier pontificates their causes were examined in the Consistorial Congregation, where, when they were not canonical, the translations were rejected; and if for some time now the rigour formerly practised about verifying the said causes has been partly relaxed, which however has not always been so, it is not for that reason that they have been admitted as a matter of course and almost blindly, where not only were the requisites prescribed by the sacred Canons lacking, but circumstances concurred wholly opposed to the granting of the grace requested, as in our case. Secondly, it is not understood to what prejudice of the royal right this deferment tends, which depends on the will of that Court; for, if the Pope is satisfied on the points you know of, or at least about the expulsion of the Bishop of Vich and the administration of the revenues of the mensa of Tarragona, he is disposed, notwithstanding the conduct held here by the Royal Ministers, to cut short all delay. As for the scandal adduced in the third place, it would rather arise in Spain from seeing that the Pope, without any regard to the well-known and most grave innovations, so injurious to all ecclesiastical authority, and before obtaining the due reparation for them, granted those graces which he would hardly grant even when the lay power did not abuse but respected the ecclesiastical, and did not meddle in those things which by every right belong to it alone. Lastly, the fourth reason is sufficiently answered in the counter-protest which is sent marked letter D, likewise registered by Monsignor Auditor in the acts of the Chancery; to which I need only add that Our Lord intends to dispose of the fruits of the Church of Seville during this time of vacancy in such a way that no one can complain that he has applied them to a use contrary to the sacred Canons, much less that he has wished to fatten the Apostolic Camera with them. The third concerns the publication which Cardinal Acquaviva has made of the said protest, even in print, and also with a translation into Italian, as appears from the annexed copy which I send you. The Pope was truly surprised at such a step, it seeming to him that he had proceeded in a way that should not be answered with such publicity. His Eminence knows with how much bitterness, and only compelled by his own duty, Our Lord suspended the proposal of the Church of Seville. He knows that His Holiness deferred the Consistory until Friday to await the ordinary post from Spain, hoping to be able to have with it some news that would have put him in a position to proceed to the said proposal. He knows besides the disposition in which His Holiness was to delay the Consistory, although three examinations of bishops had preceded it, had not the provision of the Church of Nanking forced him, for the reasons already written in the last cipher. On the said publication, the resolutions His Holiness will take for the safeguard of his reasons and those of the Holy See are not known to me. I know well the very great prejudice that has come to Our Lord, even in his own esteem and dignity with foreign nations, from the too cautious and circumspect measures observed solely so as not to displease the King of Spain over the publication of the dreadful failure done to him last year; and I also know that there is in Our Lord's power a quantity of notes written in Cardinal Acquaviva's own hand, with which, and with one in particular of the fifth of August, he assured Our Lord that the ships had sailed and were on their way to help the Christian fleet in the Levant. All these items of news and considerations, which are indicated to Your Most Illustrious Lordship for your instruction and to make timely use of them, make the Pope hope that the Catholic King, knowing Our Lord's most upright intentions, will be willing to take in good part the indispensable necessity in which His Holiness has been of having to suspend the proposal of the said Church, and will move him to supply the Pope with the means by which his royal instances may be satisfied. Se questo si ottiene, può ben essere persuasa V.S. Ill.ma che per l'aggiustamento delle altre pendenze si averà ogni possibile facilità; et il merito che ne riporterebbe il Sig. Card. Alberoni, a cui ne sarebbe giustamente attribuita la principal gloria, distruggerebbe in un istante qualunque sinistra impressione formata contro di lui, e rimoverebbe tutti gli ostacoli che ritengono la Santità Sua dal continuare verso il medesimo le dimostrazioni del suo amore. Certo è che senza di ciò non potrà mai indursi N.S. a fare nuove grazie a un soggetto che, per stare alla testa degli affari di cotesta monarchia, è considerato per autore di tutto il presente sconvolgimento e de' danni che ne derivano alla Christianità et alla publica quiet[e] ... ## Notes - 4185 'impressione' is open in Lasry's key; read from the interlinear ('sinistra impressione'). - The cipher stops at 'quiet' at the foot of f. 145v (so also in the second copy, 364D/10). If this is obtained, Your Most Illustrious Lordship may well be persuaded that every possible facility will be found for the settlement of the other pending matters; and the merit that Cardinal Alberoni would gain from it, to whom the principal glory would justly be attributed, would destroy in an instant any sinister impression formed against him, and would remove all the obstacles that keep His Holiness from continuing towards him the demonstrations of his love. It is certain that without this Our Lord will never be able to bring himself to grant new graces to a person who, for being at the head of the affairs of that monarchy, is considered the author of all the present upheaval and of the harm that comes from it to Christendom and to the public pea[ce] ... Card. Alberoni, come per altro la Maestà Sua intende di fare, vede ben V.S. Ill.ma che il Papa non potrebbe ristringersi alle sole preghiere, doglianze e minaccie fatte nelle lettere che si scrivono in piano. His own duty would oblige him to pass to deeds, and first of all to suspend the effect of those graces which the Supreme Pontiffs his predecessors granted to the Catholic Kings for the sole and only purpose of supplying them with means sufficient to keep the war against the Infidels alive at sea. And in fact the concessions of the Cruzada, of the subsidy, of the millones openly declare the end the Holy See had in granting them, binding them also to the fulfilment of various conditions, such as keeping fifty [4171] etc. in service against the Infidels. Card. Alberoni, come per altro la Maestà Sua intende di fare, vede ben V.S. Ill.ma che il Papa non potrebbe ristringersi alle sole preghiere, doglianze e minaccie fatte nelle lettere che si scrivono in piano. Il proprio debito lo costringerebbe a passare a' fatti, e primieramente a sospendere l'effetto di quelle grazie che li Sommi Pontefici suoi predecessori hanno concedute a' Re Cattolici a solo et unico oggetto di somministrar loro mezzi sufficienti a mantenere per mare viva la guerra agli Infedeli. Et in fatti le concessioni della Crociata, del sussidio, de' millioni dichiarano apertamente il fine avutosi dalla S. Sede nell'accordarle, legandole anco all'adempimento di varie condizioni, come sarebbe il tenere in corso contro gli Infedeli cinquanta [4171] etcetera. Ora, se la Spagna, in vece di fare la guerra agli Infedeli, contribuisse a loro vantaggio, o indirettamente impedendo li progressi de' Principi Cristiani contro di loro, et anco direttamente operando di concerto con gli stessi Infedeli a' danni dell'Imperatore, come potrebbe N.S., senza tradire la propria coscienza e senza fare una macchia indelebile al suo Pontificato, non mettere in opera tutta la sua autorità affinché l'uso e li proventi delle grazie sudette, date per mantenere in mare poderosa squadra a' danni del nemico comune, non si convertissero per l'allestimento e mantenimento di un'[?armata] marittima destinata a' danni dell'Imperatore, con divertirlo dal proseguire le sue vittorie contro il Turco? L'Imperatore, che [...] il Papa perché adempisca quanto gli promise nel Breve de' 16 Febbraio millesettecento 16; come può [?dunque] ritirarsi il Papa dal fare a tanto oggetto almeno quello che, anche prescindendo dall'impegno contratto, per impulso del suo proprio debito doverebbe fare? Conosce N.S. che questa minaccia parrà molto dura costì; conviene però che Ella la maneggi con delicatezza, ma in modo da fare conoscere al Re et al Sig. Cardinale principalmente che il Papa non potrà dispensarsi dall'effettuarla se cotesta Corte non si piega alle amorevoli insinuazioni, preghiere et istanze di N.S. [4322] molto più dura per il Papa la mancanza fattagli l'anno scorso; et il non essersene appunto fatto costì il minimo conto, con un disprezzo [?intollerabile], et il vedersene ogni giorno crescere le conseguenze fatali al ben della Christianità et alla riputazione del Vicario di Cristo, pongono N.S. in necessità o di esiggerne nella forma indicata un pron[to] et subito riparo, o a farne un effetto [...] [4312] da V.S. Ill.ma che un buon successo di questa nostra spedizione farebbe cessare tutti i lamenti che si sono fatti di Lei, e la reintegrerebbe pienamente nel possesso di quella particolar stima et amore con cui l'ha riguardata N.S., il quale ne farebbe provare gli effetti anco ad onta di qualunque contradizione. Il fine principale di questa nostra spedizione e l'oggetto di ogni premura di N.S. tendono a fare rivoltare contro gli Infedeli quel poderoso armamento che la Spagna prepara contro l'Italia. Se questo si ottiene, può ben essere persuasa V.S. Ill.ma che per l'aggiustamento delle altre pendenze si averà ogni possibile facilità; et il merito che ne riporterebbe il Sig. Card. Alberoni, a cui ne sarebbe giustamente attribuita la principal gloria, distruggerebbe in un istante qualunque sinistra impressione formata contro di lui, e rimoverebbe tutti gli ostacoli che ritengono la Santità Sua dal continuare verso il medesimo le dimostrazioni del suo amore. Certo è che senza di ciò non potrà mai indursi N.S. a fare nuove grazie a un soggetto che, per stare alla testa degli affari di cotesta monarchia, è considerato per autore di tutto il presente sconvolgimento e de' danni che ne derivano alla Christianità et alla publica quiet[e] ... ## Notes - 'un'[?armata] marittima': the figures give 'un tanto maritima destinata'. 'come puol unque' read 'come può [?dunque]'. - f. 182r-v: [4322] before 'u molto più dura' and [4312] before 're da VSMma' are open codes; 'in [?] lerabile' read [?intollerabile]; 'un pron [?] et subito riparo' = pron[to]. His own duty would oblige him to pass to deeds, and first of all to suspend the effect of those graces which the Supreme Pontiffs his predecessors granted to the Catholic Kings for the sole and only purpose of supplying them with means sufficient to keep the war against the Infidels alive at sea. And in fact the concessions of the Cruzada, of the subsidy, of the millones openly declare the end the Holy See had in granting them, binding them also to the fulfilment of various conditions, such as keeping fifty [4171] etc. in service against the Infidels. Now, if Spain, instead of making war on the Infidels, were to contribute to their advantage, either indirectly by hindering the progress of the Christian princes against them, or even directly by acting in concert with the Infidels themselves to the Emperor's harm, how could Our Lord, without betraying his own conscience and without making an indelible stain on his Pontificate, not put into action all his authority so that the use and proceeds of the said graces, given to keep a powerful squadron at sea to the harm of the common enemy, should not be turned to the fitting out and maintenance of a maritime [?armament] destined to harm the Emperor, diverting him from pursuing his victories against the Turk? The Emperor, who [...] the Pope to fulfil what he promised him in the Brief of 16 February 1716; how then can the Pope withdraw from doing for so great an object at least what, even apart from the engagement contracted, he ought to do at the prompting of his own duty? Our Lord knows that this threat will seem very harsh there; it is fitting, however, that you handle it with delicacy, but in such a way as to make the King, and the Cardinal principally, understand that the Pope will not be able to excuse himself from carrying it out if that Court does not yield to Our Lord's loving insinuations, prayers and instances. [4322] much harsher for the Pope the failure done to him last year; and the fact that not the least account was made of it there, with an [?intolerable] contempt, and that its fatal consequences for the good of Christendom and for the reputation of the Vicar of Christ are seen growing every day, put Our Lord under the necessity either of exacting a prom[pt] and immediate reparation for it in the form indicated, or of making an effect of it [...] [4312] by Your Most Illustrious Lordship that a good success of this despatch of ours would put an end to all the complaints that have been made about you, and would fully restore you to the possession of that particular esteem and love with which Our Lord has regarded you, who would let you feel its effects even in the face of any contradiction. The principal aim of this despatch of ours, and the object of all Our Lord's concern, tend to turning against the Infidels that powerful armament which Spain is preparing against Italy. If this is obtained, Your Most Illustrious Lordship may well be persuaded that every possible facility will be found for the settlement of the other pending matters; and the merit that Cardinal Alberoni would gain from it, to whom the principal glory would justly be attributed, would destroy in an instant any sinister impression formed against him, and would remove all the obstacles that keep His Holiness from continuing towards him the demonstrations of his love. It is certain that without this Our Lord will never be able to bring himself to grant new graces to a person who, for being at the head of the affairs of that monarchy, is considered the author of all the present upheaval and of the harm that comes from it to Christendom and to the public pea[ce] ... Quest'è assai poco; e pure, oltre all'essere molto conforme a quella distinta pietà di cui il Re fa con tanta sua lode [?professione], e al non disdire punto al suo regio decoro, sarebbe preso da N.S. per qualche sodisfazione della gravissima mancanza fattale l'anno passato, che tuttavia rimane e rimarrà sempre altamente impressa nell'animo della Santità Sua. Veda dunque V.S. Ill.ma di conseguire almeno questo poco, con sicurezza di recare con ciò una non piccola consolazione all'amarezze di N.S. ## Notes - 4123 'distint-' (open in Lasry's key) as in 364D/3 ('più distintamente'), from the interlinear both times. - f. 266r l. 16 the figures give 'lode urro nel ne dels [?]', the interlinear 'lode prossessione?': read [?professione]; l. 17 'upmim [?]' where the interlinear has 'punto'. Same hole: [?word] partly carried. --> # R165, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 17 May 1718 (Spagna 364D/12, f. 266r-v): English translation ## Translation It would be no great thing if, peace being concluded between the Emperor and Spain, the Catholic King took occasion to answer, as every duty and propriety would require, the letter written to him in Our Lord's own hand, by declaring to His Holiness that his fatherly remonstrances too had induced him to lend a hand to the conclusion of the Treaty, so as not to hinder the progress of the Christian arms against the Turk. This is very little; and yet, besides being very much in keeping with that distinguished piety of which the King makes [?profession], to his great praise, and not at all unbecoming to his royal dignity, it would be taken by Our Lord as some satisfaction for the most grave failure done to him last year, which nonetheless remains, and will always remain, deeply impressed on His Holiness's mind. Let Your Most Illustrious Lordship therefore see to obtaining at least this little, with the assurance of bringing by it no small consolation to Our Lord's bitterness. Card. Acquaviva immediatamente dopo la spedizione fatta costì del corriere sotto li 31 del caduto, la mattina del primo stante fece chiamare a sé tutti li Spagnuoli, intimando loro per ordine Regio di dover prontamente ritirarsi da Roma et astenersi di fare alcuna istanza in Dateria o in qualunque altro tribunale di Roma, sotto pena della regia indignazione, e di farne anche risentimento contro li congiunti de' trasgressori. Un ordine sì strano et ingiurioso alla maestà del Papa, eseguito per la semplice dilazione di una mera grazia, in circostanze che la contradizione delle notizie di S. Em.za a quelle dateci da V.S. Ill.ma e dal P. Daubenton circa la richiesta sodisfazione per li fatti di Vich e Tarragona non avevano dato luogo a poter discorrere e convenire insieme su la materia, e già prima non solo che si fosse tenuto il Concistoro, che seguì solamente ier mattina, ma che neanche si sapesse doversi tenere Concistoro, fanno ben prevederci che gli attentati fatti costì contro l'autorità Apostolica averanno nella loro gravezza et atrocità corrisposto a quelli già seguiti in Roma. Ella vede come siamo trattati; onde non si maraviglierà anco per questo capo degli ordini che se le danno con questo dispaccio. ## Notes - 'del caduto': the interlinear; Lasry's 4482 (key_extra 'corrente', marked probable) stands here, as in 364D/3 where the interlinear also has 'del caduto'. 4488 'primo' (open) from the interlinear. - Read from the interlinear where the figures are garbled or the group is mis-valued: 'risentimento' (figures 'riri'), 'Apostolica' (Lasry's 'questo a', as 'Camera Ap.ca' in 364D/5), 'atrocità' (figures 'noro'), 'onde'. No holes. --> # R169, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 9 June 1718 (Spagna 364D/16, f. 320r-v): English translation ## Translation Cardinal Acquaviva, immediately after the despatch of the courier sent there on the 31st of last month, on the morning of the first of this month had all the Spaniards called to him, notifying them by royal order that they must promptly withdraw from Rome and refrain from making any application at the Dataria or at any other tribunal of Rome, under pain of the royal indignation, and of resentment being taken also against the relatives of transgressors. So strange an order, and so injurious to the Pope's majesty, carried out for the simple deferment of a mere grace, in circumstances in which the contradiction between His Eminence's information and that given us by Your Most Illustrious Lordship and by Father Daubenton about the requested satisfaction for the affairs of Vich and Tarragona had left no room to discuss and agree together on the matter, and already before, not only the Consistory had been held, which took place only yesterday morning, but before it was even known that a Consistory was to be held, give us good reason to foresee that the outrages committed there against the Apostolic authority will have matched in their gravity and atrocity those already committed in Rome. You see how we are treated; so you will not wonder, on this head too, at the orders given you with this despatch. Ill.ma sotto li 31 del caduto con lo straordinario speditole costì dal Sig. Card. Acquaviva, le trasmetto per questo espresso il Breve sospensivo de' noti Indulti concessi altre volte, e poi di mano in mano rinovati da questa S. Sede a' Re di Spagna. La sola lettura del Breve medesimo, oltre tutti li fortissimi motivi [?tanto] ampiamente dedottile sì nel mio dispaccio de' due Aprile passato, come ancora nell'ultimo de' 31 Maggio caduto, servirà di sufficiente istruzione a V.S. Ill.ma, ma per ben conoscere che non ha potuto la Santità Sua dispensarsi da venir prontamente ad un tal passo, e la metterà in stato di poterlo altresì giustificare presso gli altri. Stimo per tanto superfluo il diffondermi maggiormente sopra di ciò, perché non potrei se non ripeterle le stesse cose. Solo non posso astenermi di pregarla a riassumere i miei dispacci dal principio di Agosto dell'anno passato, per osservare che, quantunque non prima di adesso eseguisca Sua Santità la sospensione de' sudetti indulti, non è già che egli non l'avesse determinata e creduta necessaria sin da quando gli giunse la certa notizia dell'orrida mancanza fattagli dalla Spagna con trasmettere in Sardegna, e per conseguenza in favore indirettamente degl'Infedeli, quelle forze marittime che erano state promesse e destinate contro di essi; ad effetto di mettere con questo passo al coperto da ogni calunnia l'onore della sua sacra persona, lacerato, come sa pur tutta l'Europa, in tante guise, e sodisfare a quelle parti che in sì grave pericolo del Cristianesimo esigeva da lui l'Apostolico ministero. Non ce ne siamo però mai apertamente espressi, con la fiducia che cotesta Corte fosse alla fine per dare qualche riparo alla gravissima offesa fatta al Papa; non potendosi ciò più sperare, mentre vedonsi proseguire costì gli stessi disegni, non meno nocivi alla Cristianità per l'impedimento che recano alla continuazione della guerra contro il Turco, non ha creduto la Santità Sua di potere differire più oltre l'uso de' rimedii più vigorosi, con sospendere almeno alla Spagna quelle grazie che a solo intuito di promovere efficacemente la guerra contro gli Infedeli le sono state dalla S. Sede concesse; le quali sono per altro sì strettamente legate a questa precisa condizione, che li stessi Re Cattolici, essendone ben consapevoli, sono più volte umilmente ricorsi a' Sommi Pontefici per essere assoluti da quel reato in cui credevano di essere incorsi per avere convertito non solo in uso contrario, ma anco in uso solamente diverso da quello prescritto negli Indulti medesimi, le somme percettene, siccome con evidenza si raccoglie da diversi Brevi di Clemente ottavo e di Innocenzo decimo, de' quali le mando annesse le copie. [...] il Breve dunque in carta pecora, che se le trasmette per ogni occorrenza in tre esemplari, della medesima stampati; e se ne mandano tanti altri parimente stampati quanti sono li Arcivescovi e Vescovi sì della Spagna come dell'Indie, essendosi avuto l'avvertenza di chiuderli negli aggiunti pieghi diretti a' [?sudetti] prelati, affinché V.S. Ill.ma senza questa briga possa più sollecitamente e segretamente dar loro il ricapito, cominciando da quelli indirizzati a' Vescovi più rimoti dalla Corte, incaminando gli altri per l'Indie a quei porti donde più prossima sia per seguire la partenza delle solite navi per quelle parti. Del resto, premendo a Sua Santità sommamente la pronta esecuzione di questo ordine, perché la publicazione di esso segua in tempo da poter produrre qualche frutto, quale sarebbe di far desistere la Spagna da ulteriori pregiudizii alla publica causa della Cristianità, non lascia la Santità Sua sopra di esso alcun arbitrio d'interpretare o sospendere la mente Pontificia; anzi vuole Sua Santità che Ella, eseguendola senza ritardo da qualunque luogo ove Ella si ritrovasse, ci rispedisca immediatamente e subito il corriero con la notizia di avere pienamente data la esecuzione a questa premurosissima Commissione. ## Notes - About twenty-two cipher lines are missing from DECODE's figure transcription (90 of 112), among them f. 322r ll. 8-10 ('La sola lettura ... dedottile'), f. 322v ll. 34, 37 ('in Sardegna e per conseguenza', 'che erano state promesse e'), f. 323v ll. 72-73 ('le somme percettene'), 323v-324r ll. 84-85, 324r ll. 100-102 ('produrre qualche frutto ... pregiudizii alla publica causa'). Same holes: [?word] partly carried, [...] unread. --> # R170, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 9 June 1718 (Spagna 364D/17, ff. 322r-324v): English translation ## Translation Following what I wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship under the 31st of last month by the extraordinary courier sent to you there by Cardinal Acquaviva, I send you by this express the Brief suspending the well-known Indults granted at other times, and then renewed from time to time by this Holy See to the Kings of Spain. The mere reading of the Brief itself, besides all the very strong reasons [?so] amply set out to you both in my despatch of the 2nd of April last and in the last one of the 31st of May, will serve as sufficient instruction for Your Most Illustrious Lordship, so as to understand well that His Holiness could not excuse himself from coming promptly to such a step, and will put you in a position to justify it also to others. I therefore think it superfluous to enlarge further on this, because I could only repeat the same things to you. Only I cannot refrain from begging you to take up again my despatches from the beginning of August last year, to observe that, although His Holiness carries out the suspension of the said indults only now, it is not that he had not determined on it and believed it necessary ever since the certain news reached him of the horrid failure done to him by Spain in sending to Sardinia, and consequently indirectly in favour of the Infidels, those naval forces which had been promised and destined against them; so as by this step to put beyond all calumny the honour of his sacred person, torn in so many ways, as all Europe knows, and to fulfil those parts which the Apostolic ministry required of him in so grave a danger to Christendom. We never expressed it openly, however, in the confidence that that Court would at last give some reparation for the most grave offence done to the Pope; since this can no longer be hoped for, as the same designs are seen being pursued there, no less harmful to Christendom for the hindrance they bring to the continuation of the war against the Turk, His Holiness has not believed he could defer any longer the use of the most vigorous remedies, by suspending for Spain at least those graces which were granted her by the Holy See solely with a view to promoting the war against the Infidels effectively; which are besides so strictly bound to this precise condition that the Catholic Kings themselves, being well aware of it, have several times humbly had recourse to the Supreme Pontiffs to be absolved from the guilt they believed they had incurred by having turned the sums received from them not only to a contrary use, but even to a use merely different from that prescribed in the Indults themselves, as is clearly gathered from several Briefs of Clement VIII and Innocent X, of which I send you the copies annexed. [...] the Brief, then, on parchment, which is sent you for every need in three copies, printed from the same; and as many others likewise printed are sent as there are archbishops and bishops both of Spain and of the Indies, care having been taken to enclose them in the added packets addressed to the [?said] prelates, so that Your Most Illustrious Lordship, without this trouble, may deliver them to them more quickly and secretly, beginning with those addressed to the bishops most remote from the Court, and sending the others for the Indies to those ports from which the departure of the usual ships for those parts is to take place soonest. For the rest, since the prompt execution of this order matters supremely to His Holiness, so that its publication may follow in time to be able to produce some fruit, such as making Spain desist from further prejudice to the public cause of Christendom, His Holiness leaves you no discretion in it to interpret or suspend the Pontifical mind; nay, His Holiness wishes that you, carrying it out without delay from whatever place you may be in, send the courier back to us immediately and at once with the news of having fully carried out this most urgent commission. Ill.ma si danno toccanti le presenti publiche emergenze sono state molto accette a N.S., a cui troppo importa di essere fedelmente et intieramente informato di tutto. Continui però Ella con la sua solita attenzione, e sinché le sarà permesso, li suoi ragguagli, con sicurezza del pieno gradimento della Santità Sua. Per altro non meno la risoluzione, quale Ella avvisa essersi presa et eseguita costì, di apporre per ordine regio il sequestro alle rendite delle Chiese di Siviglia e di Malaga, che le minaccie fatte d'insultare lo Stato Ecclesiastico non per altro che per essersi da N.S. differita la traslazione del Sig. Card. Alberoni da una all'altra delle sudette Chiese, non solo pienamente giustificano il ritardamento di tale traslazione, ma vanno con mio grande dispiacere a mettere la Santità Sua in un preciso e necessario obbligo di assolutamente e perpetuamente negarla; troppo importando che a qualsisia costo non si ammetta un esempio di violenza sì perniciosa all'autorità Apostolica et alle leggi più sacre della Chiesa. Torno a dire che ho sommo dispiacere che le cose si riducano a questo stato. Ma doveva pure considerare il Sig. Card. Alberoni che la conquista della Chiesa di Siviglia è assai diversa dalla conquista della Sardegna, e che quei mezzi che sono stati opportuni per la seconda sono esecrabili per la prima. Da queste espressioni, che sono proprie di N.S., raccolga V.S. Ill.ma quali sieno i sentimenti della Santità Sua. E giaché si è nominata la Sardegna, si contenti che io le dica che N.S. non si è scordata né si scorderà mai della terribile burla che le fu fatta l'anno passato in questi tempi da cotesta Corte, con tanto discapito del suo onore e con sequela di tanti pregiudizii della S. Sede e della Religione Cattolica; e [?perciò] non si maravigli che per fine io le aggiunga che la Santità Sua sta con impazienza attendendo l'avviso che sia giunto costì lo straordinario ultimamente speditole, e che V.S. Ill.ma abbia eseguite senza alcun minimo indugio quelle Commissioni che le furono date per mezzo di tale spedizione. ## Notes - From the interlinear: 4359 'Per' and 4425 'Stato Ecclesiastico' (open in Lasry's key); 'fatte d'insultare' (figures garbled), 'contenti' (Lasry's 4113 again for 'conte-'), 'Apostolica' (Lasry's 'questo a'), 'della Religione Cattolica, e [?perciò]' (figures 'della et tanto'; the interlinear 'E preci'), 'ultimamente' (Lasry's 'quelli'). Same hole: [?word] partly carried. --> # R171, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 21 June 1718 (Spagna 364D/18, ff. 332r-333r): English translation ## Translation The news which Your Most Illustrious Lordship gives touching the present public emergencies has been very welcome to Our Lord, to whom it matters very much to be faithfully and entirely informed of everything. Do you continue, then, with your usual attention, and as long as you are permitted, your reports, with the assurance of His Holiness's full appreciation. For the rest, no less the resolution, which you report has been taken and carried out there, of laying by royal order a sequestration on the revenues of the Churches of Seville and Málaga, than the threats made of attacking the Ecclesiastical State for no other reason than that Our Lord has deferred Cardinal Alberoni's translation from one of the said Churches to the other, not only fully justify the delay of such a translation, but are going, to my great regret, to put His Holiness under a precise and necessary obligation to refuse it absolutely and perpetually; since it matters too much that, at whatever cost, an example of violence so pernicious to the Apostolic authority and to the most sacred laws of the Church should not be admitted. I say again that I am extremely sorry that things are reduced to this state. But Cardinal Alberoni ought to have considered that the conquest of the Church of Seville is very different from the conquest of Sardinia, and that those means which were suitable for the second are execrable for the first. From these expressions, which are Our Lord's own, gather, Your Most Illustrious Lordship, what His Holiness's sentiments are. And since Sardinia has been named, be content that I tell you that Our Lord has not forgotten, nor will ever forget, the terrible trick that was played on him last year at this time by that Court, with so much damage to his honour and with so many prejudices to the Holy See and the Catholic Religion following from it; and [?therefore] do not wonder that I add finally that His Holiness is waiting impatiently for the news that the extraordinary courier lately sent to you has arrived there, and that Your Most Illustrious Lordship has carried out without the least delay those commissions which were given you by means of that despatch. Ill.ma consegnò al corriero ritornato qua da Lisbona, si è udita la piena esecuzione da Lei data agli ordini prescrittile sotto li nove del sudetto mese. N.S. ha ricevuta con molto gradimento la notizia, et ha rese le dovute lodi alla puntualità con la quale V.S. Ill.ma li ha eseguiti, aspettandosi con impazienza di saperne tutte le circostanze con il ritorno del nostro corriero. Conosce Sua Santità l'indignazione che ne concepirà la Spagna, e tutto ciò che può essere consecutivo a tale indignazione; ma, per dirla a Lei, preme molto più al Papa di non cadere nelle mani di Dio vivente non sodisfacendo alla sua obbligazione nelle circostanze nelle quali si trova la Cristianità, dalle quali gli huomini non lo possono liberare, che d'esporsi a cadere in quelle degli huomini, da cui la potente mano di Dio lo può facilmente salvare; anzi lo spera certamente, perché non ha la Santità Sua avuta altra mira nella risoluzione presa che di adempire alle parti del Ministero commessole da Dio, e di promovere i vantaggi della sua Causa. E si assicuri che non vi ha avuta la minima parte veruno riflesso alla Corte di Vienna, da cui ognuno vede il trattamento che riceviamo; se non fosse quella di parere ora essere in grado di fare il nostro dovere anche con essa, come lo siamo or che si è fatto con la Spagna, che è stata la prima a mancare, et ha dato motivo, o per dir meglio, pretesto alle offese fatteci dall'Imperatore. ## Notes - Read from the interlinear where DECODE's figure transcription and PLAINTEXT rows fail: f. 340r ll. 1-3 ('in data de' 27 del caduto, che V.S. No holes. --> # R172, the Secretariat of State to the nuncio in Madrid, Rome, 12 July 1718 (Spagna 364D/19, ff. 340r-341r): English translation ## Translation From the short despatch dated the 27th of last month, which Your Most Illustrious Lordship handed to the courier who returned here from Lisbon, we have heard of the full execution you gave to the orders prescribed to you under the 9th of the said month. Our Lord received the news with much satisfaction, and gave due praise to the punctuality with which you carried them out, waiting impatiently to learn all the circumstances of it with the return of our courier. His Holiness knows the indignation Spain will conceive at it, and all that may follow from such indignation; but, to tell you, it matters much more to the Pope not to fall into the hands of the living God by not fulfilling his obligation in the circumstances in which Christendom finds itself, from which men cannot free him, than to expose himself to falling into those of men, from which the mighty hand of God can easily save him; nay, he certainly hopes for it, because His Holiness has had no other aim in the resolution taken than to fulfil the parts of the Ministry committed to him by God and to promote the advantages of His cause. And be assured that no regard for the Court of Vienna has had the least part in it, from which everyone sees the treatment we receive; unless it be that of seeming now to be in a position to do our duty with it too, as we are now that it has been done with Spain, which was the first to fail, and gave occasion, or to put it better, pretext, to the offences done to us by the Emperor. His Holiness learned at once what the said Cardinal was saying; and because the orders given to Your Most Illustrious Lordship were entirely different from, and opposed to, what His Eminence asserted, and he could never have imagined such an outcome, he saw to it that the Cardinal learned at once that no such orders had ever been given to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. You may therefore judge what and how great His Holiness's astonishment was on reading your despatch, brought to us on the return of our said express, in which Your Most Illustrious Lordship confirms what Cardinal Acquaviva had asserted. I assure you that His Holiness cannot yet bring himself to believe that you have proceeded to a step that has no precedent, and which the Holy See has always so resisted that it has never suspended, let alone abandoned, the exercise of the authority it freely exercises in the Catholic kingdoms through its ministers; nor have the nunciatures ever been closed except by sheer force and violence. Ill.ma, il Sig. Card. Acquaviva, in seguito di un corriere di cotesta Corte giuntogli precedentemente, aveva partecipato a qualche suo amico le doglianze che si facevano costì per avere il Papa ordinato a V.S. Ill.ma di serrare la Nunziatura senza darne neppur conto al Re; anzi che, [?avendone] la pietà della Maestà Sua procurato di persuaderla a sospendere, non le era riuscito; e che però, essendo V.S. Ill.ma spogliata da Sua Santità del carattere, non era parso al Re proprio decoro di consentire che Ella restasse più ne' suoi Regni. Seppe subito la Santità Sua quanto andava dicendo il sudetto Cardinale; e perché gli ordini dati a V.S. Ill.ma, essendo totalmente diversi et opposti a quanto asseriva S. Em.za, non doveva mai figurarsi un tal successo, fece in modo che il Sig. Cardinale sapesse subito non essersi mai dati somiglianti ordini a V.S. Ill.ma. Quindi raccolga Ella quale e quanto sia stato lo stupore di N.S. nel leggere il suo dispaccio recatomi col ritorno del sudetto nostro espresso, ove V.S. Ill.ma ci conferma ciò che aveva asserito il Sig. Card. Acquaviva. Io l'assicuro che N.S. non può per anche indursi a credere che Ella sia proceduta ad un passo che non ha esempio, et al quale ha sempre la S. Sede tanto ripugnato che non ha mai intermesso, non che lasciato, l'uso di quella autorità che liberamente esercita ne' Regni Cattolici per mezzo de' suoi Ministri; né sono state mai chiuse le Nunziature se non per pura forza e violenza. A[nche] il [4416] Card. Acquaviva non ha finora mostrato di avere alcun ordine di discorrere su le presenti pendenze; se lo farà, lo vedrem[o]. ## Notes - From R173's interlinear where these figures are garbled: 'da Sua Santità del carattere' (figures 'spogliata [?] btllidaicalleodal [?]'), 'il Sig. Add MS 61575 f. 95, catalogued on DECODE as a numerical cipher of a Prussian king, holds no numbers. It is seven lines of cleartext French, spelled by ear, thanking someone for teaching the writer to write in cipher. Transcribed in full; writer and recipient unidentified. moy en me mon trant d'es cria re / en sif fer moi, en me montrant d'écrire en chiffre Blenheim Papers · to an unknown teacher · cleartext French · date unknown (volume 1702–1723) A thank-you note for lessons in cipher British Library, Add MS 61575 f. 95 · DECODE R8774, catalogued as a numerical cipher of "Frederic, Re di Prussia", 1702, with no decipherment There is no cipher on the leaf. It is a short thank-you note in French for lessons in writing in cipher, transcribed here in full. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher closed At a glance Not a cipher The document A one-page French thank-you note, in a large careful hand, spelled by ear and set out syllable by syllable. The writer thanks someone for showing him how to write in cipher. Where British Library, Add MS 61575 f. 95 (Blenheim Papers); DECODE R8774, listed as “Non-decrypted”, numerical, author “Frederic, Re di Prussia”. Why it resists There is nothing to resist: the page shows no numbers and no signs. It was filed as a cipher because its subject is cipher. How it was read Read directly: every word is legible and makes sense. A correction (not a cipher, cleartext French) has been queued for DECODE. What it says The writer thanks the recipient for the trouble taken, promises lasting gratitude and wishes a good journey. Still open The writer, recipient and date are unknown; “Frederic, Re di Prussia” cannot be checked from the leaf, and 1702–1723 is only the volume’s span.
prussia1702.html#page

One page, written in brown ink across the top half of the leaf, with a long rule below and an ink blot at the left where a signature could have been. The folio number 95 is at top right. The words are broken into syllables and spaced out in rough columns, as in a writing exercise. Spelling follows sound: eun for une , Payne for peine , d'es cria re for d'écrire , sif fer for chiffre , as seu re for assurer . The s for ch is what a German speaker would write, which fits a Prussian writer, but proves nothing about which one.
prussia1702.html#reading

Line for line, as written: par cel le cy je vient vous re mer cier en cor eun ne foy de la Pay ne que vous aves eue avec moy en me mon trant d'es cria re en sif fer et vous as seu re que je se roys tous jours re cog naissent vous sou haytant eun bon voya ge. In standard French: Par celle-ci je viens vous remercier encore une fois de la peine que vous avez eue avec moi en me montrant d'écrire en chiffre, et vous assurer que je serai toujours reconnaissant, vous souhaitant un bon voyage. "By this I come to thank you once more for the trouble you took with me in showing me how to write in cipher, and to assure you that I shall always be grateful, wishing you a good journey." Every word is legible and makes sense; the only doubt is the letter shapes of eun in the last line, which could be un with a flourish.
prussia1702.html#why

The note is about cipher. Someone who kept the Marlboroughs' keys filed it with them, and DECODE catalogued each leaf of the volume as a ciphertext or a key, with the volume's date span and a generic "numerical" symbol set. The entry follows the volume metadata, apparently without a check of the image. The correction has been queued for DECODE: not a cipher, cleartext French, no numbers.
prussia1702.html#open

Writer. "Frederic, Re di Prussia" comes from DECODE and is unverified. The hand and spelling suggest a young German-speaking writer still learning French, which fits a Prussian prince, but no name appears on the leaf. Recipient. Someone who taught ciphers and was about to travel. Not identified. Date. Unknown; 1702–1723 is the volume's span.

Seventeen squared sheets of dots in the Munich key volume, sent from Cologne in April and May 1583 by Ernst of Bavaria, candidate for the archbishopric, to his brother Duke Wilhelm V. We had taken them for grilles over lost cover letters; Albert C. Leighton showed in 1974 that the dots are the cipher itself, read with key strips bound in the same volume, and printed the whole text. ANFANG / SDEN / -YSC / HENV / ERT → Anfangs den (kayser)yschen vertrag Cologne → Munich · dot cipher on squared paper with a code list · April–May 1583 · earlier decipherment found Duke Ernst of Bavaria to Wilhelm V: the “Post Scripta” dot cipher of 1583 from Ernest of Bavaria → to Wilhelm V, Duke of Bavaria Go to the transcriptions ↓ Squared sheets of dots that we took for grilles over lost cover letters turn out to be a dot cipher of their own, deciphered in full by Albert C. Leighton in 1974. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · ry-xu (pointer to a source) · Albert C. Leighton (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Duke Ernst of Bavaria, bishop of Freising, Hildesheim and Liège, writing from Cologne to his brother Duke Wilhelm V in Munich: postscripts dated 22 April 1583 and two more sections received on 12 and 19 May, during the contest for the archbishopric of Cologne. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 96–115 (old shelfmark Kasten schwarz 13478); DECODE R9319, which images ff. 96–114. Part of catalogue entry 161. The cipher Dots on squared paper, read against a key strip laid along the sheet: three mixed 24-letter alphabets, and between the letters an alphabetical list of names and words, so that one dot can stand for a whole word. Who deciphered it Not this project. Leighton found the key strips in the same volume (f. 49, DECODE R9304), deciphered every sheet and printed the German text, checked against two chancery decipherments of the time. What it says Truce talks, the papal legate, troops and money for the cathedral chapter, the Jülich and Baden marriages, and a Calvinist tumult in Cologne; Salentin of Isenburg has “ain aufrech bayrisch herz”. Credit Albert C. Leighton (1974) for the decipherment; ry-xu (GitHub issue #88) for pointing to it. Still open No dot-by-dot transcription of ours to set beside Leighton’s text; f. 115 is not on DECODE. Until 15 October 2026 this record was filed on one page with thirteen other ciphertexts of the same key volume. They are different ciphers, each with its own page; the largest group is System A′ of the dukes’ agents in Hungary, and the other piece of 1583 is a letter to Duke Wilhelm V .
r9319.html#record

Seventeen DECODE images show sheets ruled in red into squares, 66 by 43, with dots, a few crosses and other marks; “Postscripta” heads f. 96R, “Aliud Postscript” f. 101V, and the outer leaves are docketed “Presentatur 12 May … 83 Monaci” (f. 107V) and “Presentatur 19 May 83” (f. 115V). On 21 September 2026 we described them as grilles to be laid over clear cover letters on ff. 115–118, which DECODE had not photographed, and closed the record as blocked. That was wrong.
r9319.html#leighton

A. C. Leighton described the same sheets in 1974 under the volume’s old shelfmark, Kasten schwarz 13478, ff. 96–115; his plates of f. 96R match the DECODE image. The dots fall into columns, at least three to a row, which pointed him to a strip key with several alphabets. In the same volume (f. 49) he found four parchment strips: one pair with three alphabets in normal order, the other with three mixed 24-letter alphabets and, between the letters, a list of names and words ( Imperator , Pontifex , Colonia , Capitulum …; German on the mixed pair: Kayser, Capitel, Brueder, Salentin). Laid on f. 96R, the mixed strip gave the opening at once, ANFANG / SDEN, and a dot between two letters gave a code word (between I and O, “Kayser”). A dotted stroke doubles a letter, a closing sign marks the end of a section, and a looped sign stands for E. L. ( Euer Liebden ). Leighton prints the whole text in its original spelling, divided into words, with code-list words in brackets (pp. 836–838), and leaves a few of the encipherer’s slips as written. He checked it against two chancery decipherments he found in the same archive: ff. 96R–101R in Kasten schwarz 3634 ff. 285–287a, headed “Extrait aus H. Ernst Ziffer 22 April 83”, and ff. 104R–107R in Kasten schwarz 3636 f. 42. f. 103V holds a faulty first attempt at the opening. With the same key he also deciphered a further undated dot letter, Kasten schwarz 3636 ff. 43R–45½R, on Count Arnold of Manderscheid’s vote. The sender is Ernst of Bavaria, elected archbishop of Cologne on 23 May 1583 after Gebhard Truchsess was deprived for turning Protestant; the recipient is his brother Wilhelm V. The first postscript is dated “Datum (Cöln) den zwenundzwainzigisten tag april”.
r9319.html#texts

Leighton’s article (1974) is in copyright, so his text is not copied here. It is free to read on the Bavarian State Library’s scan of the journal: pp. 836–838 . ff. 96R–101R, Cologne, 22 April 1583 : the imperial commissioners’ truce talks with the cathedral chapter, Archduke Ferdinand and the legate, Salentin of Isenburg, Württemberg, the Baden marriage, and the canonries of the Bishop of Metz. ff. 101V–102R, another postscript : the chapter’s letter to the Catholic estates, and a new election day for 15 May. ff. 104R–107R, received 12 May : the bishop of Vercelli’s arrival, a Calvinist tumult in the city, a ride to Düsseldorf and the Jülich marriage talks, Count Adolf of Neuenahr, the summons sent to Philipp Truchsess. ff. 108R–115V, received 19 May : French intrigues, the papal deprivation and the election day, the chapter’s troops and money (ten thousand crowns from the Pope, hopes of Spanish help), and Parma as a possible commander.

A Florentine letter in the Sienese cipher file: the orator Donato Acciaiuoli writes from Rome to Lorenzo de’ Medici seven weeks after the Pazzi conspiracy (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 11, DECODE R4800). George Lasry recovered the homophonic key of its two cipher blocks from the ciphertext alone with CTTS and Claude, about 90% certain: Forlì and Faenza to send two squadrons each, Gianfrancesco Gonzaga offers 80 men-at-arms for 7,000 ducats. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (94% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by George Lasry (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (94% of the cipher) The letter Donato Acciaiuoli, Florentine orator in Rome, to Lorenzo de’ Medici, “ex Urbe die 13 junii 1478”: a clear letter with two cipher blocks on its second page. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, no. 11; DECODE R4800, catalogued “1500–1599” with no sender or receiver. The cipher Homophonic substitution on 57 signs: three to five signs for each vowel, one to three for the consonants, a few nulls, and the numerals 80 and 7 written as dotted numbers. No word division, no nomenclator. How it was deciphered George Lasry with CTTS and Claude, 15–17 October 2026: transcription by Claude, key recovered by Claude by crib analysis. No key or decipherment of this letter is known. What it says The lord of Faenza, like the lord of Forlì, is to stay in his lands and send two squadrons into the field; Gianfrancesco Gonzaga will come into Lorenzo’s service with at least 80 men-at-arms for 7,000 ducats. Still open One sign lost in a hole and six doubtful words. Credit George Lasry: transcription, key, reading, translation and context (report of 17 October 2026). The project transcribed the letter in September 2026 but did not break it. The Sienese cipher file Concistoro 2308 holds pieces in many different keys; this one is a Florentine cipher, with its own page. The other pieces of the file are listed on the collection’s page .
siena11.html#letter

The letter is in clear except for two blocks on its second page: block A, 206 symbols in five lines, continues a clear sentence about the briefs written to the lord of Forlì; block B, 187 symbols in five lines, follows the clear words et della legha and ends in the clear Vale . The signature reads “Donatus Acc. or.”; the address on the first page, “Mag.co ac gen.so Viro Laurentio Medici tamquam fratri hon.do, Florentie”. No. 11, block A: the clear words e veduti brevi e quali scriviamo a dto S.re di Furli , then five lines of cipher, et a quelo di Faenza, che si contenteranno … Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 11 p. 2, via DECODE R4800. George Lasry’s key to no. 11: the signs as cut from the manuscript with their number of occurrences, homophones under their letter, then the nulls and separators. Image: George Lasry, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 report (17 Oct 2026), signs cut from ASSi Concistoro 2308.
siena11.html#reading

George Lasry’s reading of the two blocks, quoted from his report (nulls omitted; 80 and 7 are numerals written in the cipher; ? marks a doubtful reading): … et a quelo di Faenza, che si contenteranno, et egli stieno nele tere loro et mandino dua squadre per uno e di gente d’arme in campo. Et maraviglomi di? Faenza, havendo hauto lo aviso che ? ?v m date piu di fa, di ma non? el sapevo. Del signor Giovan Francescho da? Gonzagha si e spicato dile altre pratiche et volentieri vera a s?ervigi vostri con 80 huomini d’arme il meno, et no? fanti; domanda 7 milia ducati per queste genti et mille per la persona sua; et Bacio? viene et diravene a boca. “… and to him of Faenza, that they will be content and that they should stay in their own lands and each send two squadrons of men-at-arms into the field. And I marvel at(?) Faenza, having had the news that ? … were given several days ago, and I did not(?) know it. As for Signor Giovan Francesco da(?) Gonzaga: he has freed himself from his other negotiations and will gladly come into your service with at least 80 men-at-arms and no(?) foot soldiers; he asks 7,000 ducats for these troops and 1,000 for his own person; and Baccio(?) is coming and will tell you of it by word of mouth.” (his translation) Context. The letter was written seven weeks after the Pazzi conspiracy of 26 April 1478. On 1 June Sixtus IV excommunicated Lorenzo, and with Ferrante of Naples and Siena went to war on Florence; Florence pressed its Romagnol clients, Pino III Ordelaffi of Forlì and Galeotto Manfredi of Faenza, and hired condottieri. George Lasry takes block B’s Gonzaga to be Gianfrancesco Gonzaga (1446–1496), third son of Marquis Ludovico III of Mantua, who died on 12 June 1478, the day before this letter. Acciaiuoli was next sent to Louis XI and died in Milan on the way in August 1478. How a letter to Lorenzo came into the Sienese file is unexplained; interception of the courier, Siena being Florence’s enemy, is the obvious hypothesis.
siena11.html#method

George Lasry, with CTTS and Claude, 15–17 October 2026: Claude transcribed the 393 symbols and recovered the key by crib analysis; George Lasry gives the result as “about 90 % certain”. Counted here on his reading, 357 of the 381 plaintext letters and numerals of the cipher passages stand in words without a query mark (93.7%). He marks two probable encipherer’s slips ( ri where di is expected, e a for da ). The project transcribed the letter on 24 September 2026 (409 tokens under 44 sign names) and failed to break it: homophonic annealing did not converge, the Sienese key of Antonio Bichi (Rome 1478, DECODE R4752) did not fit, and the index of Florentine keys has no key for Acciaiuoli. George Lasry’s key has 57 signs: the project’s transcription had merged look-alike signs, the obstacle he names for the whole file.
siena11.html#open

One sign lost in a hole in block A (“? ?v m date piu di fa”). Six doubtful words, graded M: di? , non? , da? , s?ervigi , no? , Bacio? . Whether the Gonzaga condotta was concluded is unchecked in the published letters of Lorenzo (Rubinstein, vol. III).

And I marvel at(?) Faenza, having had the news that ? ... were given several days ago, and I did not(?) know it. As for Signor Giovan Francesco da(?) Gonzaga: he has freed himself from his other negotiations and will gladly come into your service with at least 80 men-at-arms and no(?) foot soldiers; he asks 7,000 ducats for these troops and 1,000 for his own person; and Baccio(?) is coming and will tell you of it by word of mouth. Farewell. Contents From: Donato Acciaiuoli, Florentine orator To: Lorenzo de’ Medici Place: Rome Date: 13 June 1478 — dated in the clear text The letter is in clear except for two cipher blocks on P2. Block A continues a clear sentence about the briefs being written to the lord of Forlì: the same is to be written to the lord of Faenza, that they will be content, should stay in their own lands and each send two squadrons of men-at-arms into the field; Acciaiuoli adds that he marvels at Faenza, having had news that something (one sign is lost in a hole) was given several days earlier without his knowing it. Block B, which follows the clear words 'et della legha', reports on Giovan Francesco Gonzaga: he has freed himself from his other negotiations and will gladly enter Lorenzo's service with at least 80 men-at-arms and no foot soldiers, asking 7,000 ducats for these troops and 1,000 for his own person; a certain Baccio(?) is on his way and will explain the matter by word of mouth. Historical context and dating The letter was written seven weeks after the Pazzi conspiracy of 26 April 1478. On 1 June Sixtus IV excommunicated Lorenzo de' Medici and, with Ferrante of Naples and Siena, went to war on Florence; Alfonso of Calabria's army entered the Chianti from Sienese territory in July [Rubinstein, Lettere di Lorenzo de' Medici III, 1977; Martines, April Blood, 2003]. Donato Acciaiuoli (1429-1478), the Florentine orator in Rome, was next sent to Louis XI and died in Milan on the way (August 1478) [D'Addario, DBI 1, 1960]. Florence meanwhile pressed its Romagnol clients, Pino III Ordelaffi of Forlì (Girolamo Riario took Forlì only in 1480) and Galeotto Manfredi of Faenza, and hired condottieri [Mallett, Mercenaries and Their Masters, 1974]. Block B's Gonzaga is most probably Gianfrancesco Gonzaga (1446-1496), third son of Marquis Ludovico III of Mantua, who died on 12 June 1478, the day before this letter [Lazzarini, DBI 57, 2001]; whether the condotta was concluded is unchecked in the published Medici letters. How a letter to Lorenzo came into the Sienese Concistoro's cipher file is unexplained; Siena was Florence's enemy in 1478, and interception of the courier is the obvious hypothesis, but the file gives no evidence. Four clear lines open the slip: the writer has a headache (“doglia di testa”) and has not written more, addresses “la V. S.” and speaks of “questa via de accordo”. The cipher follows in two passages, in manuscript lines 5 and 6, with a last group at the right end of line 8; 53 cipher symbols in all. Below, a second hand wrote out the decipherment, resolving Stella as “del re d’Aragona” and nichil as “la pr…”. No. 9, lines 4–8: the cipher after nichil and before colo sentimento di Stella , the second passage in line 6, and below them the decipherment, la . pri chas Lglone questa vernata … d(e)l re d’Ragona ; the last group sits at the right of line 8. siena9.html#reading

George Lasry’s reading, quoted from his report (cipher in bold; clear code words and uncertain readings in brackets with ?): [la pratica?] [di?] Chastiglone questa vernata con lo sentimento di [re d’Aragona] e nutrire questa guerra uno altro anno Francesco? i? “[the negotiation?] [of?] Castiglione this winter with the assent of [the King of Aragon]; and to sustain this war one more year. Francesco? i?” (his translation) Context and date (George Lasry, unverified). Castiglione, perhaps Castiglione della Pescaia, was the Aragonese foothold on the Tuscan coast: Alfonso V took it in 1447 and held it for more than a decade; his army wintered in the Sienese Maremma in 1447–48 before the failed siege of Piombino, and in the war of 1452–54 the Neapolitan army operated from there again, with Siena as Alfonso’s ally. A report that Castiglione is to be held “this winter” with the king’s assent, and the war sustained another year, fits either campaign; the winter of 1447–48 fits best.

George Lasry, with CTTS and Claude: Claude transcribed the slip and recovered the key from the second hand’s decipherment, which fixes the two passages sign for sign and confirms every value it covers. Counted here on his reading, 36 of the 44 letters in the cipher passages stand without a query (81.8%): the three words of line 5 and the three of line 6. The sign before Chastiglone and the last group are outside what the decipherment covers. The project transcribed the slip on 24 September 2026 (46 cipher tokens under 28 sign names) and closed it as too short for a ciphertext-only attack. That transcription took the second hand’s lines for ordinary clear text, noting only that they might be a decipherment, and dated the slip c. 1495–1516 from the persons in the clear lines. The report’s reading replaces both.

Transcription no09.txt No. 9 (ASSi Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2) - DECODE R4798 Images: decode/img/IMG_R4798_I27941_P1.jpg (text side, slip c. 3000x700 px in a 4000x2248 photo); _P2.jpg (dorse) Transcriber: agent J, 24 Sept 2026, from the photographs (clear lines 1.7x, cipher lines 3x in 4 overlapping segments, doubtful signs 4-5x; crops/agentJ/p9_*.png) WHAT IT IS - A narrow slip (poliza) of 8 lines, no salutation, no date, no address: an enclosure to a letter. Place: unknown Date: 1440s–1450s? — Castiglione and the King of Aragon (Alfonso V) point to the Tuscan wars of 1447–48 or 1452–54; unverified A slip of paper, not a full letter. Four hurried clear lines open it: the writer excuses himself (he has a headache, 'doglia di testa', and has not written more), addresses 'la V. S.', and speaks of 'questa via de accordo', this way of agreement. The sensitive part follows in cipher, with the key words disguised: [the negotiation?] [of?] Castiglione this winter, with the assent of 'Stella' (the King of Aragon), and 'to sustain this war one more year'. Below, a second hand has written out the decipherment line for line, resolving Stella as 'del re d'Aragona' and nichil as 'la pr...' (la pratica?); this contemporary solution confirms every locked value of the key. A last cipher group at the right may read 'Francesco'. Historical context and dating Castiglione (della Pescaia?) was the Aragonese foothold on the Tuscan coast: Alfonso V of Aragon and Naples took it in 1447 and held it for more than a decade; his army wintered in the Sienese Maremma in 1447–48 before the failed siege of Piombino in summer 1448, and in the war of 1452–54 the Neapolitan army sent against Florence again operated from there, with Siena as Alfonso's ally [Ryder, Alfonso the Magnanimous, 1990]. A report that Castiglione is to be held 'this winter' with the king's assent, and the war sustained 'another year', fits either campaign; the winter of 1447–48, when the king himself lay on that coast, fits best. Nothing on the slip dates it, sender and addressee are unnamed, and the identification of Castiglione with Castiglione della Pescaia is a conjecture; the date remains unverified. Open points. The clear code word nichil (la pratica?), the final cipher group 'Francesco?', and the persons mentioned in the clear lines (a Guido and someone 'da Rimino'?) remain unidentified. smallwood1777.html

A field letter from the days after Brandywine in which five words were erased and replaced by the marks *, §, §§, † and §. The editors wondered whether they were a simple code. § stands once for a number and once for a route, so the marks are blanks; the erased words are lost. he has * Troops · our united Force amounts to § · exerted to §§ · I have † this County Lieut. · my Baggage I shall send by § Chester County → Washington · erasures marked with printer's symbols · 19 September 1777 · not a cipher Smallwood to Washington, 19 September 1777: five erased words from William Smallwood → to George Washington A Maryland general's field letter, written days after Brandywine, in which five words were erased for safety and replaced by symbols; the symbols hide nothing that can be recovered, because they are blanks, not a code. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher closed At a glance Not a cipher · 5 marks, 4 kinds The letter Brig. Gen. William Smallwood to George Washington, from James Mechlans Tavern, Chester County, Pennsylvania, 19 September 1777, on his march to join the main army. Where The signed original is privately owned (Joseph Rubinfine, 1994); a Sprague transcript is in the George Washington Papers at the Library of Congress. Printed in the Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series 11, p. 272. What it is Clear English. Five words were erased on the original and replaced by the marks *, §, §§, †, §. The editors wondered whether they were a simple code. Why it is not a cipher § stands once for a number of men and once for a route or carrier. One sign with two unrelated meanings is not a substitution; the marks are footnote-style blanks. Still open The five erased words. They are not in the letter and were not found elsewhere; the original and the Sprague transcript were not seen.
smallwood1777.html#the-letter

Smallwood had been sent with the Maryland militia to harass the British rear after Brandywine (11 September 1777). On 17 September Washington told him to “form a junction with the Main Army as soon, as you possibly can” and named Warwick Furnace on French Creek as his next halt. Two days earlier Smallwood had written that he was “afraid the Express has fallen into the Enemys hands”. The letter of the 19th, sent from a tavern in West Caln Township, reports that Colonel Mordecai Gist has joined him and that he is marching. Its numbers and its intentions were erased before it went. The edition’s text, with the marks as printed: Last Night Colonel Gist joined me he has * Troops—our united Force amounts to § . I am now on my march and rest assured every Effort shall be exerted to §§ —as expeditiously as possible which I hope to effect Tomorrow—the Shameful neglect in the Commissarys Department throws many Obstacles in my way and retards my March … I have— † this County Lieut. and others of Integrity with me but cannot ascertain my Route so precisely as to point it out. my Baggage I shall send by § —but believe I shall fall more down to the Right with the troops. No image of the letter is available: the original is in private hands and the Library of Congress transcript was not reached. The full text, with each mark and the slot it fills, is in the repository’s transcription.txt .
smallwood1777.html#the-marks

Mark Slot What fits the slot * “he has * Troops” a number: Gist’s strength § “our united Force amounts to §” a number: the combined strength §§ “exerted to §§ as expeditiously as possible” a verb phrase; Washington’s order of the 17th makes “join you” or “form a junction” likely † “I have—† this County Lieut.” a verb or participle § “my Baggage I shall send by §” a route, place or person Three things decide the question. The marks are the printer’s reference marks used for footnotes, not invented cipher signs. The same mark, §, fills a number in one place and a route or carrier in another, so it cannot stand for one word, letter or figure. And the editors report that the words were erased on the original: the information was taken out of the letter, not written into it in another form. Whatever the marks referred to, a message carried by word of mouth or a slip sent separately, it is not with the letter. Five marks of four kinds would in any case be far too few to recover a key from.
smallwood1777.html#what-remains-uncertain

The five erased words. The reading of §§ as the junction with the main army is an inference from Washington’s letter, not a decipherment; the numbers and the baggage route are unknown. Whether the marks are Smallwood’s own or the transcriber’s rendering of blank erasures. The Sprague transcript at the Library of Congress would show how they were copied; it was behind a bot check when tried. The conclusion does not depend on it.

SP 106/7 f. 33 (DECODE R597), catalogued as a partly decrypted letter, is an English instruction sheet for a syllabic code in two keys, used with Baron Stosch, the British spy at Rome and Florence. The syllable is written over every group of its worked example, and the whole sheet is transcribed. 316 509 139 134 435 509 702 593 506 408 Le s ad her en s du Pre te nd 371 = changement de clef · 110, 220 & all above 900 = nulls Secretary of State's office → a correspondent of Stosch · syllabic code, two keys · c. 1731 Instructions for the Stosch–Walton cipher, c. 1731 Go to the full text ↓ TNA State Papers 106/7, f. 33 (DECODE R597). DECODE lists it as a partly decrypted French letter in a nomenclator of letter pairs, with some lines not deciphered. It is an English sheet of instructions sent with a cipher that “serves only to correspond with Baron Stosch and Mr Walton”, and every group of its worked example has its syllable written above it. The sheet was transcribed in full; there is no ciphertext without its plaintext. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not applicable closed At a glance Not applicable · instruction sheet, fully transcribed The document The catalogue took R597 for a ciphered letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. It is an English instruction sheet for a cipher to be used with “Baron Stosch and Mr Walton who reside at Rome”, where “Rome” is corrected to Florence. Where TNA SP 106/7, images 0091–0092, DECODE R597 (status “Partially decrypted”). Stosch moved to Florence in 1731, so the sheet dates from about then. The cipher A syllabic code of three-digit groups from 100 to 999 in two keys, A in black ink and B in red, used alternately. Group 371 means “changement de clef”; the nulls are 110, 220 and so on, plus every group above 900. How it was read The writer put the syllable over every group of his worked example, so the sheet explains itself; the whole sheet is transcribed. The lines DECODE calls undeciphered are the same key B example written as one unbroken string. What it says The example is Les Adherens du Pretendant se donnent beaucoup de mouvement à Rome , first in key A, then switching to key B after “donnent”. Still open Three figures are doubtful, and keys A and B themselves are not on the record.

DECODE R597 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0091-0092)”) has two images. Its date, 1702–1837, is the span of the volume. [When you write you put no Stops, as in our Ordinary Cypher, but write thus, 371436433342218446670 4175534530236208477.] You have several Nulls to intermix as 110. 220. &c and all above 900 are so. You make use of no Numbers under 100 or above 999. The example sentence means “The Pretender's adherents are very busy in Rome”. That is the kind of news Stosch sent home about the court of James Francis Edward Stuart.
sp106r597.html#the-system

Code. Three-digit groups stand for syllables and letter pairs (le, s, ad, her, en, du, pre, te, nd …). DECODE's “letter pairs rather than words” is right. A repeated syllable keeps its group within one key (s = 509 twice, en = 435 twice in key A). Two keys. Key A and key B give different groups for the same syllable (be 446 / 436, au 447 / 433, mo 612 / 678). The writer switches at will, and 371 announces the switch. No separators. The groups run on and the decipherer cuts them into threes. This is the point where the sheet contrasts the method with “our Ordinary Cypher”, which used stops. Nulls. The round hundreds-and-tens groups 110, 220 and so on, and every group from 901 to 999.
sp106r597.html#what-remains-uncertain

In key A, 702 appears for both “du” and “up”. One of the two is probably a slip by the writer or a misreading (grade C). In key B, the group for “tà” is written 023, which falls below the stated range of 100–999 (C). The run-on demonstration does not match the separated groups digit for digit (…446670… against 446|678, and …6208477 against 620|477). The writer copied it loosely (C). Only the 30 groups of the example are known. Keys A and B are not on the record. Whether one of the 16 SP 106 key records on DECODE is one of them has not been checked. The writer and the recipient are not named. The date c. 1731 is inferred from the Florence correction.

Two Italian letters (DECODE R704, R721) in a third cipher of the SP 106/10 codebreaker’s file: groups of a letter and one or two figures, with his syllables above them. Identified and separated from the file’s other ciphers; not yet transcribed or deciphered. Split on 14 Oct 2026 from sp106box10. Z6 n54 m56 g42 n24 m62 Z11 n23 g62 m12 … (the codebreaker’s syllables above: dal … to ge … me … sa) intercepted Italian letters · letter-and-figure syllabary · c. 1623–24 · attempted, not solved Two intercepts in a letter-and-figure syllabary, TNA SP 106/10 Two Italian letters in a third cipher of the same codebreaker’s file, glossed by him between the lines; identified and set apart, not yet transcribed or deciphered here. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Two Italian letters, sender and recipient unknown, intercepted in England and worked on by the English codebreaker whose file dates from 1623–25. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 186–187 and 190–192 (DECODE R704, 46 lines, ~700 groups; R721, 26 lines, ~300 groups; group counts DECODE’s). The cipher Each group is a letter followed by one or two figures. The codebreaker wrote Italian syllables above them, so it is syllabic and the plaintext is Italian. What was done The system was told apart from the file’s other ciphers, and two records DECODE files with it were moved out (R720 and R722 belong to the 1625 code). Still open Everything: no transcription yet, and the codebreaker’s glosses have not been aligned against the groups. The two letters belong to one codebreaker’s file, which holds several ciphers; each has its own page (a different cipher in each): the three-figure “Venetian Cifer” ( sp106box10 ), the two-figure nomenclator of his key sheet R725 ( sp106r725 ) and a second three-figure code in a letter of 1625 ( sp106r722 ).

Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10, via DECODE R704 (rotated here). The groups are a letter (Z, n, m, g and others) followed by one or two figures, in numbered lines, with no clear text between them. The codebreaker worked these letters the way he worked the others in the file, writing a syllable above each group, so his partial decipherment is on the page. That is the method that rebuilt the “Venetian Cifer”, and it has not yet been applied here. DECODE points from R720 to R704 (“possibly related”); R720 is covered in three-figure groups and is a worksheet on the 1625 letter, not on this system. R722, filed here at first following DECODE’s pointers, is that 1625 letter. Two further records, R723 and R724, were fetched and have not been examined.
