TNA SP 106/10 ff. 241–243 (DECODE R927), catalogued as an undeciphered letter in the masonic alphabet. The pencilled pigpen key on its flap does not fit; the cipher is homophonic, and its key was recovered from the ciphertext alone after a hand transcription of the last page. With all three pages transcribed, the letter runs f. 243 to f. 241, f. 242 is a second copy of f. 243, and after a sign-by-sign re-reading 95.6% of its symbols read as sense, the rest under blots or name signs: a client at Nancy writing in December to a patron, about a gentleman’s marriage and an envoy to congratulate His Majesty on his recovery. ⊓: ⊐· ◻· ⊓: ⊓: ◻· ⊔· ⌟: ⌟: ◻: ◻· ⌟: ◻· m o n s i e u r m e c o n t i n u e r Nancy → “Monsieur” · homophonic pigpen, French · December, year unknown (17th century) A French letter in a homophonic pigpen cipher, SP 106/10 ff. 241–243 Go to the full text ↓ The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 241–243 (DECODE R927), described as an “undeciphered letter in the masonic alphabet, say 800 codegroups”, with no key, sender, recipient or date. The September 2026 search found no earlier decipherment or published key, but George Lasry reports that the letter was decoded by Sheila Richards in Secret Writings (1973); this reading is an independent re-solution, not a first break. f. 243 was transcribed by hand and the key recovered from the ciphertext alone; f. 241, its continuation, and the image catalogued as f. 242 followed on 2 October 2026 (it is f. 243 again, with the flap down, as WAINUT showed in October), and after every unread word was read again sign by sign on 3 October, 95.6% of the letter’s symbols read as sense. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (96% of the cipher) Credits · WAINUT (verification, transcription) · George Lasry (pointer to a source) · Sheila R. Richards (earlier solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (96% of the cipher) The letter A French letter of the seventeenth century from a client or servant at Nancy, in December, to a “Monsieur” whose favour he asks; signed with a name read “Nicle”(?). It runs f. 243 → f. 241; the image of f. 242 is the same leaf as f. 243 with the flap folded down. A proposed identification of the persons is given below as a hypothesis. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 241–243; DECODE R927, catalogued as an “undeciphered letter in the masonic alphabet”. The cipher A homophonic pigpen: nine cell shapes, each with one to three dots and sometimes an inner stroke, several symbols for the common letters, two of them polyphonic; a few special symbols for names. The pencilled key on the flap does not fit. How it was deciphered The key was recovered by annealing on a hand transcription of f. 243 and fixed with probable words. On 2 October 2026 ff. 241 and 242 were transcribed by hand and decoded with it, and four values were added. On 3 October every sign of every unread word was cut out at three to four times the size and read again; two more values were fixed and the share read rose from 84.0% to 95.6%. What it says Sorrow that the recipient, after the marriage of “ce gentilhomme”, believed something “au prejudice de l’entiere affection que j’ay vouée a vostre service”; a proposal to send someone to congratulate “Sa Majesté” on recovering from a long illness; the writer’s “zele … a son tres humble service”. Credit George Lasry reports that Sheila Richards decoded the letter in Secret Writings (1973). The book was not seen here; this reading is an independent re-solution. Still open Two short stretches of f. 241 under ink blots and a stain, and a few single signs, at the resolution of the only images; the 14 special symbols in name positions, which no surviving key explains; and so the sender’s identity, the recipient and the year. With these, the reading of f. 241 builds coherent sentences but reads at 90.1% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. The foot of f. 243 turned to the writer's orientation. The last lines decipher as … et vous supplie tres humblement, monsieur, me continuer l’honneur de vostre bienveuillance et croire que je vous honnor[e] . Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 243, via DECODE R927 (rotated here).
sp106r927.html#the-document-and-the-false-key

There are three images: f. 241, f. 242 with a paper flap pasted over part of it, and f. 243. The archive photographed the text sideways. Turned 90° anticlockwise, it runs in horizontal lines with word spaces. The flap carries a pencil grid, the standard dotted pigpen (a–i one dot, k–s two, t–z three). Applied to the letter it gives oeaeydakdorsefekdoi… , with g/q at 16% of the text and t almost absent. None of the 48 rotations, reflections and dot orders, and none of the 9! reassignments of shapes to cells, gives any language.
sp106r927.html#the-system

Each symbol is one of the nine cell shapes, followed by one, two or (rarely) three dots, and sometimes with an inner stroke. The shape does not fix a group of letters: e is ◻·, ◻ with an inner mark, and one or two rarer forms; s has five or six symbols; i three. Working key (shape named by its open side; the digit is the dot count): a ⊔1 b ⊓1 c ⊏1, ⊏ with bar 1 d Γ1 e ◻1 (+ inner-mark forms) f/q L1 g ⊔2 h ⊏-bar 2 i ◻2 (+ variants) l ⊏2, ⊏3 m ¬1 n ⌟1 o ⊐1 p ◻3 q L2 r Γ2, Γ3 s ⊓2 (+ variants) t ⊐2, ⊔2 u/v ⌟2 y ¬2 L1 serves for both f ( affection , effets ) and q ( que ). It is either a polyphonic symbol or two variants not separated in transcription. Two circle or “9”-shaped symbols and a few stacked composites are unresolved. They stand where names or abbreviations are expected.
sp106r927.html#the-reading-of-the-last-page-f-243

First worked as the last page; the transcription of f. 241 on 2 October 2026 showed that the letter begins here (section 04). On 3 October every sign of the words not yet deciphered was cut out at three to four times the size and read again: the errors had been the open side of corner shapes, dot counts and inner strokes, and two signs the writer cancelled with an ink blot. Two values were corrected in the key (F*1 = l , from “que les occasions” twice; D*1 = o , from pouvois ). A joint re-annealing of every value over the three pages raised the model score but turned g and h against gentilhomme , longue and humble , so it was not adopted. The raw decryption after the re-reading of 3 October, one line per written line: ienepouuoisreceuoid / unennuyplussensible / ayant_apprisquedunri / agedecegentilhomme / lequelsaluadernierement / _ndelapartde_monmaitre / _usauiescreuquelqu / choseaupreiudice / delentiereaffectionque / iayuoueauostreseruice / silfutestepersnnenfui / iepeusseprendreconfia / nceuouseussiescongnupr / luyqueienecherisrien / tantquelesoccasionsdeuous / entesmoingnerdeseffets / iescrisa_cequecegentil / hommealloetfaircpardela / etuoussupplietreshunblem / monsieurmecontinuerlhonneur / deuostrebienueullanceet / croirequeieuoushonnor (an _ is a special symbol or a sign lost to a blot or a hole; the first decryption of 19 September, before the re-reading, began ieneponunisreceuoid / … / lequessaluiderviedement .) Regularised, with the doubtful parts marked: Je ne pouvois recevoir d’un ennuy plus sensible, ayant [..] appris que du voiage de ce gentilhomme, lequel salua dernierement [67] de la part de [6] mon maistre, vous aviés creu quelques choses au prejudice de l’entiere affection que j’ay vouée a vostre service. S’il fut esté personne en qui je peusse prendre confiance, vous eussiés congnu par luy que je ne cheris rien tant que les occasions de vous en tesmoigner des effets. J’escris a [@] ce que ce gentilhomme alloit faire par dela, et vous supplie tres humblement, Monsieur, me continuer l’honneur de vostre bienveuillance et croire que je vous honnor[e] … Translation: “I could not have received a keener sorrow than on learning that, from the marriage of this gentleman, who lately greeted [name] on behalf of [name] my master, you had believed some things to the prejudice of the entire affection I have vowed to your service. Had there been anyone in whom I could confide, you would have known through him that I cherish nothing so much as the occasions to show you its effects. I am writing to [name] about what this gentleman was going to do over there, and I beg you most humbly, sir, to continue me the honour of your goodwill, and to believe that I honour you …” The first decryption had read the middle of the page as “Je ne vous dis rien” and left most of it open.
sp106r927.html#the-first-page-f-241

On 2 October 2026 both remaining pages were transcribed by hand, every symbol read by eye from enlarged, deskewed strips, and decoded with the key (polyphonic symbols resolved word by word by a French language model). Two findings changed the shape of the letter: The page order is f. 243, then f. 241. f. 243 ends “et croire que je vous honnor-”; f. 241 begins “-e et cheris ce qui se peut” and ends with the subscription and the dateline. What was called the last page above is the first, and f. 241 is the close. f. 242 is not a second copy. It was first taken for one, line for line the same. WAINUT pointed out (October 2026), and the images confirm, that images P2 and P3 show the same leaf, with the same holes, blots and special symbol, photographed with the flap folded down and lifted. The agreement between the two transcriptions therefore checked the transcription, not the text. The foot of f. 241, turned to the writer’s orientation: the close of the letter, … vous conjurant me faire [..] faveur d’asseurer Sa Majesté du zele que j’ay a son tres humble service, estant, mo[nsieur], vostre tres humble et fidel serviteur [Nicle?] , and in the last line the dateline De Nancy le [..] decembre . Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 241, via DECODE R927 (rotated here). f. 241, regularised after the re-reading of 3 October; [..] marks symbols not read as sense, [name] a special symbol: [… que je vous honnor]e et cheris ce qui se peut. S’y vous trouviés a propos de disposer [67] d’envoier ledit [@] de la part de Sa Majesté vers [6] pour se resjouir de sa santé apres la longue maladie qu’il a eue, je m’asseure que les personnes que vous aimés n’en seroint marris, et de mon costé je leur ouvriray mon coeur de tout ce que je jugeray estre du [..] [67] et du [..] (WAINUT conjectures du service du [67] et du vostre ), vous conjurant me faire la faveur d’asseurer Sa Majesté du zele que j’ay a son tres humble service, estant, Mo-sieur, vostre tres humble et fidel serviteur [Nicle? or Ville?]. De Nancy le [day] decembre. “… and cherish you as much as can be. If you thought fit to arrange for [name] to send the said [name] on behalf of His Majesty to [name], to rejoice at his health after the long illness he has had, I am sure that the persons you love would not be sorry for it; and for my part I will open my heart to them on all that I judge to be of [..], begging you to do me the favour of assuring His Majesty of my zeal for his most humble service, being, sir, your most humble and faithful servant [Nicle?]. Nancy, the [..] of December.” Three readings here come from an independent transcription and key by WAINUT (October 2026), whose 20 symbol values all agree with ours: voiage on f. 243 (we had read mari-age with one symbol unread), Mo-sieur before the subscription, and the separation of the special symbols into three: a “67” (a king, “Sa Majesté”), a “6” (the writer’s master, recovering from a long illness) and a circled symbol [@], a man who could be sent from one to the other. The signature is still open between Nicle and Ville : the two transcriptions differ in the dots of two symbols, which the images cannot settle. Who (a hypothesis, WAINUT). If the signature is Ville , the writer may be Henri de Livron, marquis de Ville, gentleman of the chamber of Charles IV, Duke of Lorraine, and his envoy to Charles I in 1628–29; [6] would be Charles IV, [67] Charles I, the “Monsieur” perhaps Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, and the year perhaps 1629. Ville appears in the Calendar of State Papers Venetian XXI (April 1628) and Domestic 1628–29 as the Duke’s envoy, and in 1629 dealing with Holland. No document names the persons of this letter, and the identification fails if the signature is Nicle . Measured (a word counts when its decrypt differs from the regular word by at most one letter): 843 of the letter’s 882 symbols read as sense (95.6%) , f. 243 98.3% and f. 241 92.5%; leaving out the 14 special symbols in name positions, 97.1%. On 2 October, before the sign-by-sign re-reading, the figure was 84.0% (f. 243 81.7%, f. 241 86.5%). On 2 October four values were added to the key: H3 = z ( zele ), C*2 = q ( ce qui ), and two polyphones, C1 = f / q ( faveur , confiance against que , qu’il ) and F2 = l / h ( plus against cheris , gentilhomme ); C3 = l and A*2 = q are provisional, one occurrence each. Neighbouring records. R922–R933 were opened on DECODE: R923–R925, R928 and R929 are the digit code of the Henrietta Maria and Goffe letters of 1645–46, R930 a strip of alchemical-type symbols, R931–R932 numeric, R933 a key sheet with English names. None is in this pigpen, and none carries a decipherment or clear copy of R927.
sp106r927.html#method

The glyph boxes and dots were segmented automatically, then corrected by eye from enlarged crops. The solver is simulated annealing over a homophonic key, scored by French, English, Latin and nine other quadgram models, with a letter-frequency penalty. It was tested first on synthetic homophonic text, with and without 10% noise. On the automatic transcription every language failed (best −4.5/char, no words). On the hand transcription French scored clearly best (−4.39), and the solver output contained que dun , de la part de , plus . The key was then fixed from whole words and the solver run again.
sp106r927.html#what-remains-uncertain

Writer, recipient and year: the letter is dated at Nancy in December and signed with a name read “Nicle”(?), perhaps a contraction; the recipient is “Monsieur”; the gentleman whose journey is mentioned is not named. WAINUT’s hypothesis (above) would make the writer the marquis de Ville and the year 1629; it rests on the signature. The names sit in the special symbols. No docket or address leaf survives in the record, and without a year or a name the calendars cannot be searched. The formulae and spelling point to French of the seventeenth century. The special symbols (circle/“9” forms, stacked composites): not decoded, probably names or titles. f. 243 reads in full but for two signs lost to a blot (line 3) and a paper hole (line 7); there is no second copy (the f. 242 image is the same leaf). The closing formulae are secure (H), the rest C. f. 241: the close and the dateline are secure (H). Counted by words, its reading reads at 90.1% (24 October 2026), under 95%. Two stretches stay unread: b_ruiledu … et du uoii in line 13 (“de tout ce que je jugeray estre du [..] [67] et du [..]”) and bienr before the subscription (now deciphered sieur after WAINUT), under ink blots and a stain, plus single signs at three line ends and the day of the date. f. 241 has no second copy, the National Archives have not digitised SP 106, and DECODE holds only these 2,300-pixel images, so this is the limit until the leaf or a better photograph is seen. They are the reason f. 241 is at 92.5% while the letter is over 95%: the project’s threshold for a complete text (95% of the cipher gives sense) admits gaps blocked from outside, and these are. Writer’s spellings kept as read: alloet , fairc , hunblem , persnne , bienveullance .

Two French despatches of the Dutch envoy decode with William V’s 1782 Grand Chiffre (DECODE R1024), checked on a control letter with known plaintext; digits the DECODE transcription could not place were resolved with a French language model. They report the Prussian refusal to guarantee the Dutch possessions overseas. P. van de Spiegel) inv. 190 · DECODE R1026 (29 Dec. 1787, two pages) and R1027 (4 Mar. 1788, one page). The two French despatches are in the 1782 Grand Chiffre of Stadholder William V (DECODE R1024), as DECODE’s description suggests. A control letter with its plaintext on DECODE confirms the key. The sign the DECODE transcription could not place is the writer’s 1 with a hooked foot, and the blocks of the key that DECODE left out are nulls; with that, both letters are deciphered complete (23 October 2026). No earlier decoding of these two letters was found. Van Reede’s 1793 letter to the Secret Committee is in another code, with its own page . Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letters Despatches from Arend Willem van Reede, the Dutch Republic’s envoy in Berlin, to the Grand Pensionary Van de Spiegel: R1026 (29 December 1787), R1027 (4 March 1788), and a 1793 letter to the Secret Committee (R1893). Where DECODE R1026, R1027 and R1893, with no decipherment. The key is DECODE R1024, William V’s 1782 “Grand Chiffre” (Koninklijk Huisarchief A29, inv. 301). The cipher A one-part French code, 4,732 entries from 1 to 5000 in alphabetical order, with whole words, names, syllables and letters. DECODE’s J+ sign does not stand for one digit. How it was read R1024 decodes word for word an undated Van Reede letter (R1028) whose plaintext DECODE gives. Each J+ group was tried with all ten digits and chosen by a French character-level language model; 105 groups were settled that way and 452 of 472 groups now have a value. What it says The treaty of alliance Prussia signed with the Republic in April 1788: the King “could not guarantee our possessions overseas”, and the article was reworded to cover only an attack by a European power. Still open The 1793 letter (R1893) is in marked three-digit groups (696 groups, 513 distinct forms) for which no key has been found.

R1026 (29 December 1787) and R1027 (4 March 1788) are Van Reede’s own despatches to Laurens Pieter van de Spiegel, in dot-separated groups of one to four digits with clear French at the head and foot. R1026 carries an interlinear gloss over its first groups, dites … avant hier , which is the first check on any key. The two letters share 49 groups. Van Reede’s letter of 24 March 1793 to the Secret Committee (DECODE R1893) is in another system, three-digit groups with marks over single digits, and is written up on its own page . R1026, first page: the gloss dites … avant hier above the first groups. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.26 inv. 190, first page, via DECODE R1026. The key is DECODE R1024, the “Grand Chiffre” of William V (Koninklijk Huisarchief A29, inv. 301, dated 1782): a one-part French code in which the numbers run with the alphabet, up to 5000. Whole words, names ( le Comte de Finkenstein , Monsieur de Herzberg ), syllables and letters all have values, so rare words are spelt out: ul·er , simple·ment .

R1028, an undated Van Reede letter headed Chiffre de Mr de Reede , has its plaintext written out on DECODE. Its groups, decoded with R1024, give la reponse A donner au [Roi] à la communication que Sa Majesté vient de faire A leurs haut Puissance les voici le Ministre d’Angleterre A ajouter dans son rapport qu’on esperer·oit ic[i] qu’on approuver·oit A Londres… , matching the clear version word for word. The key is right and complete enough. The same key on R1026 decoded cleanly in some lines ( il doit y avoir ce matin … une conference à ce sujet ) and made nonsense in others. Every nonsense word came from a group containing DECODE’s J+ , which the transcriber defined as “a sign that is not represented by other signs”. The first pass took it as 3, the second as any digit chosen by a language model. Both were wrong: it is the writer’s hooked 1 ( JJ8J is 1181 le Roi ). 275J , read 2750 dites after the gloss, is 2751, in a null block: the gloss writer was guessing too.

Superseded (23 October 2026): the per-group digit choice described here was withdrawn once J+ was seen to be a hooked 1; the readings below are built on the figures as re-read on the images ( R1026-R1027_reread_log.md ). The first method: resolve_j.py reads the DECODE transcription, keeps plain digits as written and treats each J+ as unknown. For each group it lists every digit filling whose number is in the key, and a search that keeps the 40 best partial texts chooses among them, scored by a six-character French language model built from eighteenth-century diplomatic correspondence (the Politische Correspondenz text already in the repository). Groups without J+ are never changed. 79 groups in R1026 and 26 in R1027 were resolved this way. The model can choose a wrong but grammatical word, and it cannot repair a plain digit the transcriber misread; both kinds of error remain in the passages marked below.

The reading of 23 October 2026 ( R1026_reading.md , English R1026_en.md ), cipher and clear together, in the writer’s spelling; [?word] marks a word the groups carry only in part: Berlyn le 29 Decem. 1787. Monsieur, Avant hier les deux Ministres ont proposé au Roi le projet de l'alliance tel que vous l'avés, Monsieur. Comme ils persistoyent à differer d'opinion, j'ai prié Monsieur de Herzberg de detailler separement les sentiments dans le rapport et de motiver le sien, et il l'a fait. La reponse est arrivée hier au soir et elle me paroit bonne. Il doit y avoir ce matin à dix heures une conference à ce sujet encore entre le Roi et ses deux Ministres. J'espère qu'il n'y aura pas de changement. Le seul jusqu'ici dont il [?soit] question, c'est que le Roi a dit qu'il ne pouvoit pas garantir nos possessions d'outre Mer. Je ne l'ai pas demandé, mais bien qu'au cas d'elles fussent attaquées par une Puissance Européenne on [?fournit] en argent le subside. Peutêtre Sa Majesté entend elle par garantir fournir le subside, mais quand cela seroit, je ne desespere pas encore d'obtenir ce point. L'article sept que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous envoyer separement est supprimé comme desagreable pour l'Angleterre, à la requisition du Comtte de Finkenstein. Monsieur de Herzberg a rendu le Traité temporaire et l'a fixé à vingt ans. Voila jusqu'a present la seule difference entre ce qui a êté arreté hier et ce que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous envoyer. Depuis que ceci a été chiffré, Monsieur, j'ai été au sortir d'une Conference que les deux Ministres ont eu avec le Roi, une visite à leurs Excellences, qui m'ont dit que mon audience ne pouvoit avoir lieu que Mercredi. Le Ceremonial a été reglé d'une maniere convenable, et quoique peu versé dans les formes, je [?vois] le plus [?estimé] d'[?ici] de reconnoitre l'attention de L.H.P. par les plus grandes politesses. Le Roi a bien voulu y mettre le comble en decidant de lui même, et quoique cela ne se fut pas pratiqué du temps de Mr de Tessin, Ambassadeur de Suede, que j'aurois le jour [?la] l'honneur de diner à sa table. J'apprens qu'il a êté decidé dans la conference de ce matin que sans articuler le mot de possessions d'outre Mer on diroit simplement que si la Republique etoit attaquée par une Puissance Européenne le Roi lui fourniroit les secours stipulés, laissant ainsi la chose comme indecise. Cependant si leurs hautes Puissances m'ordonnent d'insister pour obtenir qu'on [?énonçoit] l'article plus clairement, je crois que je pourai l'obtenir, d'après la manière dont ceci m'a êté dit. Si j'ai bien compris je n'ai pas à m'attendre à d'autres changements. J'ai l'honneur d'être avec un très profond respect, Monsieur, votre très humble et très obeissant serviteur, A. W. van Reede. In English. Two days ago the two ministers, Finckenstein and Hertzberg, put the draft alliance to the King as Van de Spiegel had sent it; a further conference between the King and the ministers is set for ten this morning. The only point raised so far is that the King said he could not guarantee the Republic’s possessions overseas. Van Reede had not asked for that, only that if they were attacked in Europe the King would help with money or supplies. Hertzberg wrote his own view into the report; article seven was struck out as disagreeable to England at Finckenstein’s request; and the treaty was made temporary, for twenty years. After the conference he adds that the article is to drop the words possessions d’outre Mer and say simply that if the Republic is attacked by a European power the King will furnish the aid stipulated, leaving the point undecided; he expects no further change. This is the defensive treaty signed at Berlin on 15 April 1788, which guaranteed the stadholderate and the Republic’s territory in Europe; the Anglo-Dutch treaty of the same day covered the possessions overseas.

Berlin le 4 de Mars 1788. Monsieur, Les nouvelles de Russie entrées ce matin portent que Messieurs de Segur et de Cobentzel sont fort capots de ce que l'Imperatrice doit avoir [?decidement] refusé la triple alliance. Monsieur de Keller n'a point cependant encore de reponse, et ne croit la recevoir qu'après que l'Imperatrice aura celle qu'elle attend de Vienne à la demande qu'elle a faite à l'Empereur s'il etoit resolu ou non à une attaque vigoureuse et soutenue contre les Turcs; demande qui, à ce qu'on croit, a decidé l'Empereur à faire la declaration connue à la Turquie. Monsieur de Keller croit encore que l'Imperatrice voudra attendre le retour du premier Courier expedié à Londres, qui a êté suivi de deux autres, avant de s'expliquer sur les propositions du Roi. N'y ayant rien de plus, Monsieur, qui puisse meriter votre attention, j'ai l'honeur de vous presenter mes respects, et d'être, Monsieur, votre très humble et très obeissant serviteur, A. W. van Reede. In English. News from Russia: Ségur and Cobenzl, the French and Austrian envoys at St Petersburg, are put out because the Empress is said to have refused the triple alliance of Britain, Prussia and the Republic. Keller, the Prussian envoy, has no answer yet and expects none until the Empress has Vienna’s reply to her question to the Emperor; Joseph II has made his declaration of war on Turkey (9 February 1788). A courier has gone to London, followed by two more, before anyone will declare on the proposals.

Four words the groups spell as slips : R1026 [?soit], [?fournit], [?énonçoit] and R1027 [?decidement] (spelt de-ci-demi-ent ). The bars above and below groups are the code’s inflection signs (a bar above cuts letters, one below adds the ending), but the key gives no instruction for them, so these readings rest on sense. Three faint words in the clear passage of R1026 (“je [?vois] le plus [?estimé] d’[?ici]”, “le jour [?la]”), on the 1,240-px DECODE image; a better image of the Nationaal Archief original would settle them. The groups once listed as open are closed: 2637 is cependant (mis-numbered 3637 in the key transcription), and 1250, 331, 2800, 3160, 3660, 3153, 2751, 50 and 1201 fall in the key’s null blocks. Grades. The decoded groups are not graded one by one. The structural sentences quoted in English (the conference, the refusal to guarantee the overseas possessions, the reworded article, Joseph II’s declaration) rest on runs of groups without J+ and are certain; words chosen by the model are probable. No contemporary decipherment, copy or print exists (log). `[?word]` = partly carried, `[…]` = unread. ## Reading Berlyn le 29 Decem. 1787. Monsieur, Avant hier les deux Ministres ont proposé au Roi le projet de l'alliance tel que vous l'avés, Monsieur. Comme ils persistoyent à differer d'opinion, j'ai prié Monsieur de Herzberg de detailler separement les sentiments dans le rapport et de motiver le sien, et il l'a fait. La reponse est arrivée hier au soir et elle me paroit bonne. Il doit y avoir ce matin à dix heures une conference à ce sujet encore entre le Roi et ses deux Ministres. J'espère qu'il n'y aura pas de changement. Le seul jusqu'ici dont il [?soit] question, c'est que le Roi a dit qu'il ne pouvoit pas garantir nos possessions d'outre Mer. Je ne l'ai pas demandé, mais bien qu'au cas d'elles fussent attaquées par une Puissance Européenne on [?fournit] en argent le subside. Peutêtre Sa Majesté entend elle par garantir fournir le subside, mais quand cela seroit, je ne desespere pas encore d'obtenir ce point. L'article sept que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous envoyer separement est supprimé comme desagreable pour l'Angleterre, à la requisition du Comtte de Finkenstein. Monsieur de Herzberg a rendu le Traité temporaire et l'a fixé à vingt ans. Voila jusqu'a present la seule difference entre ce qui a êté arreté hier et ce que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous envoyer. Depuis que ceci a été chiffré, Monsieur, j'ai été au sortir d'une Conference que les deux Ministres ont eu avec le Roi, une visite à leurs Excellences, qui m'ont dit que mon audience ne pouvoit avoir lieu que Mercredi. Le Ceremonial a été reglé d'une maniere convenable, et quoique peu versé dans les formes, je [?vois] le plus [?estimé] d'[?ici] de reconnoitre l'attention de L.H.P. par les plus grandes politesses. Le Roi a bien voulu y mettre le comble en decidant de lui même, et quoique cela ne se fut pas pratiqué du temps de Mr de Tessin, Ambassadeur de Suede, que j'aurois le jour [?la] l'honneur de diner à sa table. J'apprens qu'il a êté decidé dans la conference de ce matin que sans articuler le mot de possessions d'outre Mer on diroit simplement que si la Republique etoit attaquée par une Puissance Européenne le Roi lui fourniroit les secours stipulés, laissant ainsi la chose comme indecise. Cependant si leurs hautes Puissances m'ordonnent d'insister pour obtenir qu'on [?énonçoit] l'article plus clairement, je crois que je pourai l'obtenir, d'après la manière dont ceci m'a êté dit. Si j'ai bien compris je n'ai pas à m'attendre à d'autres changements. J'ai l'honneur d'être avec un très profond respect, Monsieur, votre très humble et très obeissant serviteur, A. W. van Reede. ## Notes - `soient` + two bars (group 97) gives "soie"/"soit"; "soit" is the sense, hence `[?soit]`. `fournir` with a bar above and below (group 133) is read `[?fournit]`. `E Nonce ois` (groups 294-296) gives "énonceois"; the writer presumably meant `oit` (164) for `ois` (163), hence `[?énonçoit]`. - In the clear passage, "je [?vois] le plus [?estimé] d'[?ici]" and "le jour [?la]" are faint and uncertain. - "possessions d'outre Mer ... lui fourniroit les secours stipulés" is underlined in the letter (quoting the article). Translation R1026_en.md # R1026 — Van Reede to Van de Spiegel, Berlin, 29 December 1787: English Translation of `R1026_reading.md` (same holes; modern spelling of names: Hertzberg, Finckenstein). ## Translation Berlin, 29 December 1787. Sir, The day before yesterday the two Ministers put to the King the project of the alliance as you have it, Sir. As they went on differing in opinion, I asked Monsieur de Hertzberg to set out the views separately in the report and to give the reasons for his own, and he did so. The answer arrived yesterday evening and it seems good to me. There is to be a conference on this subject again this morning at ten, between the King and his two Ministers. I hope there will be no change. The only point [?raised] so far is that the King said he could not guarantee our possessions overseas. I did not ask for that, but only that, should they be attacked by a European Power, the subsidy [?be furnished] in money. Perhaps His Majesty understands by "guarantee" furnishing the subsidy; but even if that were so, I do not yet despair of obtaining this point. Article seven, which I had the honour of sending you separately, is suppressed as disagreeable to England, at the request of Count Finckenstein. Monsieur de Hertzberg has made the Treaty temporary and fixed it at twenty years. That is, so far, the only difference between what was settled yesterday and what I had the honour of sending you. Since this was put into cipher, Sir, I have been, on coming out of a Conference that the two Ministers had with the King, on a visit to their Excellencies, who told me that my audience could not take place before Wednesday. The ceremonial has been settled in a fitting manner, and although I am little versed in forms, I [?consider it] the most [?esteemed] [?here] to acknowledge the attention of Their High Mightinesses with the greatest courtesies. The King was pleased to crown it by deciding of his own accord, although this was not done in the time of Monsieur de Tessin, Ambassador of Sweden, that I should have [?that] day the honour of dining at his table. I learn that it was decided at this morning's conference that, without spelling out the words "possessions overseas", it would simply be said that if the Republic were attacked by a European Power the King would furnish it the stipulated aid, thus leaving the matter as it were undecided. However, if Their High Mightinesses order me to insist on having the article [?stated] more clearly, I believe I shall be able to obtain it, from the way this was said to me. If I have understood rightly, I need not expect other changes. I have the honour to be with a very profound respect, Sir, your very humble and very obedient servant, A. W. van Reede. Monsieur, Les nouvelles de Russie entrées ce matin portent que Messieurs de Segur et de Cobentzel sont fort capots de ce que l'Imperatrice doit avoir [?decidement] refusé la triple alliance. Monsieur de Keller n'a point cependant encore de reponse, et ne croit la recevoir qu'après que l'Imperatrice aura celle qu'elle attend de Vienne à la demande qu'elle a faite à l'Empereur s'il etoit resolu ou non à une attaque vigoureuse et soutenue contre les Turcs; demande qui, à ce qu'on croit, a decidé l'Empereur à faire la declaration connue à la Turquie. Monsieur de Keller croit encore que l'Imperatrice voudra attendre le retour du premier Courier expedié à Londres, qui a êté suivi de deux autres, avant de s'expliquer sur les propositions du Roi. N'y ayant rien de plus, Monsieur, qui puisse meriter votre attention, j'ai l'honeur de vous presenter mes respects, et d'être, Monsieur, votre très humble et très obeissant serviteur, A. Translation R1027_en.md # R1027 — Van Reede to Van de Spiegel, Berlin, 4 March 1788: English Translation of `R1027_reading.md` (same holes). ## Translation Berlin, 4 March 1788. Sir, The news from Russia that came in this morning says that Messieurs de Ségur and Cobenzl are quite dumbfounded that the Empress is supposed to have [?decidedly] refused the triple alliance. Monsieur de Keller, however, has still had no answer, and does not expect to receive it until the Empress has the one she is awaiting from Vienna to the request she made to the Emperor, whether he was resolved or not on a vigorous and sustained attack against the Turks; a request which, it is believed, decided the Emperor to make the declaration to Turkey that is now known. Monsieur de Keller further believes that the Empress will want to await the return of the first courier sent to London, which was followed by two others, before declaring herself on the King's proposals. There being nothing more, Sir, that could deserve your attention, I have the honour to present my respects to you and to be, Sir, your very humble and very obedient servant, A. W. van Reede.

The Visconti chancery's own cipher books are lost. Eighteenth-century copies of fifteenth-century keys are kept in the Milan State Archives, Carteggio Visconteo-Sforzesco cart. 1597, and are on DECODE as anonymous key records dated "1450–1555". Two of them, nos. 23 and 24, are headed "Filippo Maria Duca di Milano". No. 23 (R5323) reads the Duke's other slips. No. 24 (R5324) did not, but it fits this one from the first word: cim = per, then the letters of "vostre", then the code word cima = lettere. The key has one to four signs for each letter (a = ꝺ, ꝡ, c, ∴; e = a, b, ħ, L; o = ɣ, ɼ, ꝺ, ʒ), word signs for et, que, qui, in, de, con, qua, da, che, per, come and ciò, code words for Dux Mediolani, lettere, date, havemo, Papa, Re de Ragona, Ambassadore, questo, cosa and vuy, and six nulls. Three code words on the slip are missing from the copy and were identified against the clear text: cab = quello, ba = Conte, cel = se. One shape, ꝺ, stands for a, c or o, and context decides. The full table is in targets/visconti1447/key.md .

In le altre cose etiandio faremo integramente secondo li recordi et conseglii vostri. Dat. Cusaghi die vigesimo tertio ianuarii [..]. Filippus Maria Anglus, Dux Mediolani etcetera, Papie Anglerieque comes ac Ianue dominus. In English. We have your letters of the 11th and thank you warmly for your faithful and wise advice, which shows you do not fall short of your forebears. Following your advice we will send another ambassador of ours to the Pope and the King of Aragon, besides Pietro da Pusterla and Antonio da Trezzo, to do with His Holiness and His Majesty whatever the Count's affairs require; he will be told to act in concert with the Count and with you, and to do as you direct. In other matters too we will follow your advice. Cusago, 23 January 1447. The Duke was then courting Sforza, at war with him the year before, against Venice: the slips of these months press him to come north with his troops. He died seven months later, on 13 August 1447.

One cipher line at the foot of BL Add MS 4136 f. 33 (DECODE R2989), John Wood to Cecil, 6 September 1568, in the symbols of Moray’s cipher to Wood. The phrase Bain prints as cipher does not align with it, and a solver finds dozens of unrelated English readings that fit its 39 symbols better than real text: it has no unique solution, and needs the Hatfield original. g x ob r3 Z ± x x x2 f x2 Z g Δ x2 e … g x ob / 39 symbols; the line opens and closes with the same three Edinburgh → Cecil · symbol cipher of the Moray–Wood family · 6 September 1568 John Wood to Cecil, 6 September 1568 to William Cecil One line of 39 cipher symbols from Moray’s agent: too short to have a unique solution, and the phrase printed as its decipherment does not fit it. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The line John Wood, the Regent Moray’s agent, to William Cecil, Edinburgh, 6 September 1568: one line of cipher copied at the foot of a Throckmorton leaf, with a traced signature “M. Jhone Wod”. Where British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 33 (old f. 10), in the Forbes Papers; DECODE R2989 (catalogue item 97). Tomokiyo lists it as a cipher “yet unidentified”. The cipher 39 symbols, 16 kinds: saltires with hooks, long-tailed z, g, o with a bar, a triangle, a plus-minus sign. The same families as Moray’s cipher to Wood of July 1568. How it was tried Bain’s calendar prints one phrase of this letter as cipher; it was aligned against the line in every tested form. A solver was then run from 200 random starts to see whether the line determines a reading at all. Why it resists The phrase does not fit, and 92 mutually different “English” decryptions score better than real English text: the line is too short to fix a key. What would finish it The original letter at Hatfield (Cecil Papers vol. 1), which may show where the cipher sits and whether it was deciphered. Other ciphers The Throckmorton text on the same leaf is his Cipher 3, already deciphered by Tomokiyo. Throckmorton’s letter of 10 July 1559 on the previous leaf has its own page , and so has the margin code beside it. f. 33, foot of the leaf: the docket “Mr John Wod to Secretary Cecil, 6 Sept 1568”, the cipher line and the traced signature. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 33, via DECODE R2989.
wod1568.html#the-line

f. 33 (old 10) is Throckmorton to Cecil, 8 August 1559, deciphered by Tomokiyo (his Cipher 3; Forbes p. 195). At its foot is one line docketed in the left margin “Mr John Wod to Secretary Cecil, 6 Sept 1568” with a traced signature. Transcription ( wood_line.txt ): g x ob r3 Z ± x x x2 f x2 Z g Δ x2 e XX 3 · x zl x ob x3 x2 x x2 Z zl o d ± g x ob / (J) o · Z Δ x2 zl 34 symbols on the main line and 5 after the marker (J), 16 kinds in all. The families (x with variants, z with variants, g, o, e, f) match Tomokiyo’s transcription of Moray to Wood, 13 July 1568; Wood was Moray’s agent in London that summer, so this is very likely a second sample of the same Scottish cipher. Tomokiyo’s labels could not be aligned symbol for symbol without his image, so the two texts were not pooled.
wod1568.html#tried

The printed phrase. Bain, CSP Scotland II no. 804, prints the letter from the Hatfield original and marks one phrase as cipher: “and says he must neidis haif it be on meinis or uthir”. An exhaustive alignment, with each symbol a letter, a null or a string of up to four letters, forwards and reversed, with and without the (J) group and over every substring of eight letters or more, finds no consistent fit. The line opens and closes with the same three symbols, which the phrase cannot produce. Either the copy reproduces a different ciphered passage of the letter, or the original shows the words in a form the copy does not. HMC Salisbury I has no entry for the letter. No unique solution. A solver (simulated annealing) fitted a one-letter-per-symbol key against quadgram statistics of Bain’s calendar from 200 random starts; 185 end above the median score of real 39-letter text, and 92 differ from each other in more than a third of their letters, all gibberish ( nonunique.py ). The line is undetermined by its own text; only the Hatfield original, with whatever decipherment it carries, can settle it.
